column17: The CoA's previous greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction target was 40 percent below 2009 levels by 2030. To help meet this target, steps were taken to reduce energy consumption in commercial and residential buildings, reduce transportation GHG emissions, and increase waste diversion rate to landfills up to 80% by 2020. The different sectors chosen to quantify the metrics are green space, energy production, commercial buildings, residential buildings, transportation & mobility, water consumption, materials management & recycling, food security, and green space access.

column17: The last Atlanta Community-Wide Inventory was conducted in 2023. This was developed with guidance from the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Inventory (GPC) with the following sectors calculated CO2e through ClearPath: Energy, Transportation, Solid Waste, Water & Wastewater, and Agriculture Forestry & Other Land Use (AFOLU). The emissions are divided between 3 measurement scopes: physically within the city (scope 1), outside the city (scope 3), and the use of electricity, steam, and heating/cooling from grids (scope 2). A new methodology change for the 2021 & 2023 inventories was to convert the Electricity Factor Set from SERC South to Georgia Power GRID, this is to create more of an accurate local model of GHG accounting.

column17: Over the last decade, agencies and organizations across Atlanta have produced a range of reports and frameworks establishing a vision for the future of the city. Resilient Atlanta builds on these efforts by bringing together decades of planning and applying a resilience lens to projects previously identified or already underway. This Strategy sets specific Visions, Targets, and Actions in order to ensure that our future Atlanta is a more equitable, connected, transparent, and sustainable city. In total 4 visions (aspirational guides that will lead to a resilient region), 16 targets (measured goals for tracking progress toward achieving the visions) and 57 Actions (policies, programs, or practices that the City and partners will implement to reach targets).https://resilientcitiesnetwork.org/downloadable_resources/Network/Atlanta-Resilience-Strategy-English.pdf

column17: To tackle the serious consequences of burning fossil fuels, in 2017, the CoA passed the Clean Energy Resolution, which pledged to transition the city to 100 percent clean energy for City operations and community-wide by 2035. Transforming the way electricity is produced and used is a tremendous opportunity to help the City develop in ways that are more equitable, resilient, sustainable, healthy, and profitable. The choices we make now can serve as a stimulus to advance equity, create jobs, improve public health, and slash Atlanta's contribution to climate change. The Clean Energy Resolution defines “clean energy” as “energy derived from wind, solar, existing and low impact hydroelectric, geothermal, biogas, and wave technology sources” and directs the City of Atlanta Mayor's Office of Resilience to develop a plan for the city to transition to 100 percent clean energy by 2035. The resolution also states that this transition plan would include “interim milestones, budget estimates, equity metrics (such as, but not limited to, energy burden), estimated financial impacts, financing mechanisms, and the percentage of clean energy that shall be locally and distributivity generated.” In response, OSR led in the drafting of the Clean Energy Atlanta Plan and was voted on and adopted in a resolution from City Council in March of 2019. As specifically recognized in the Clean Energy Atlanta Plan, this is not only about climate related GHG mitigation, but also a commitment and goal for climate adaptation. As stated in Clean Energy Atlanta, Electricity generation requires a tremendous amount of water, which is used to cool power plants and to produce steam which is then used to generate electricity. In 2010, power generation was responsible for 40 percent of freshwater withdrawals in Georgia. To meet Atlanta's 2018 electricity demands, approximately 2.2 billion gallons of water were consumed from Atlanta's waterways. This exceeds Atlanta's direct use of water by more than 10 percent. The increasing use of renewable energy under business-as-usual practices will reduce water needs for electricity. However, the planned addition of more nuclear power and combined-cycle natural gas power plants removes some of these water-saving benefits. Under business as usual, projected water consumption needed to meet Atlanta's electricity demand are 2 billion gallons in 2035. The CoA only has approximately 1-2 months of backup water supply with the addition of the new Westside Quarry Park reservoir. Atlanta's clean energy goals are directly linked to water usage, and decreasing our dependence on water-intensive means of energy production which enhances our resilience and will help Atlanta further adapt to climate related droughts that are already historically impacting the Midwest (100atl.com). The 2018 City of Atlanta Green Infrastructure Action Plan is directly connected to Atlanta's resilience strategy and sets climate adaptation goals in terms of mitigating flooding with the increase of frequency and intensity of storms the City is and will continue to face more and more. Green infrastructure (GI) is a cost-effective way for the CoA to address localized flooding and water quality concerns from stormwater runoff, while improving the resiliency of our watersheds and natural resources in the face of rapid growth and climate change. These types of infrastructure investments also provide significant environmental, economic, and community benefits to City of Atlanta residents. This Action Plan is needed to help address institutional and funding barriers, steer policy, increase effectiveness, and engage multiple city departments, citizens, the development community, and environmental groups in implementing GI at scale across the City. As part of its 2022 strategic action plan, the Department of Watershed management goes into further detail it's focus on multiple objectives to support the adaptation goal of establishing and maintaining a safe and reliable 30-day emergency water supply, while also making Atlanta more resilient and adaptable to climate-related flooding and urban heat impacts through the implementation of DWM's Green Infrastructure Strategic Action Plan. DWM's 2018 GREEN INFRASTRUCTURE STRATEGIC ACTION PLAN: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1u65BWi5qBFA-iYQmdBLm9wAVE7yHJnyf/view?usp=sharing, DWM 2022 Strategic Action Plan https://www.atlantawatershed.org/sp2022/

column17: The Local Net Zero Accelerator (LNZA) programme has been funded by the Department for Net Zero and Energy Security and the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) has been tasked with implementing the programme with its member Local Authorities. Each Authority has chosen a neighbourhood and there is approximately £545,000 over 2 years for each Authority to explore how neighbourhood wide net zero measures can be funded. They are particularly interested in gathering evidence to attract impact investors and patient capital. In Birmingham, Castle Vale has been chosen and the focus of the LNZA will be on the creation of a community energy co-operative using roof top solar. Profits from the co-operative will be modelled and the impact of using these profits to invest in retrofit measures analysed. This will involve equipping homes with sensors, undertaking retrofit assessments, understanding possible heat network opportunities as well as the development of a neighbourhood investment portfolio.

The programme includes the Whole House Retrofit Project which has implemented multiple measures to improve the energy and thermal efficiency of 300 homes in Bromford, East Birmingham, including external wall and roof insulation, and the installation of solar panels and air source heat pumps. Overall, these activities will save 1.5 tonnes of carbon dioxide (tCO2) per property per year, on average, leading to a total annual saving of over 3,000 tCO2 per year.

column17: WM-Adapt is a UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) funded research project led by the University of Birmingham in collaboration with the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) and the Birmingham Voluntary Services Council (BVSC). It focuses on driving climate change adaptation in the West Midlands through community engagement, climate risk assessment, and the establishment of a Regional Adaptation Network. The project also belongs to the Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change (MACC) programme. Funded by UKRI and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), MACC aims to enhance the nation's preparedness for the impacts of climate change by building capacity, knowledge, and skills for practical and scalable climate adaptation solutions. So far, five out of 16 planned Climate Adaptation World Café events have been held across the West Midlands, covering: World Cafes - facilitated conversations used to stimulate group discussion in café-like setting - are being staged as part of the WM Adapt project. Funded by the UKRI (£2m), WM Adapt aims to maximise adaptation to climate change in the West Midlands and beyond. It is a transdisciplinary action research project with collaboration between researchers in the School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences and School of Engineering, in partnership with the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) and the Birmingham Voluntary Services Council (BVSC).

column17: The City of Chicago actively works with the US Army Corps of Engineers on the Chicago Shoreline Protection Project, which provides storm damage protection to the Lake Michigan shoreline and Lake Shore Drive, a major transportation artery in the City of Chicago. The existing shoreline structures, built in the early 1900s, had deteriorated and no longer functioned to protect against storms, flooding, and erosion. Construction features of the project include: Reach 2 - steel sheet pile and concrete stair-step revetment from Wilson to Fullerton avenues; Reach 2F - beach nourishment with attached breakwater at Fullerton Avenue; Reach 3 - steel sheet pile and concrete stair-step revetment at Solidarity Drive; Reach 4 - steel sheet pile and concrete stair-step revetment between 23rd and 57th streets, with beach stabilization at 31st and 40th streets; Reach 5 - reconstruction of the breakwater at the South Water Purification Plant. The local sponsors and cost share partners for the project are the City of Chicago Department of Transportation, and the Chicago Park District. (text has been copied from the US Army Corps of Engineers website: https://www.lrc.usace.army.mil/Missions/Civil-Works-Projects/Chicago-Shoreline/)

•Nationally:-Essex County Council (ECC) makes representations on the climate agenda to central government including working with our local MPs to lobby on climate related issues and representing local government at committee hearings in Parliament.-ECC is an 'ally' member of UK100: a network of local leaders who have pledged to lead a rapid transition to net zero with clean air in their communities, ahead of the government's legal target. Cllr Peter Schwier is on a teaching panel for the Climate Leadership Academy 2025 run by UK100. ECC is also part of their Countryside Climate Network-ECC sits on both the Environment Board and the Climate Board of ADEPT, the Association of Directors of Environment, Economy, Planning and Transport. ADEPT brings together directors from county, unitary, metropolitan and combined authorities, along with local enterprise partnerships, sub-national transport bodies and corporate partners drawn from key service sectors. ADEPT members look after roads and transport, environment, local economy and wellbeing, alongside future plans for local areas. The Board aims to share knowledge and understanding of strategic issues and policies relating to climate change and the environment and to develop collaborative responses where needed. The Board advocates that environmental matters - and tackling and adapting to climate change - must be at the heart of decision making.

•Regionally:-the East of England Local Government Association's Regional Climate Change Forum - now called Climate East - which Cllr Peter Schwier continues to chair: this group brings together local authorities from across the East of England to share information and approaches to climate action and to amplify action taken by individual authorities. ECC has helped to shape the group's overall direction and is active in workstreams on funding and resourcing, as well as climate adaptation. ECC helped shape the most recent cross-region Climate East conference on resilience including leading workshops on nature-based solutions to reduce flood risk and also developed a logo and identity for the Forum 
- ECC works closely with District Authorities on climate action and district authorities are represented on the Essex Climate Action Commission.
-ECC also works closely with Parish Councils through the Essex Association of Local Councils (EALC). ECC ran a series of climate action forums and events to inform and support Parish Councils, and set up a £0.5m climate action challenge fund which parishes and community groups could apply to for funding to deliver climate action projects. The Essex Climate Action Commission has been involved in the Local Climate Engagement Programme since 2022, supporting towns and parishes to develop local nature plans (https://www.essexclimate.org.uk/local-climate-engagement-programme). 
- ECC also supports the Rural Community Council of Essex (RCCE) with bespoke webinars and attendance at its events.

The Essex Waste Partnership (EWP), made up of Essex County Council (ECC) and the 12 Essex Borough, City and District Councils, works collaboratively to develop and deliver a cost efficient and sustainable waste system for Essex. The EWP has worked collaboratively with partners, citizens and businesses to develop the Waste Strategy for Essex (WSfE). This 30-year countywide framework for the delivery of waste management has been formally adopted by all 13 partnership councils. The WSfE sets an ambitious approach to Essex waste management with a priority focus on 
1. Move to a Circular Economy - where natural resources are used efficiently and products are designed to be durable, easy to repair and recyclable
2. Apply the waste hierarchy - by designing services that prioritise waste reduction, reuse and recycling, and recovering energy and materials from waste that can't be recycled
3. Collaborate and Innovate -	with each other and with Government, businesses and communities to create a more sustainable waste system
4. Educate and Engage - by listening to feedback and delivering information and initiatives to support residents and businesses to reduce waste and recycle more

Partnership working groups have been established to deliver the ambitions and targets of the WSfE focussed on specific areas of work including the decarbonisation of waste management

The key WsFE targets include 
- Ensuring all residents have access to recycling services for plastic, paper, card, metal, glass, food and garden waste by 2026 
- Ensuring all residents have access to recycling services for plastic film by 2027 
- Stopping the use of landfill by 2030 
- Reusing, recycling or composting 65% of waste by 2035, with an ambition to achieve 70% or more 
- Halving the amount residual waste by 2042 
- Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from waste management, contributing to achieving our next zero targets by 2050

The WSFE and assorted action plans can be found at https://www.loveessex.org/waste-strategy-essex 

Waste composition analysis of residual waste has been undertaken across Essex giving detailed information on what's in our waste, enabling more effective service design and intervention targeting. Joint development and delivery of shared information and education activities across the EWP area has ensured effective engagement with citizens, including hard to reach and underrepresented groups on the need to reduce waste and utilise the available reuse and recycling services.

Behavioural change insight and interventions are being delivered across the county to test new approaches focussed on service delivery change, communications and education to reduce waste and divert from hight to low carbon waste treatment rotes

These documents provide legal justification for the introduction of net zero standards in new developments and guidance on how local authorities can mandate energy efficiency standards higher than national building regulations, even prior to the adoption of formal local plan policy.

CaPU also produced the Renewable Energy Offsetting Framework in April 2025 as a guidance document for Local Planning Authorities.. The Framework sets out the process for calculating an Energy Offset Contribution where it is justifiably triggered and outlines how the contribution will be used to deliver the 'missing' renewable energy generation elsewhere.

CaPU has continued supporting Local Authorities across Essex to incorporate the net zero new development policy into their local plans. As of July 2025, CaPU has been working in an advisory capacity for five plans. The Tendring Colchester Boarders Garden Community Inspectors Report was published and policy passed examination; the CaPU and ECC submitted a hearing statement for the Uttlesford examination of policy; CaPU will continue to support Chelmsford in its Reg 19. The Colchester plan has been delayed and Basildon has had another Regulation 18 consultation and consultation on their town centre masterplan that CaPU responded to. The SUDs team at ECC also provides bespoke planning advice on sustainable drainage and green infrastructure to new housing developments. Further, ECC hosts a staff member, paid for by the District, Borough & City Councils to provide support for the emerging bio-diversity net gain market, encouraging investment in increased green infrastructure within housing developers for investment in new biodiverse spaces nearby; increasing carbon sequestration, climate resilience and space for nature.

Manchester City Council (MCC) engages across national, regional, and local levels of government to shape and deliver climate action.
At the national level, MCC works directly with key departments including DESNZ, DEFRA, and DLUHC (formerly MHCLG). Engagement takes place through consultations, policy forums, and funding negotiations, ensuring Manchester's priorities on retrofit, clean energy, and resilience are reflected in national policy and supported by targeted resources.
At the regional level, MCC plays a central role in the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), where devolution has provided access to climate-related funding and powers. This has enabled large-scale programmes such as retrofit accelerators, clean transport investment, and green skills initiatives. The Greater Manchester Strategic Infrastructure Board further aligns investment across infrastructure providers, strengthening regional adaptation and resilience.
Through leadership roles, Manchester has significant influence nationally. Council Leader Cllr Bev Craig is Deputy Chair of the Local Government Association and Chair of Core Cities UK, advocating for urban climate action at the highest levels. Within GMCA, she leads the Economy, Business, and International portfolio, embedding climate action into economic growth strategies.
This multi-level engagement secures funding, informs national regulatory frameworks, and accelerates delivery of local projects, ensuring Manchester's climate action is equitable, well-resourced, and aligned with both regional and national goals.

The City of New Orleans has joined both the State of Louisiana and thousands of cities worldwide to set a science based target to reduce climate pollution. Both the City's and the State's Climate Action Plans were originally aligned with the Biden Administration's goal of reaching net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. With the change in federal administration, there is now increased uncertainty around the continuation of federal climate programs and funding. This makes it even more critical for New Orleans to accelerate implementation of its local climate actions while building strong partnerships across all levels of government.

The City's Climate Action Plan include cross governmental collaboration with entities such as the New Orleans Regional Transit Authority, the New Orleans City Council (as the utility regulator of Entergy New Orleans) and Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans, a quasi-state entity. In addition, the City is working closely with the New Orleans Regional Planning Commission (RPC) on its Comprehensive Climate Action Planning process, ensuring that local and regional strategies are coordinated and complementary. 

Together with these partners, the City is continuing to pursue available federal funding opportunities for infrastructure and climate programs while also identifying innovative financing pathways to sustain progress if federal resources are scaled back. More information on the City's infrastructure and climate funding efforts can be found at: https://nola.gov/next/resilience-sustainability/about/federal-infrastructure-task-force/

Nottingham is actively engaged in national and regional collaborations to drive forward climate action, ensuring that its efforts are aligned with broader goals across the UK. As part of the UK Core Cities Network, Nottingham works closely with other major cities such as Belfast, Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, Glasgow, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle, and Sheffield. This collective advocacy group holds regular consultations and briefings with central government departments, focusing on carbon neutral and net zero strategies, while addressing key climate components measured by the CDP (Carbon Disclosure Project).

Through these interactions, Nottingham shares valuable insights and experiences with fellow cities, enabling the exchange of best practices around climate action. The Core Cities Network also advocates for stronger national-level policies and greater government action to address the climate crisis, amplifying Nottingham's voice on the national stage and ensuring that local initiatives receive the support they need.

In addition to national cooperation, Nottingham collaborates with local authorities across the region through partnerships such as the Midlands Net Zero Hub. This regional collaboration strengthens efforts by pooling resources, expertise, and strategies to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy. By participating in these regional and national networks, Nottingham is able to take a leadership role in driving climate action while benefiting from the collective knowledge and experience of other local authorities.

These partnerships not only reinforce Nottingham's commitment to achieving carbon neutrality but also ensure that the city remains at the forefront of innovative climate solutions, benefiting both its residents and the wider region.

column17: Secção de Municípios para a Ação Climática da Associação Nacional de Municípios Portugueses (ANMP), da qual Torres Vedras é membro.A criação de Secção da ANMP intitulada “Secção da Ação Climática”, tem, entre outros, os seguintes objetivos: Promover um processo planeado de incorporação da ação climática ao nível municipal, designadamente ao nível dos PDM em fase de revisão, ampliando as vantagens de integração de disposições de adaptação, mitigação e gestão e conhecimento nas políticas locais e nos instrumentos de planeamento; Proporcionar a partilha de boas práticas entre municípios em torno do desígnio comum da ação climática; Promover a capacitação dos municípios nos eixos principais da ação climática, nomeadamente da adaptação e mitigação às alterações climáticas ao nível local; Permitir o desenvolvimento de relações de cooperação entre municípios, facilitando a implementação e desenvolvimento de projetos, bem como contribuir para um espaço de reflexão no que respeita a programas, legislação, candidaturas e instrumentos de financiamento que apoiem a ação climática; Intensificar a exigência de mais meios técnicos, legais e financeiros para que os municípios possam cumprir a sua missão indispensável e indelegável nas políticas nacionais e europeias de ação climática.

column17: Associação adapt.local - Rede de Municípios para a Adaptação Local às Alterações Climáticas foi criada em dezembro de 2016, decorrente do projeto ClimAdaPT.Local, em que os municípios beneficiários do projeto, mediante a assinatura de uma Carta de Compromisso, formalizaram a constituição de uma parceria informal, liderada por municípios, e envolvendo outras instituições, designadamente de ensino superior, centros de investigação, organizações não-governamentais e empresas, com a finalidade de dinamizar a adaptação local às alterações climáticas em Portugal. Em maio de 2022, como consequência da dinâmica e do trabalho desenvolvido, a adapt.local formalizou-se como uma associação de direito privado, sem fins lucrativos, reforçando assim a sua capacidade de atuação e de intervenção.A adapt.local assume como missão promover um processo contínuo de planeamento adaptativo que aumente a capacidade dos municípios portugueses e de outras entidades, públicas ou privadas, em incorporar a adaptação às alterações climáticas nas suas políticas de atuação e nos seus instrumentos, afirmando a importância da escala local para a conceção e implementação de soluções de adaptação mais eficazes, eficientes e equitativas.Torres Vedras integra a Direção da adapt.local, enquanto órgão responsável pela administração e gestão corrente, pela representação legal e pela coordenação da representação externa da adapt.local. No mandato 2022-2025, compõem a Direção, para além de Torres Vedras, os seguintes Municípios associados: Loulé, Bragança, Castelo Vide e Figueira da Foz.

The City of Vancouver regularly sends referrals to Vancouver's three Host Nations on a project basis related to their territorial jurisdiction. A referral is a key initial stage in the City's engagement process with the Musqueam Indian Band, Squamish Nation, and Tsleil-Waututh Nation. It is an invitation to the local Nations from the Planning, Urban Design, and Sustainability department to participate in on City projects. It includes a high level description of the project, highlights proposed engagement opportunities, and funding available for the Nations engagement. The City also passed the UNDRIP Action Plan in 2024 with 18 action groups and aims to strengthen relationships between the 4 government. 

At a department level, the Sustainability Group is working to build relationships and a shared understanding with Host Nations on the City's Climate Plan work. One of the goals of the Climate Plans is to embed equity and reconciliation into both the process and Climate Plan outcomes. The Sustainability Group submitted a referral for the City's Climate Plans to the Musqueam Indian Band, the Squamish Nation and the Tsleil-Waututh Nation in 2024. The purpose of the referral is to collaborate with Host Nations on areas of mutual alignment and interest and gather their input and feedback on Climate Plans. The Sustainability Group has had several meetings with two of the Host Nations and maintain a keen interest in deepening relationships and collaboration with all three Nations. 

We've been collaborating more deeply with Squamish Nation given their recent release of their Climate Legacy Strategy. After a review of their Strategy, the Sustainability Group wrote a policy alignment brief that highlighted where our government shared policy priorities on climate change. This then led to a series of meetings to better understand the opportunities for collaboration between both governments through the referral process. We are now at the stage of doing thematic workshops on both adaptation and mitigation plans to deepen our work together.

column17: The City regularly collaborates with local governments both neighbouring, nationally, and internationally. This can typically be more informal in nature, taking the form of knowledge-sharing or coordinating strategic engagement with senior levels of government. The City also relies on formal collaboration with utilities: for example, Memoranda of Understanding formalize the collaborative nature of our relationships with local utilities FortisBC and BC Hydro. The City regularly collaborates formally with Provincial and regional government agencies. For instance, City membership in regional committees helps to inform regional climate action efforts with Metro Vancouver, our regional government. Also, elements of our Climate Emergency Action Plan build on CleanBC, the provincial climate policy of which the City of Vancouver was a collaborator. Another example is in building regulations. The City of Vancouver sets its own building efficiency standards, within the Vancouver Building Bylaw, under the Vancouver Charter. The provincial BC Energy Step Code uses an approach to measuring energy performance that is similar to that used by the City of Vancouver for many building types. The City consulted on the development of the Step Code, with the goal of alignment of energy standards across the province. The City also seeks data from senior levels of government to inform Climate Emergency Action Plan (CEAP) and Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (CCAS) policy development, and continued climate action monitoring and reporting (e.g., GHG inventory inputs).

column17: Climate-related hazards are considered further through a hazard, risk and vulnerability assessment (HRVA), a legislated requirement of local governments through the (Province-level) Emergency and Disaster Management Act (EDMA). The HRVA considers current and future risks of human caused and natural hazards including many that are climate-related. The HRVA also focuses on vulnerable conditions that influence the adaptive capacity of individuals and predispose them to adverse impacts. Risk mitigation actions will focus on who and what is disproportionately impacted by the hazards assessed.

column17: Many components of the City's GHG reductions will be conditional on involvement from senior levels of government. Examples of these changes and priorities include right-to-charge rules for electric vehicle owners in multi-unit residential buildings, ride-hailing legislation that aligns with zero emissions principles and complements sustainable travel, supporting the All On Board campaign, accelerated transit electrification, a bold vision for the Regional Transportation Strategy, energy performance benchmarking for buildings, counting district energy systems with heat from renewable energy as a contributor towards the targets in BC's new renewable gas standard, and electricity pricing that supports electrification. At implementation level, the City will seek to leverage opportunities from existing Federal and Provincial programs, rather than developing standalone programs (e.g., pilot projects in partnership with the provincial government to retrofit affordable market rental housing and non-market housing). The City's Climate Emergency Action Plan (CEAP) and the province's CleanBC will contribute to reducing Vancouver's emissions from a baseline of 2.8 million tonnes in 2007 to below 1.4 million tonnes by 2030. To achieve this goal, the most stringent mix of policies must be adopted at both the City and provincial level. Modelling is being done in 2025-2026 to forecast the impact of CEAP and CleanBC policies on GHG emissions under several policy scenarios. Preliminary results indicate that we will need to identify additional policies to meet our 50% emissions reduction targets by 2030.

• Glasgow City Council provides consultation responses relating to policy developments at both UK and Scottish Government level, relating to their plans to mitigate and adapt to climate change including for the Scottish National Adaptation Plan 3 and the Circular Economy (Scotland) Bill. 
• Glasgow City Council also has a statutory duty to report on climate ambitions, targets, action and progress towards those targets annually under The Climate Change (Duties of Public Bodies: Reporting Requirements) (Scotland) Order 2015.
• Glasgow City Council works with the Scottish Government to build capacity and facilitate knowledge exchange across bodies. 
• The Council has worked very closely with Scottish Government on the roll-out of its Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy (approved at the City Administration Committee on the 16th November 2023) required by The Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategies (Scotland) Order 2022; this has taken part in several different platforms to provide input and updates on what should be included in the policy work and where issues are that need to be resolved. This has led to the Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy being more robust and more achievable.

• On behalf of Glasgow City Region, the council-led Clyde Metro Team is supporting the development of Clyde Metro's Case For Investment. The Scottish Government confirmed Clyde Metro as a key future mass transit transport investment priority, bringing together Strathclyde Partnership for Transport (SPT) as programme lead, Glasgow City Council for Glasgow City Region, and Transport Scotland to look at a long-term integrated approach to transport infrastructure and services across the region. It will also look at corridor master planning to enable Clyde Metro's reach to extend beyond the value of improved connectivity to deliver wider transformation benefits to sustainability, environment, housing, placemaking, economy, health, and social strategies. 
• Through the Metropolitan Glasgow Strategic Drainage Partnership (MGSDP) City Deal investment of circa £45m, Glasgow is proactively working in partnership with key stakeholders to deliver a programme of drainage schemes targeting areas of the city where rainfall adversely impacts communities. These schemes will reduce flood risks and impacts, improve water quality, bring greenspace improvements through blue-green interventions, and increase drainage capacity. The MGSDP covers a wide area and partners include: Scottish Water, SEPA, Scottish Canals, Scottish Natural Heritage, Housing Associations, and Glasgow City Region City Deal partners.
• Climate Ready Clyde is a place based adaptation initiative including neighbouring local authorities, government agencies with a view to also engaging private sector bodies to accelerate adaptation action.
• Glasgow is also the heart of the Glasgow City Region. Glasgow is bound on all sides by other local authorities and many of its services, such as public transport, cross the boundary from one of the regions authority areas and into the city. Thus, there are potentially economies of scale to be realised form working together across the region. To date, work has been done to look at a regional approach to EV charging infrastructure to build economies of scale, encourage private sector intervention, and to provide consistency of service and infrastructure availability across the region. In addition, the region has taken a similar approach to looking at the retrofit of building stock, identifying similar building types across the region and seeking to identify opportunities to reduce costs and build supply chain to support the retrofit of buildings in the region.
• Glasgow Economic Leadership (GEL) is the strategic leadership body for economic development in Glasgow and Glasgow City Region (the latter is comprised of eight partner councils). Its aim is to align and boost private and public investment in Glasgow / city region. The Board brings together senior leaders from academia, industry and the public sector. GCC is both a board member and attendee, with the council leader Cllr. Susan Aitken acting as a co-chair. 
• GCC forms part of the management team of Clydeplan, which principally prepares and maintains an up-to-date Regional Spatial Strategy (RSS) for the Glasgow City Region.
• GCC works with Glasgow and Clyde Valley (GCV) Green Network Trust partnership supports initiatives which increase the Glasgow City Region green network e.g. the Clyde Gateway which integrates sustainable urban drainage systems.
• Glasgow works with Convention of Scottish Local Authorities (COSLA), a councillor-led, cross-party organisation, to provide advice, expertise, experience, and opinion on a series of different topics, including climate change and net zero, actively working with representatives from every Scottish Local Authority at a senior management and political level.
• The Council also works with other authorities on major national policy pieces. This has most recently been seen in relation to the delivery of Low Emission Zones in the 4 major cities in Scotland.

Glasgow is one of eight Scottish cities that are part of the Scottish Cities Alliance (SCA), alongside the Scottish Government. The Alliance works together to promote the country's economic potential and look at ways to collective further work in relation to a series of issues including in relation to climate change and net-zero, thereby ensuring that it has a wide scope across the urban landscape of Scotland/UK. 

Glasgow City Council were a partner in a Horizon 2020 funded project, RUGGIDISED, looking at smart grid capacity, renewable technologies and intelligent street lighting, EV charging hubs and demand site management. The city was a lighthouse city alongside partners from Rotterdam and Umea. The project has now come to an end. This was an opportunity for the city to participate in knowledge exchange, fostering innovation locally. 

In addition to this, Glasgow participated as a follower city in the CIRCuIT (Circular Construction in Regenerative Cities) Horizon 2020 project, for peer to peer learning. This project included a network of European Cities, and explored three innovative intervention areas: urban mining and reverse cycles (the re-use and recycling of materials); extending building life through transformation and refurbishment; and designing for disassembly and flexible construction.

column17: Effective climate action aligned to the goals of the Paris agreement requires alignment of targets and actions between levels of government. The priority actions described in CoM's Climate change mitigation strategy are aligned to the framework described under the Victorian Government's Climate Change Act 2017, which requires the Victorian Government to set five yearly interim greenhouse gas emissions targets. The City of Melbourne submitted a Council Emissions Reduction Pledge under the Act, which is a formal commitment to reduce emissions within the municipality from 2021 to 2025, as part of Victoria's overarching goal to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. This pledge involves identifying and addressing major sources of emissions, setting interim targets, and developing strategies to deliver environmental, social, and economic benefits to the community, aligning with the requirements of the Climate Action Act.

Policy responsibility for key climate change areas such as energy, buildings, transport and waste is multilateral, with varied responsibilities between city, government regulators and private energy, buildings, transport and waste management providers. 

City of Melbourne collaborates at an officer-to-officer level through various networks facilitating knowledge sharing and advice. For example, the development of our Climate Change Mitigation Strategy to 2050 included external workshops and collaboration with Local Government (horizontal) stakeholders including: Local Governments, ICLEI, Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy (GCoM), Victorian Local government Greenhouse Alliances and peak bodies, Resilient Melbourne, Climate Emergency Australia, Council of Capital City Lord Mayors(CCCLM), Municipal Association of Victoria, City of Sydney, City of Adelaide, Australian Capital Territory and Brisbane City Council. Council staff are active on the CCCLM Climate Working Group, actively exchanging information on climate action amongst climate leads across Australian Capital Cities. This network is coordinated by a Canberra secretariat who can inform the network on Federal Government priorities and funding opportunities. 

In the past 12 months, the Climate Change and City Resilience Branch (CCCR) has provided advocacy submissions for State Government 5-year Climate Strategy, Building Electrification Regulatory Impact Statement, and Commercial Building Disclosure. More recently the CCCR Branch has installed a new team of three to help coordinate climate advocacy and networks for the organisation. 

In August 2025, the Lord Mayor of City of Mayor, Nicholas Reece was appointed Regional Chair and Board Member for Oceania for GCoM demonstrating Council's ongoing commitment and leadership in climate action and willingness to work collaboratively with the Oceania region. 
The Lord Mayor will also travel to Rio de Janeiro for the C40 World Mayors Summit and COP30 Local Leaders Forum in November 2025. At the Summit, the Lord Mayor hopes to present examples of City of Melbourne's annual climate agenda including the Garden City program (accelerating urban greening) and getting off gas initiative (converting 11 council assets to electricity). The Lord Mayor will also demonstrate Melbourne's support for Australia and the Pacific hosting COP31 in Adelaide and willingness to host important lead in events. 

To enhance Melbourne's position as a global leader on climate and biodiversity action, we undertake bold advocacy on behalf of our community and advocate for other levels of Government and the private sector to take bold action on climate change. Our current advocacy priorities include : 1. Building for extremes by funding local infrastructure and nature based solutions required for resilience to extreme weather and community led resilience initiatives with a focus on vulnerable communities including those experiencing homelessness (state and federal governments); Accelerating the transition to zero emissions buildings by regulating for climate-adapted new buildings and precincts by 2030, and regulation and incentives for existing mid-tier commercial buildings to achieve zero carbon by 2040 (state and federal governments); Heat and Health - retrofit and upgrade of social and affordable housing for heat and health (state); Circular Economy - create a regulated product stewardship scheme for key waste streams, starting with soft plastics (federal). Other priorities include adaptive reuse of buildings, getting off gas, responding to Inquiry into Ecosystem Decline in Victoria, including wine and spirits in the Container Deposit Scheme (state) and introducing vehicle emissions standards (federal).

In Tokyo, the Zero Emission TMG Action Plan (https://www.kankyo.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/climate/own_efforts/zero_emi_plan.html) corresponds to the Administrative Operations Version and the Tokyo Environmental Master Plan (https://www.kankyo.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/basic/plan/master_plan/index.html) corresponds to the Regional Policies Version. The Climate Change Adaptation Act (https://www.env.go.jp/earth/earth/tekiou/page_00608.html) requires local governments to formulate a local climate change adaptation plan. In Tokyo, the Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan (https://www.kankyo.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/policy_others/zeroemission_tokyo/adaptation/plan.html) corresponds to the plan.

O Programa de Eficiência Energética de Curitiba é desenvolvido em alinhamento com o marco regulatório nacional estabelecido pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL), que orienta e fiscaliza a destinação de recursos obrigatórios pelas concessionárias de energia para projetos de eficiência energética em todo o país. Essa vinculação assegura que as iniciativas locais não apenas cumpram critérios técnicos e de transparência, mas também estejam integradas a uma política pública nacional de uso racional de energia.
No contexto municipal, a iniciativa Curitiba Mais Energia tem avançado com a instalação de sistemas fotovoltaicos em equipamentos públicos, como nos terminais de transporte coletivo e prédios institucionais. Esses projetos são viabilizados pela sinergia entre o município, o governo estadual e os instrumentos normativos da ANEEL, permitindo que Curitiba amplie o acesso a recursos regulatórios e fortaleça sua estratégia de transição energética.
Essa articulação multiescalar evidencia como programas federais e regulatórios podem ser territorializados em escala municipal, potencializando impactos locais e contribuindo para metas climáticas regionais e nacionais. Além disso, a integração com o Programa de Eficiência Energética da ANEEL reforça a capacidade de Curitiba em dialogar com diferentes níveis de governo e de inserir suas ações em um marco mais amplo de descarbonização do setor elétrico brasileiro.
Programa de Eficiência Energética - A programação inclui ainda os painéis instalados no Palácio 29 de Março; no Complexo Imap, no Parque Barigui, e na Galeria Quatro Estações, no Jardim Botânico.A próxima etapa do Curitiba Mais Energia inclui sistemas fotovoltaicos nas coberturas dos terminais rodoviários Santa Cândida (465 kWp) e Boqueirão (512 kWp), com serviços em andamento; além do Terminal do Pinheirinho (925 kWp), com licitação em fase final. https://www.aen.pr.gov.br/Noticia/Em-comemoracao-aos-seus-330-anos-Curitiba-ganha-Piramide-Solar-do-Caximba

A elaboração do Plano de Ação Climática do Estado do Paraná foi conduzida de maneira colaborativa e participativa, envolvendo a coleta sistemática de dados e de feedback de municípios e órgãos estaduais e regionais, de forma a subsidiar a formulação de diagnósticos e ações. Esse processo se deu por meio de consultas técnicas, oficinas regionais e integração de contribuições provenientes de diferentes níveis de governo, o que permitiu tanto a harmonização metodológica quanto a consolidação de uma visão ampla sobre riscos climáticos, vulnerabilidades e potenciais de mitigação.
A escolha de coletar dados e/ou feedback de outros níveis de governo reflete a prática de ouvir e integrar as experiências locais às análises em escala estadual, fortalecendo a legitimidade e a aplicabilidade do plano. Já a opção por facilitar o compartilhamento de informações entre os diferentes níveis de governo demonstra o esforço em construir canais de cooperação e de disseminação de dados, garantindo que informações críticas sobre impactos climáticos e estratégias de resposta circulem entre governos municipais, regionais e estadual. Essa abordagem assegura coerência entre iniciativas, evitando duplicidades e fortalecendo a governança climática multiescalar.
Um aspecto de destaque foi a complementaridade estabelecida entre o estudo estadual e os diagnósticos municipais já realizados, em especial o caso de Curitiba. O Plano de Ação Climática do Paraná incorporou e expandiu a avaliação de riscos climáticos conduzida no âmbito do PlanClima de Curitiba, possibilitando a convergência entre análises locais e regionais. Essa integração reforçou a consistência técnica, ampliou a escala de observação dos riscos e oportunidades e forneceu uma base mais sólida para a priorização de medidas de mitigação e adaptação.
Essa complementaridade é particularmente relevante no contexto da atuação do município de Curitiba no grupo C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group. Ao demonstrar que a cidade se apoia em diagnósticos regionais, ao mesmo tempo em que contribui para o aperfeiçoamento das estratégias estaduais, evidencia-se a capacidade de liderança e de articulação em diferentes esferas de governo. Tal prática favorece diretamente o atendimento dos critérios de liderança do C40, que exigem dos municípios não apenas a robustez técnica de seus planos, mas também a demonstração de coordenação com outros níveis de governo, integração de informações e capacidade de influenciar políticas públicas em escalas mais amplas.
Dessa forma, a experiência do Paraná exemplifica um modelo de governança climática colaborativa, no qual a interação entre estado e municípios fortalece os resultados de ambos. Essa abordagem aumenta a resiliência regional, qualifica as medidas de mitigação e adaptação, e projeta Curitiba como uma referência em liderança climática urbana, alinhada às melhores práticas internacionais reconhecidas pelo C40.

A 5ª Conferência Municipal do Meio Ambiente de Curitiba ocorreu no dia 5 de novembro de 2024, no Salão de Atos do Parque Barigui. O evento, com o tema “Emergência Climática: o desafio da transformação ecológica”, reuniu cerca de 200 pessoas para debater e elaborar propostas sobre as mudanças climáticas que seriam encaminhadas para as etapas estadual e nacional da conferência. 
Detalhes do Evento: 
Tema: 'Emergência Climática: o desafio da transformação ecológica'.
Data: 5 de novembro de 2024.
Local: Salão de Atos do Parque Barigui.
Organização: Secretaria Municipal do Meio Ambiente (SMMA).
Objetivo: Coletar propostas para a proteção ambiental e o enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas.
Contexto:
Esta conferência é a etapa municipal que antecede a Conferência Estadual e a 5ª Conferência Nacional de Meio Ambiente, que teve como tema a emergência climática e a transformação ecológica, culminando com o evento nacional de 6 a 9 de maio de 2025. 
Resultados:
A conferência resultou na definição de 10 propostas prioritárias para a cidade, focadas na mitigação e adaptação às mudanças climáticas. 
As discussões foram orientadas pelos eixos temáticos da conferência nacional: mitigação; adaptação e preparação para desastres; transformação ecológica; justiça climática; e governança e educação ambiental.

Um exemplo significativo de colaboração foi a Conferência da Mata Atlântica, realizada em Curitiba em parceria com o Governo do Estado do Paraná. O evento reuniu atores municipais, estaduais, sociedade civil organizada, setor privado, universidades e organizações internacionais em torno de uma agenda comum de preservação, restauração e governança da Mata Atlântica, bioma estratégico tanto para mitigação quanto para adaptação climática.
A conferência foi concebida como um espaço de diálogo e de construção coletiva, articulando diferentes níveis de governo e setores da sociedade para discutir soluções práticas e inovadoras. Entre os destaques, estiveram os blocos temáticos de preservação, mitigação de gases de efeito estufa, adaptação climática, financiamento, governança e transição justa, com ênfase em justiça climática.
Essa iniciativa fortaleceu a integração entre as estratégias municipais e estaduais de ação climática, ampliando a escala de impacto das políticas e reforçando o papel de Curitiba como cidade líder na articulação regional. Além disso, consolidou a cooperação com parceiros estratégicos, criando sinergias para implementação de projetos de restauração ecológica, desenvolvimento de mercados ambientais e estruturação de mecanismos de financiamento climático.
A Conferência da Mata Atlântica ilustra, portanto, como a cooperação multiescalar e multissetorial pode gerar avanços concretos no enfrentamento da crise climática, ao mesmo tempo em que fortalece a governança climática no Brasil e atende às exigências de liderança internacional, como as do grupo C40.

Toward the goal of a sustainable and climate resilient city, the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IMM) develops multi-stakeholder collaborations integrated with European Union projects and missions, and establishes comprehensive relationships with provincial/district municipalities, public institutions, universities, NGOs, and residents.

In particular, through projects supported by the European Commission, such as the 
--> Net Zero Cities - Climate Neutral and Smart Cities Mission, 
--> the Adaptation to Climate Change Mission, 
--> the Pilot City Project (Build4GreenIST), and 
--> the UP2030 Horizon Europe Project, 

IMM adopts a multi-layered approach extending from climate action planning to implementation. Through these projects, Istanbul is implementing both carbon-neutral urban transformation and climate change adaptation strategies at the local level.

The main benefit of the missions included was to strengthen cooperation, develop know-how through experience sharing, and create synergy to mobilize other stakeholders of the city on climate change.

As part of the Net Zero Cities - Climate Neutral and Smart Cities Mission, the city's action and investment plan for achieving climate neutrality by 2030 (which is called 'Istanbul Climate City Contract', abbreviated as 'CCC') was prepared and signed. 

A “Commitment Document”, expressing the support of the city's stakeholders, was also signed. This shows that achieving the city's climate goals is the responsibility of more than just the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, but also of district municipalities, academic institutions, NGOs, citizens' representatives and the private sector.

In our ongoing projects, we prioritise effectiveness and awareness-raising efforts. We believe that effective results can be achieved through structures that are embraced and accepted by the general public. To this end, we organise workshops, training programmes and conferences with various groups within the scope of our projects.

As part of the UP2030 project, various workshops were held. Kadıköy was selected as the project's pilot region. Four workshops on the energy potential of installing solar panels on building roofs were held, with active participation from representatives of the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IMM), district municipalities, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), the private sector and the Kadıköy City Council. 

Furthermore, '4 public events' were held to introduce the project to citizens and stakeholders. 

'4 surveys' were conducted to measure citizens' awareness of climate action.

The Build4GreenIST project, implemented under the NetZeroCities framework, aims to support the development of a 'Green and Carbon Neutral Building Transition Guide' that can be understood and utilized by a wide range of audiences — from citizens to practitioners and decision-makers — to raise awareness and foster responsibility in the city's green transformation. To achieve this goal, the project has incorporated several key actions, including 'Learning Processes and Social Inclusion', 'Workshops for All Stakeholders and Citizens, Capacity Building' , 'Technology Training for Practitioners' , and 'Peer-to-Peer Learning with Other Cities - B40 Cities'. 

These activities have been designed to highlight the significance of the Guide, facilitate knowledge exchange, and provide training across different sectors. In addition, the project featured major events such as the 

--> Launch Event, 
--> Mid-Term Conference, 
--> Final Event, all of which brought together diverse participants through impactful panels and high-level knowledge sharing.

As part of the Build4GreenIST project, energy consumption was measured using sensors installed in the designated pilot residential area (Bayrampaşa KİPTAŞ Houses), with the data monitored via the 'GreenIST Mobile Application'. 

Over 65% of users regularly interacted with GreenIST messages via the GreenIST app. Those who engaged with at least three notifications per week achieved energy savings of 12-20% compared to the baseline level. User surveys revealed a notable increase in awareness of the relationship between daily activities and energy costs. Among active users, a measurable change in temperature set points was observed (typically 1-1.5 °C lower at night).

16-27 October UN World Climate Change Action Days

In order to raise awareness about climate change around the world, the United Nations has designated 16-27 October as 'World Climate Change Action Days'. As the Climate Change Directorate, we will be holding a series of events this week to raise social and institutional awareness.

October 23, 2024

As the Climate Change Branch Directorate, we organised a ferry event to bring together women who are vulnerable to climate change, raise awareness about the climate crisis and gender equality, and discuss the power of women in society.

Our event was attended by a total of '500 women', including female students from the Istanbul ISMEK Institute and scholarship recipients from the Istanbul Foundation.

October 24, 2024

As the Climate Change Branch Directorate, we got together with kids at the Sarıyer Büyükdere Tree Nursery on Thursday, 24 October 2024, in collaboration with the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality Children's Directorate and the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality Urban Ecological Systems Directorate. We had a fun chat with the kids about fighting climate change and its effects. Then we did a seed bomb workshop and planted some trees.

IMM CLIMATE RESPONSIBLES
October 25, 2024

Climate responsibles have been appointed to coordinate between Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IMM) units and raise institutional awareness of climate change, representing IMM internal units, affiliated organisations and subsidiary companies. These officers will be responsible for implementing climate change-related actions and providing data during the monitoring phase, and will develop strategies by assessing risks to ensure the achievement of the targets set out in the Climate Change Action Plan. 

A total of '350 climate responsibles', consisting of one primary and one alternate officer, have been appointed from all units, affiliated institutions, and subsidiaries of the IMM.

In this context, as the Climate Change Directorate, we gathered with Climate Responsibles from Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality units and affiliates, as well as IPA, on Friday, 25 October 2024. We conducted a workshop using the game titled 'The Future of the World' to enhance institutional capacity on the issue of climate change.

However, a heat plan also makes sense for all other municipalities and is promoted by the Ministry of the Environment. For the preparation of the thermal planning the city of Heidelberg has commissioned two planning offices as the ifeu Research Institute. With the involvement of Stadtwerke Heidelberg, a timetable was drawn up, how all buildings in the city area will be supplied exclusively with green heat either with district heating or heat pumps. La Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima (MML) se comprometió en el 2019 ha desarrollar un Plan Local de Cambio Climático (PLCC), el cual busque reducir las emisiones de Gases de Efecto Invernadero e incrementar la resiliencia de Lima Metropolitana frente a los efectos del cambio climático. El PLCC se elaboró bajo la Ley Marco sobre Cambio Climático y su reglamento y el Sistema de Planificación de la Acción Climática de C40. El PLCC Lima fue aprobado mediante Ordenanza N°2353, Ordenanza que declara de interés metropolitano el desarrollo de acciones frente al Cambio Climático y aprueba el Plan Local de Cambio Climático de la Provincia de Lima 2021-2030 el 05 de junio del 2021. El PLCC Lima reúne información de la ciudad desde un enfoque climático, que está orientada al análisis para la reducción de emisiones de GEI, el desarrollo de la resiliencia, todo bajo un enfoque de género, intergeneracional y de interculturalidad. Los contenidos permiten comprender la formulación del Plan acorde con las características de la provincia de Lima y el estado actual en que se encuentra la ciudad, como punto de partida para abordar la gestión del cambio climático. El PLCC Lima, está alineada al Acuerdo de París, la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático y su reglamento, Además tiene el compromiso de que Lima sea una ciudad carbono neutral y resiliente al 2050.Los tres objetivos generales del plan son: 
Gobernanza: Asegurar la gobernanza climática a través del fortalecimiento de los sistemas de planificación, información, comunicación y educación, garantizando la participación activa de la ciudadanía en la acción climática bajo un enfoque de género, intergeneracional e intercultural que incluya a la población vulnerable en la provincia de Lima. 
Mitigación: Reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero de la Provincia de Lima en 30% respecto al escenario tendencial.
Adaptación: Incrementar la resiliencia y reducir la vulnerabilidad frente al cambio climático, mejorando continuamente las capacidades de adaptación ante peligros climáticos en la población de la provincia de Lima. El PLCC Lima cuenta con 09 estrategias: Salud y Seguridad alimentaria, Movilidad sostenible, Gestión de riesgos de desastres ante los efectos del cambio climático, Gobernanza, Educación y Comunicación, Ecosistemas y verde urbano, Agua y Saneamiento, Energía y Ecoeficiencia, Gestión de Residuos Sólidos, Calidad del Aire. El PLCC Lima cuenta con 114 tareas que consisten en 1 272 acciones estratégicas (algunas de ellas se repiten o completan a través de los años).Se cuenta con un Grupo Técnico para la Implementación y Seguimiento del PLCC Lima (GTIS) el cual fue aprobado mediante Resolución de Alcaldía N°278. 

Así mismo, con fecha 31 de marzo del 2023, mediante ORDENANZA N°349-MDVMT se aprobó el Plan Local de Cambio Climático del Distrito de Villa María del Triunfo; adicional a ello, con fecha 01 de marzo del 2023, mediante R.G.M. N° 215-2023-GM/MDSJM se aprobó el Plan Local de Cambio Climático al 2030 de la Municipalidad Distrital de San juan de Miraflores. 

Adicional a ello, la Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima mediante la ORDENANZA N° 2499-2022 de fecha 14 de septiembre del 2022, aprobó el Plan de Desarrollo Metropolitano de Lima 2021-2040 - PLANMET, en cuya Síntesis del Diagnóstico Urbano de Lima Metropolitana consideró la evaluación del componente Ambiental y de Riesgo de Desastres.

El Análisis de Riesgos Climático realizado por la Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima a nivel de la provincia de Lima, sirve como insumo a los municipios locales para la definición de acciones concretas para reducir su vulnerabilidad y fortalecer su resiliencia, siendo de gran apoyo debido al alto costo de realizar este tipo de análisis y facilitándole la información a los municipios locales, que no disponen con el financiamiento para este tipo de análisis. Es por esto que el mismo fue aprobado mediante Decreto de alcaldía N°22 en el año 2021.

Adicional a ello, mediante Decreto de Alcaldía N° D000797-2025-AL-MML de fecha 3 de junio del 2025, se aprobó el Plan de Prevención y Reducción del Riesgo de Desastres del Cercado de Lima 2025-2030, el cual es un instrumento para gestionar el riesgo de desastres en este distrito, estableciendo objetivos y acciones para reducir la vulnerabilidad de la población e infraestructura ante fenómenos naturales. Este plan cuenta con 05 principales objetivos: 
1. Fortalecer el conocimiento de riesgo ante peligros priorizados, para la oportuna toma de decisiones a nivel del Cercado de Lima.
2. Evitar la generación de nuevas condiciones de riesgo territoriales, poblacional y de sus medios de vida en el contexto del desarrollo sostenible.
3. Reducir los riesgos existentes en el Cercado de Lima, mediante proyectos de inversión pública en zonas críticas identificadas.
4. Mejorar las capacidades institucionales para intervención articulada con los actores del Sistema Nacional de la Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres.
5. Fortalecer la participación de la población y sociedad organizada del Cercado de Lima, para el desarrollo de una cultura de prevención.

Las causas y consecuencias del cambio climático trascienden a sistemas sociales, sectores, atribuciones, disciplinas de conocimiento, territorios y fronteras. Por ello, fortalecer la gestión pública y la colaboración institucional es un elemento indispensable para el diseño y la implementación de la política climática en el largo plazo. Este fortalecimiento se puede conducir en tres distintas y complementarias formas de gestión: vertical, horizontal y de profundidad. 

Coordinación vertical: reconoce la importancia de implementar estrategias de acción climática basadas en el trabajo colaborativo y cercano entre el Gobierno Federal, los gobiernos subnacionales y los gobiernos municipales como agentes de cambio. El rol de las ciudades en la política climática, al no operar de manera aislada a las necesidades y los compromisos nacionales, puede habilitar o restringir la factibilidad de medidas a nivel nacional y regional, y viceversa. El trabajo conjunto entre los diferentes niveles de gobierno permite, entonces, el diseño de una política climática coherente y unificada a nivel nacional. Por ello, la contribución de la Ciudad de México al alcance de los compromisos internacionales y nacionales de acción climática requiere del fortalecimiento de la coordinación con el Gobierno Federal y las Alcaldías. A nivel vertical, se coordina con el Gobierno de México la integración del componente subnacional y el componente urbano de la Contribución Nacionalmente Determinada (NDC, en inglés), y se reportan los avances de la Ciudad de México para la integración de las Comunicaciones Nacionales y el Sistema de información de la agenda transversal de cambio climático a nivel subnacional (plataforma de reporte). También a nivel vertical, la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente coordina los procesos de acompañamiento a las Alcaldías en el diseño de sus Programas de Acción Climática, a ser aprobados por el Gobierno de la Ciudad y reportados también a la Federación. 

Coordinación horizontal: busca fortalecer la coordinación entre pares dentro de una misma estructura de gobierno. Reconoce la oportunidad de aprendizaje, intercambio de información y colaboración entre ciudades y entre diversos sectores dentro de una misma ciudad. La gestión pública en materia climática en un ámbito horizontal permite, sobre todo, impulsar la transversalidad del cambio climático en las políticas públicas y la atención de los retos compartidos a nivel cuenca o a nivel metropolitano. La coordinación horizontal es indispensable para mejorar la construcción de una política climática integral en la Ciudad de México. En el marco de la Comisión intersecrtarial de Cambio Climático(CICC), que es el órgano intersectorial integrado por las diversas dependencias, instituciones y el Congreso de la Ciudad de México, se impulsa la formulación e instrumentación de políticas colaborativas para hacer frente al cambio climático en la ciudad. Por ende, es tarea primordial el fortalecimiento de la CICC para el diálogo e intercambio de información intersecretarial, la construcción de capacidades institucionales y sectoriales para favorecer la transversalidad de la acción climática y el seguimiento de las medidas de mitigación y acción climática que integran la Estrategia de Acción Climática 2021-2050(ELAC) y el Programa de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México 2021-2030(PACCM). 

Coordinación de profundidad: busca ampliar la coordinación y la apropiación de la política climática por parte de la ciudadanía, los colectivos y demás actores involucrados en su diseño e implementación. Enfrentar el cambio climático no solo requiere de instituciones y marcos de gestión efectivos en la ejecución y planeación de políticas, también es necesaria la construcción ciudadana en sus diversas expresiones para poder actuar. Una coordinación efectiva con la sociedad y los actores colectivos de la Ciudad permitirá fortalecer la transparencia, la participación ciudadana, la rendición de cuentas y la representatividad necesarias para la gestión vertical y horizontal de la política climática. En nuestra ciudad, el principal instrumento de operación de esta gestión es el sistema de participación ciudadana, institucionalizado en la Ley de Participación Ciudadana de la Ciudad de México. Para conocer más respecto a la integración de medidas de acuerdo al tipo de coordinación, se puede consultar el capítulo 'CONDICIONES HABILITADORAS PARA UNA ACCIÓN CLIMÁTICA AMBICIOSA' de la ELAC y el PACCM, en el documento adjunto o en el siguiente enlace: https://www.sedema.cdmx.gob.mx/storage/app/media/DGCPCA/PACCM_y_ELAC_uv.pdf

In the context of its participation in international city networks, such as C40 and Eurocities, the City of Milan and its political representatives advocate for enhanced support to local climate action by international organizations, such as the United Nations and the European Union. For instance, in 2023 the Mayor participated in a meeting with the EU Commissioners Simson and Gauer, together with other C40 mayors, to pledge for a closer cooperation between the Commission and European cities. He also attended the UN Climate Ambition Summit in New York, showcasing city leadership and calling for the halving of fossil fuel use by 2030 and the creation of good green jobs to accelerate the just
energy transition.
In 2024, the Mayor endorsed an Open Letter to future European parliamentary candidates on 'Championing Climate Action in Cities' and a letter to the President of the European Commission entitled 'Building a sustainable future for everyone, everywhere - For a strengthened European Green Deal with an urban and social beating heart'. Milan also supported a C40-GCoM Open Letter to the Presidents of Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) calling for direct funding to cities to implement local climate actions. 
In May 2025, together with other 15 Mayors of major European cities, the Mayor of Milan met the Commission's Executive Vice-president, Teresa Ribera, the Commissioner in charge of drafting the EU housing plan, Denmark's Dan Jørgensen, and the Executive Vice-president in charge of Cohesion, Raffaele Fitto, to launch a European Housing Action Plan, calling on the EU to take bold and immediate steps to address the continent's spiralling housing crisis.
Moreover, since 2018 the City of Milan is a member of Urban 20 (U20), G20 cities' engagement group, bringing together mayors from major G20 cities to inform the discussions of national leaders at the G20. In 2021, during the Italian G20 Presidency, Milan co-chaired the U20 together with the City of Rome. 
As an Italian Municipality, Milan should benefit from Italy's endorsement of the Coalition for High Ambition Multilevel Partnerships (CHAMP), a platform to enhance collaboration between national and subnational governments in climate policy and finance (https://www.champ-climate.org/).

DISTRICTS The City of Paris has initiated a process to decentralize its administration and enhance the role of district councils. This decentralization involves delegating more powers to the districts and establishing a collaborative framework that combines the expertise of central services with local level coordination hierarchical lines of authority and functional responsibilities. The central administration works in collaboration with the district councils to assess needs collect data and develop localized strategies for implementing urban ecological and climate policies. 

RESIDENTS In the context of ecological transition this approach involves reimagining neighborhood level development by exploring the interplay between environmental protection and quality of life for residents. One example is the Embellish your neighborhood initiative which is a participatory method for transforming Paris in collaboration with its residents. Through this initiative residents have the opportunity to prioritize interventions such as increasing green spaces creating pedestrian areas establishing bicycle paths and installing furniture suited to new uses. By providing residents with a neighborhood diagnosis they can actively contribute to making their neighborhood or street more pleasant accessible and environmentally friendly. This approach integrates climate action into the daily lives of Parisians fostering a holistic perspective. 

METROPOLITAN At a broader level the City of Paris collaborates with the Greater Paris Metropolis which has committed to a Metropolitan Climate Air and Energy Plan (PCAEM). The goal of this plan is to align the efforts of the 131 municipalities within the Greater Paris Metropolis in promoting climate resilience energy transition and air quality It encourages synergies and supports local and metropolitan level actions. This approach is pioneering in France involving a significant number of residents approximately 7 million and covering a vast territory of over 800 km2 across the 131 municipalities. 

NATIONAL Furthermore, it is a legal requirement for French cities to submit their climate action plan proposals to national and regional authorities for review before adoption by the city council. This ensures alignment with broader policies and regulations at the national and regional levels.

CLIMATE CITY CONTRACT The City of Paris, on the basis of its fourth Climate Action Plan adopted in late 2024, developed its Climate City Contract within the Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities EU Mission.

The 112 selected cities are invited to develop Climate City Contracts, which include an overall plan for climate neutrality across all sectors such as energy, buildings, waste management and transport, together with related investment plans. Climate City Contracts are co-created with local stakeholders and citizens, with the help of a Mission Platform (which is currently managed by the project NetZeroCities). The clear and visible commitments put together by the cities in the Climate City Contracts enable them to engage with the EU, national and regional authorities, with investors and with their citizens to deliver on their ambitious climate neutrality objective.

The City of Paris, after submitting its Climate City Contract, obtained the EU Mission Label for this endeavor.

The EU Mission Label is an important milestone in the cities' work. It acknowledges successful development of Climate City Contracts and it is intended to facilitate access to EU, national, and regional funding and financing sources, in particular private investment. 

The Mission Label gives the city access to the Climate City Capital Hub, an international finance resource launched in June 2024 that supports cities:
- in accessing financial advice in cooperation with advisory services of the EIB
- in structuring their financial needs and
- in introducing projects to a range of capital providers, including lenders and investors from the public and private sectors

column17: The Philadelphia Water Department (PWD) released Climate Resilience and Planning Guidance in 2022. March 2024 updates include updated climate science, guidance and tools for each major climate impact. Precipitation and air temperature projections are based on Global Climate Model (GCM) output from Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5). Outputs from a new suite of GCMs (CMIP6), which were released with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report, are currently being analyzed by the PWD Climate Change Adaptation Program (CCAP) and will be included in future updates. The Office of Sustainability is also very involved in regional planning and utilizes collaboration with multiple levels of government in creating various levels of climate adaptation goals. One example being the coordination between local, state, and federal efforts to address flood risk in Eastwick, an environmental justice neighborhood in southwest Philadelphia, and put together an action plan to aid in adaptation.

column17: San Francisco has performed multiple climate risk and vulnerability assessments as mandated by the Federal Government. The San Francisco Department of Public Health monitors and reports on the state of the City's climate risk and vulnerability. The Department, through the Program on Health, Equity, and Sustainability, has previously released a report titled Climate and Health that identifies the scope of local climate impacts and associated potential health outcomes, and highlights populations and locations especially vulnerable to these health impacts. The Office of Resilience and Capital Planning (ORCP) also monitors and reports on the City's climate risk and vulnerability. ORCP has developed in-depth vulnerability and consequences profiles developed for 29 asset classes, focused on 13 hazards: earthquakes, tsunami, landslide, flooding, pandemics, hazardous materials, extreme heat, high wind, drought, and wildfires/large urban fires (including poor air quality from wildfire smoke).

column17: The Office of Resilience and Capital Planning (ORCP) oversees the collaborative ClimateSF working group. ClimateSF brings together key City agencies whose services could be critically impacted by climate change. These agencies are taking collective action through planning, policy, and guidance, championing a coordinated vision on climate resilience that streamlines City responses and promotes an equitable, safe, and healthy city for generations to come. This group meets biweekly and includes: the Office of Resilience and Capital Planning, the Department of Public Health, the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Authority, the Department of the Environment, the San Francisco Port, the San Francisco International Airport, and San Francisco Planning. This working group has aided the development of multiple programs and plans, including: the 2025 Hazards and Climate Resilience Plan, the 2021 Climate Action Plan and 2025 update, the Waterfront Resilience Framework, the Ocean Beach Climate Adaptation Plan, the SFMTA Climate Roadmap, and the Sustainable Neighborhoods and Environmental Justice frameworks for the San Francisco General Plan.

창원시는 기후변화 대응과 관련하여 국가·광역·주민 단위 등 다양한 수준의 정부 및 이해관계자와 협력체계를 구축·운영하고 있다.

1. 기후 요소 협력 범위
1)국가 차원의 온실가스 인벤토리, NDC 이행 점검, 국가 기후적응대책 등과 연계하여 지역 데이터를 제공·검증.
2)광역 지자체(경상남도)와는 광역 탄소중립 계획 및 재난대응 연계사업을 공동 추진.
3)시민·민간단체와는 에너지 절약·탄소중립 시민 캠페인 및 생활 속 실천운동을 공동 실행.

2. 참여 수준
1)국가 정부: 기초 지자체 온실가스 인벤토리 작성·제출, 기후적응 이행평가 참여, 국가정책 협의체 참여.
2)광역 정부(경상남도): 광역-기초 공동 적응사업(산림·물관리·재난대응) 추진, 광역계획과 지역계획 정합성 검토.
3)시민·주민: 지역 단위 실천 프로그램(자전거 출퇴근 챌린지, 공유텀블러, 주민참여형 에너지 절감 캠페인) 직접 참여.

3. 참여 목적
1)국가 목표 부합: 창원시 온실가스 감축성과가 국가 NDC 달성에 기여할 수 있도록 데이터와 사업성과를 상향 보고.
2)적응 계획 연계: 지역 기후취약성 평가 결과를 국가 NAP 및 광역계획에 반영, 중앙정부 예산 확보의 근거로 활용.
3)성과 공유: 정책·사업 성과를 디지털 플랫폼을 통해 공개하고, 상위 정부 및 시민사회와 지속적으로 피드백 교환.
4)정책 정합성 강화: 창원시 자체 사업(적응·감축·교육)이 국가정책 및 법제와 충돌하지 않도록 정기적인 협의·조정 실시.

창원시는 기초지자체 단위에서 생산되는 정량적 데이터와 정책 성과를 국가 및 광역정부와 긴밀히 공유하고, 주민·민간과의 협력 네트워크를 통해 실천력을 높이며 정책 정합성을 확보하고 있다. 

이러한 다층적 협력은 창원시 단위 사업이 국가 NDC 및 법제도와 연동되어 상위 정부 목표 달성과 지역 주민 삶의 질 개선에 동시에 기여하는 기반이 되고 있다.

In accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Reduction and Management Act, Taiwan adopts a phased and hierarchical approach to greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation and management:
1.Central Government: Formulates the National Climate Change Action Plan and GHG Reduction Promotion Projects, integrating national economic, energy, and environmental conditions to serve as the overarching policy framework.
2.Central Sectoral Authorities: Based on the national action plan, sector-specific authorities (e.g., energy, manufacturing, transportation, residential, commercial, and agriculture) prepare GHG emission control action plans. These plans include sectoral reduction targets, implementation schedules, and economic incentive measures.
3.Local Governments (e.g., Taipei City Government): Following central government guidance, local governments revise and implement their GHG Control Action Plans. These plans must be approved by the central government and are subject to review and updates every five years.
