column17: As part of the City of Boston's Climate Ready Boston program, the City regularly engages with other cities, State government, and Federal government in support of the City's adaptation and resilience goals. For example, the City participates in the Metropolitan Area Planning Council's Metro Mayors Task Force, which is a group of cities in the Greater Boston region focused on coordination and knowledge sharing around climate resilience priorities. The City participates in the Resilient Mystic Collaborative, a group created by the Mystic River Watershed Association to coordinate among cities along the Mystic River around climate resilience priorities. The City participates in the Charles River Climate Compact, a group created by the Charles River Watershed Association to coordinate among cities along the Charles River around climate resilience priorities. And the City participates with the Neponset River Watershed Association on proposals for regional coordination among cities along the Neponset River around climate resilience priorities. Boston also serves on the steering committee of the Greater Boston Regional Advisory Group (GBRAG), which develops updated regional climate risk assessments for the Greater Boston region. In terms of State engagement, the City serves on various working groups with the State's on-going Massachusetts Climate Change Assessment project led by the Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs, which develops additional information and guidance for municipalities on climate vulnerabilities in Massachusetts. The City also works closely with the Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency (MEMA), the Massachusetts Office of Coastal Zone Management (CZM), and other State agencies around grant opportunities to move identified resilience projects forward. In terms of Federal engagement, the City works closely with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT), the Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and other partners on areas of shared priority for climate action and resilience. In particular, the City regularly works with FEMA on grant proposals to move identified resilience projects forward.

A Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima oficializou o compromisso voluntário do Brasil na redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, conforme mestas estabelecidas no Acordo de Paris de 2015. Entendendo a responsabilidadde local nas emissões de GEE para o enfrentamento às emergências climáticas, o município de Belo Horizonte estabeleceu uma Política Municipal Climática, sendo o Inventário de Gases de Efeito Estufa um dos principais instrumentos desta Política, que possibilita a autoavaliação do governo local quanto às emissões e o entendimento da abrangência de seu impacto no meio ambiente (https://prefeitura.pbh.gov.br/meio-ambiente/inventario-de-emissao-de-gases-de-efeito-estufa). Por meio deste inventário é possível conhecer as emissões setoriais e propor ações para atingir as metas pactuadas.
São coletados dados de entidades nacionais como a Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustível (ANP) que fornece os números relativos à venda de combustível, e estaduais como a Companhia Energética de Minas Gerais (CEMIG), a Companhia de Saneamento de Minas Gerais (COPASA) e Companhia de Gás de Minas Gerais (Gasmig) que disponibiliza os dados referentes ao uso do gás natural, para elaboração do Inventário de emissões de gases de efeito estufa do município de Belo Horizonte que vem armazenando e disponibilizando dados deste o ano de 2001. Também são considerados os dados enviados pela Superintendência de Limpeza Urbana (SLU) de Belo Horizonte que informa sobre os resíduos sólidos grados no município, pelo ASJA que é o grupo internacional responsável pelas usinas localizadas nos aterros sanitários, e dados da Companhia Brasileira de Trens Urbanos (CBTU) que informa o consumo de energia elétrica em alta tensão correspondente à tração das máquinas e consumo de diesel utilziado na operação dos trens. As informações são parametrizadas na plataforma ecosystem da empresa Waycarbon.
As emissões do Setor de Unidades Estacionárias, que estão subsetorizadas em emissões residencial, comercial/institucional e industrial, são essencialmente emissões de GEE relacionadas ao consumo energético em cada perfil. As emissões do Setor de Unidades Móveis, subsetorizadas em emissões por modal de
transporte rodoviário, ferroviário e aéreo, refletem as emissões de GEE da matriz energética dos
sistemas de transportes implantados no Município. As emissões do Setor de Resíduos estão subsetorizadas em emissões por disposição de resíduos em aterro sanitário (CTR BR 040 e CTR Macaúbas), tratamento biológico de resíduos (compostagem), incineração (aproveitamento energético de madeira e pneus) e tratamento/lançamento de efluentes líquidos.
Segundo o padrão GPC 2014, os setores podem ser classificados a partir de fronteiras
geopolíticas operacionais, denominadas escopos. Os escopos apresentam as seguintes
características e delimitações: 
Escopo 1: Emissões de GEE provenientes de fontes localizadas dentro das fronteiras do
município.
Escopo 2: Emissões de GEE provenientes do consumo de energia a partir da rede de
transmissão e distribuição de energia elétrica dentro das fronteiras do município.
Escopo 3: Todas as outras emissões de GEE que ocorreram fora das fronteiras do
município, como resultado dentro das fronteiras do município.
Além do inventário anual do município, Belo Horizonte tem realizado o inventário de emissões de GEE dos principais eventos que ocorrem na cidade e com participação do município, como o Inventário de emissões de GEE do Arraial de Belo Horizonte, o Inventário de emissões de GEE da Virada Climática de Belo Horizonte e o Inventário de emissões de GEE da Virada Cultura de Belo Horizonte. Esses inventários feitos para os eventos que ocorrem no município também apresentam a quantidade de árvores a serem plantadas e mantidas para mitigar as emissões realizadas.

A análise da vulnerabilidade de uma cidade às mudanças climáticas é fundamental para a indicação de medidas de adaptação, considerando os riscos e a vulnerabilidade do município à emergência climática. Em decorrência disso, o município de Belo Horizonte realizou uma análise de vulnerabilidade às mudanças climáticas com projeção para o ano de 2023, com a metodologia utilziada no Quarto Relatório de Avaliação do Painel Intergovernamental de Mudanças Climáticas. Este estudo foi uma parceria público-privada entre a Prefeitura de Belo Horizonte e a WayCarbo. O cálculo de cada
índice e a escolha das variáveis mais adequadas para caracterizá-los dependeram
estritamente dos atributos socioeconômicos e biogeográficos do contexto local, da
disponibilidade de dados de qualidade e das prioridades estabelecidas pela Secretaria do
Meio Ambiente da Prefeitura Municipal de Belo Horizonte. Diante disto e das preocupações inerentes aos eventos de mudanças no clima, estabeleceu-se os seguintes indicadores de
potenciais impactos para a composição desta análise de vulnerabilidade: Inundação; Deslizamento; Dengue; Ondas de Calor. A partir desses indicadores, foi elaborado um mapa com os dados de vulnerabilidade. 
Belo Horizonte possui forte engajamento em redes internacionais e nacionais voltadas à sustentabilidade e à ação climática. Desde 1993 é membro do ICLEI - Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade. A cidade também participou do programa Urban-LEDS e Interact-BIO, desenvolvido pelo ICLEI , que apoia estratégias de baixo carbono em municípios e implementação de serviços ecossistêmicos e promoção da biodiversidade. Como a WRI Belo Horizonte já desenvolveu projetos na área de mobilidade, áreas verdes, bem como construção de Mapa de Áreas Prioritárias para SbNs, atualmente, a cidade, em conjunto com Campinas, desenvolve o projeto de pesquisa e articulação comunitária de Calor e Saúde. Belo Horizonte tem participado ativamente em iniciativas da rede C40 Cities, destacando-se como finalista no programa Cities Finance Facility (CFF), liderado pelo C40 e GIZ, com o projeto “Infraestrutura verde-azul nas sub-bacias dos córregos Capão e Piratininga”. Essa candidatura evidencia o compromisso da cidade em implementar soluções urbanas resilientes, com inclusão social, mobilidade ativa e infraestrutura sustentável. 
Além disso, foi cidade-piloto no Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories (GPC), em parceria com o WRI, C40 e ICLEI, aprimorando a elaboração de inventários de emissões de gases de efeito estufa.
Mais recentemente, Belo Horizonte tem participado do UrbanShift, consórcio formado por ICLEI, C40 e WRI, que fortalece a governança integrada e o planejamento climático em cidades. Esse conjunto de iniciativas demonstra a inserção ativa da PBH em redes de cooperação climática, ampliando sua capacidade técnica e institucional para enfrentar os desafios das mudanças climáticas.

Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (AMM) collaborates with multiple levels of government and affiliated organizations in the design, implementation, and monitoring of its climate adaptation goals. At the national level, engagement is primarily with the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change, ensuring alignment with Türkiye's National Adaptation Plan (NAP), Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), and other strategic frameworks. Data on municipal adaptation projects are reported upwards, contributing to national monitoring platforms and policy development.

At the regional level, AMM works with provincial directorates responsible for environment, water resources, and disaster risk management. Regional hydrological and meteorological data, provided by institutions such as the State Hydraulic Works, are integrated into AMM's vulnerability and risk assessments. This ensures that municipal adaptation measures—such as flood protection, drought preparedness, and heat-resilient infrastructure—are grounded in the best available science and aligned with regional strategies.

At the lower level of government, AMM engages with district municipalities across all 25 districts of Ankara. Local data on water consumption, land use, and climate vulnerabilities are collected and aggregated at the metropolitan scale. This enables monitoring of climate action impacts at the community level and ensures that adaptation benefits are distributed equitably. District municipalities also provide feedback through workshops and coordination mechanisms, ensuring bottom-up input into metropolitan adaptation strategies.

In addition to vertical governance, AMM collaborates extensively with affiliated municipal organizations. The General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) plays a critical role in climate adaptation by monitoring dam and reservoir levels, implementing leak detection programs, upgrading wastewater treatment systems, and leading water conservation campaigns. These activities directly address drought risk and water scarcity. The General Directorate of Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations (GDEGBO) contributes by developing sustainable public transportation systems—such as electric bus deployment, metro expansion, and park-and-ride facilities—which simultaneously mitigate emissions and reduce exposure to air pollution and urban heat. The Department of Disaster Affairs and the Department of Health Affairs also cooperate with regional and national authorities to integrate disaster risk reduction and health-related adaptation into municipal action plans.

The purpose of these engagements is multifold:

To facilitate the integration of municipal adaptation goals into the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) and other national climate strategies.

To enable systematic progress tracking and data sharing with higher levels of government.

To collect localized data and community-level feedback to inform adaptation planning.

To facilitate knowledge exchange and capacity building across government levels.

To integrate adaptation objectives into assessments and policies developed at different tiers of government.

Through this collaborative, multi-level governance structure, Ankara Metropolitan Municipality ensures that its adaptation goals are not developed in isolation but are embedded in national and regional frameworks. This enhances coherence between local, regional, and national actions, optimizes the allocation of technical and financial resources, and increases the resilience of the city's most vulnerable communities.

Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (AMM) engages with national, regional, district-level, and affiliated municipal organizations to design, implement, and monitor its climate mitigation goals. This multi-level governance model ensures that greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction targets are consistent with Türkiye's national climate policy while reflecting the specific needs and opportunities of the metropolitan area.

At the national level, AMM aligns with the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change and the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources. These engagements facilitate consistency between Ankara's local mitigation targets and Türkiye's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) under the Paris Agreement. Data on municipal GHG inventories, energy efficiency projects, renewable energy deployment, and electrified transport initiatives are reported to national monitoring platforms. This allows the national government to track progress against its international commitments while supporting AMM through technical guidance and financial resources.

At the regional level, AMM collaborates with provincial directorates on energy efficiency, clean air, and industrial emissions. Regional energy distribution companies and grid operators also play a role by enabling the integration of renewable energy projects developed within Ankara. Joint work on air quality monitoring and industrial emissions ensures that metropolitan mitigation measures are harmonized with regional enforcement of environmental regulations.

At the lower level of government, AMM coordinates with district municipalities to implement mitigation measures at the community scale. Examples include energy efficiency retrofits for municipal buildings, renewable energy installations on local facilities, waste segregation programs, and green space development. District-level data on waste generation, energy use, and transport demand is aggregated by AMM, enabling comprehensive reporting of mitigation impacts across the metropolitan area. Feedback from districts is also collected to identify barriers and opportunities for accelerating decarbonization.

In addition, AMM works closely with affiliated municipal organizations that are directly responsible for implementing sector-specific mitigation actions. The General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) contributes by improving energy efficiency in water pumping, treatment, and distribution systems, as well as deploying renewable energy at water infrastructure sites. The General Directorate of Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations (GDEGBO) plays a central role through the electrification of the bus fleet, metro expansion, and the development of sustainable urban mobility systems that reduce fossil fuel dependency. The Environmental Protection and Control Department implements waste-to-energy and recycling initiatives, while the Department of Urban Planning integrates low-carbon strategies into new development areas.

The purpose of these engagements includes:

Facilitating integration of AMM's mitigation goals into Türkiye's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and broader national climate strategies.

Sharing progress data on GHG inventories and mitigation actions with national platforms for transparency and accountability.

Collecting local data and community feedback to ensure that mitigation actions reflect real urban needs.

Supporting knowledge exchange and capacity building across all government levels.

Ensuring alignment between local investments—such as renewable energy, green infrastructure, and electrified transport—and regional and national policies.

Through these engagements, AMM ensures that mitigation actions are scaled effectively, benefit from national-level technical and financial resources, and contribute directly to Türkiye's international climate commitments. This integrated approach avoids fragmentation, strengthens accountability, and enables the municipality to lead in the transition to a low-carbon economy.

By embedding climate mitigation goals in a collaborative governance framework that spans multiple levels of government, Ankara Metropolitan Municipality maximizes the efficiency and impact of its GHG reduction strategies. This ensures that actions taken at the metropolitan level not only lower emissions but also create environmental, social, and economic co-benefits for residents across all districts of the city.

Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (AMM) engages extensively with other levels of government and affiliated organizations in the development, implementation, and monitoring of its climate action plans, including the Green City Action Plan (GCAP) and the Ankara Climate Change Action Plan (ACCAP). The purpose of these engagements is to ensure coherence with national policies, alignment with regional strategies, and integration of local community needs.

At the national level, AMM works closely with the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change to align its local climate action plans with Türkiye's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and long-term decarbonization strategies. Data on emissions inventories, renewable energy deployment, and sectoral climate actions are shared with national authorities through official reporting processes. This engagement ensures that local actions contribute directly to national commitments under the Paris Agreement, while allowing AMM to access technical support and funding opportunities.

At the regional level, collaboration with Ankara's provincial directorates facilitates the incorporation of critical datasets—such as hydrology, meteorology, and air quality—into AMM's planning framework. This strengthens the scientific basis of municipal climate actions and ensures that measures to reduce emissions and build resilience are consistent with regional development priorities.

At the district level, AMM engages with 25 district municipalities to gather localized data and feedback. Districts provide valuable input on community-level waste management systems, land use planning, renewable energy installations, and sustainable mobility. This bottom-up engagement guarantees that climate action plans are not top-down documents but reflect the diverse needs of different communities within the metropolitan boundary.

Additionally, AMM collaborates with its affiliated municipal organizations. The General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) contributes by implementing energy-efficient water treatment and distribution systems, promoting water-saving campaigns, and deploying renewable energy at water facilities. The General Directorate of Electricity, Gas and Bus Operations (GDEGBO) leads the electrification of bus fleets, metro expansion, and other sustainable transport projects, which are central to achieving mitigation goals. The Department of Environmental Protection and Control ensures that waste-to-energy, recycling, and circular economy initiatives are embedded in the climate action plans.

The overall purposes of these engagements are to:

Ensure integration of AMM's climate action plans into Türkiye's national climate strategies and reporting processes.

Provide mechanisms for progress tracking, upward data sharing, and transparent monitoring.

Collect data and feedback from regional and district-level governments to inform action design.

Facilitate knowledge sharing and capacity building across different levels of government.

Integrate local mitigation and adaptation measures into broader national and regional assessments.

Through these coordinated engagements, Ankara Metropolitan Municipality ensures that its climate action plans are scientifically robust, inclusive, and aligned with multi-level governance frameworks. This integrated approach enhances the effectiveness of local actions while ensuring their contribution to national and global climate objectives.

column17: The 2012 Climate Action Plan included an Advisory Committee composed of approximately 30 experts and decision-makers representing community, city, county, state, and federal entities most relevant to implementation of the CAP. State and federal agencies participating included the Maryland Energy Administration and the USDA Forest Service. The 2024 Climate Action Plan Update was adopted in January 2024. We spent months receiving input from people around Baltimore with a focus on reaching frontline communities, including attending nearly 100 community events to seek input. Community members, representatives from local organizations, and technical experts were deeply engaged in the development of the plan, particularly through the Resident Advisory Council (RAC) and the Technical Advisory Council (TAC). A group of 14 residents, called the RAC, helped with every part of making this plan. Over 80 applications to join the RAC were received. Members were selected based on why they want to help Baltimore become sustainable. Careful consideration was given to the composition of the group to ensure members came from diverse backgrounds and neighborhoods. Of the 14 members, half of the members identified as African American, Hispanic, Latino, Latinx, Native American, Indigenous, or Mixed Race. Six members were 35-50 years of age, two were 51-64 years of age, two were over 65 years of age, two were 25-34 years of age, one was 18-24 years of age and one was under 18 years of age. Each member brought unique perspectives, knowledge, and interest to the group. Two RAC members were students who shared a youth perspective. Members of the City's Sustainability Commission joined the RAC. RAC members were also compensated for their time to remove any potential financial barriers to participating in RAC work. Twenty-eight technical experts met regularly for months to help shape the CAP Update. TAC members came from different fields of practice, backgrounds, and areas of focus to help us identify actions that are well-rounded, effective, ambitious, and achievable. We also spoke with several other groups and conferred with regional and national experts in climate change and in specific fields referred to in the CAP Update. Examples of these groups included the Mayor's Sustainability and Resiliency Subcabinet, the Sustainability Commission, and Community Resiliency Hubs. Community members shared ideas and concerns so that we could craft a plan that elevates and addresses climate issues and sparks ideas that are important to people in Baltimore, especially frontline communities. We attended community events like farmer's markets, festivals, and GROW Center pop-ups. We held open houses where people shared their thoughts. We held in-person and virtual workshops to discuss what goes into this plan, to consider how actions in the CAP Update could have additional benefits, and to ensure the actions are well-considered and increase the overall well-being of the people, communities, businesses, and all others in Baltimore. As part of the engagement process, the City circulated a community survey asking residents about a range of topics. We wanted to know how extreme weather affects you, the modes of transportation used across the city, if climate change impacts how Baltimoreans feel in their homes' and in their neighborhoods', and how our community wants Baltimore City to respond to climate change. Over 500 people responded to the survey. Of these, 25% of identified as African American or black; 39% of respondents were between the age of 25 and 35. City leaders, RAC members, TAC members, and many others helped us spread the word about CAP Update events, meetings, and its public comment period. We sent promotional toolkits and emails to hundreds of neighborhood associations and community groups as well as to the offices of public officials and others and asked them to spread the word. We distributed fliers at events and local libraries. We posted on social media to help people share their ideas. We made the draft CAP Update available for comment online and provided presentations and tutorials to walk you through the CAP Update so you could share comments. To show our respect for the time people invested, we paid people to participate in public meetings. Moving forward, we will continue to work with community members across Baltimore to co-create solutions and work together as we implement the actions in the CAP Update.

The 2024 DP3 Update process engaged an Advisory Committee consisting of City, State, and Federal agency representatives, community organizations, and citizens, to provide input and oversight during the plan update process. The DP3 identifies actions to be implemented by, in collaboration with, or under the direction of City, State, and Federal agencies. The 2023 DP3 Update was submitted to Maryland Emergency Management Agency (MEMA) and FEMA for review and approval and it was formally adopted in December 2023. 

 

The planning process utilized a variety of outreach and engagement methods to integrate stakeholders into the process. This included hosting in-person and virtual meetings, deploying surveys, developing a website, and regular communication through email. These engagement efforts served to facilitate obtaining stakeholder input on identifying the hazards of concern, assessing risk and vulnerability, updating capabilities, providing status updates on the 2018 mitigation actions, updating and developing goals and objectives, and developing the mitigation strategy. Regular communication and engagement with the stakeholders permitted continuity throughout the process and kept the project on schedule. 

 

A Core Planning Team (CPT) was convened to discuss the priorities for the 2023 DP3 update. Over the course of the next nine months, City representatives, stakeholders, and community members engaged regularly to inform the development of the plan, ensuring community needs and concerns were addressed. The 2023 planning process prioritized expanded stakeholder and community engagement. A Hazard Mitigation Advisory Committee (HMAC) is an advisory team that provided oversight during the planning process. Their role was to advise the CPT on the community needs and concerns to ensure community representation and inclusion during the planning process. The HMAC aimed to include agencies and organizations that lead and support implementation of the mitigation strategy. C Social Equity Subcommittee was convened to prioritize the representation of socially vulnerable populations within Baltimore City. These stakeholders included representatives from community organizations and Resiliency Hub leaders. The 2023 DP3 update includes outreach and engagement recommendations to increase the representation of all Baltimore neighborhoods and communities.

부산시와 부산기후변화 협의체를 구성하여 해마다 2회 이상 기후변화 관련 이슈에 대한 정책 세미나 포럼 등을 수행해오고 있으며, 이를 통해 지역 주민들에게 기후변화 등에 관한 과학적 근거에 따른 많은 정보와 전문가들의 의견을 전하고 있다.
2025년 8월 7일부터 8월8일에는 APEC기후센터, 기상청, 부산광역시 주관으로 부산시에서 “APEC 기후난제에 대한 대응-기후변화의 복합성과 대응 방향 모색 (Addressing APEC's Climate Challenges: Complexity of Climate Change Adaptation and the Way Forward)” 이라는 주제로 2025 기후 심포지엄을 개최하였다.
아시아 태평양 지역을 포함한 전 세계 저명한 과학자, 정책입안자, 학계, 시민사회, 민간부문 등 이해관계자 약 200명이 참석하여 관련 발표와 논의를 진행하였다.

2025년 5월20일부터 5월 25일 까지 6일간 부산시 소재 벡스코에서 전 세계 기상 -해양-빙권 분야 석학들 참여하는 2025 IUGG 기상-해양-빙권 국제학술대회(BACO-25)를 개최하였다.
BACO-25는 '서로 연결된 지구(Our Interconnected Earth)'라는 주제로 기후위기와 환경문제의 과학적 해법을 모색하고, 해양·대기·극지 과학의 최첨단 연구 성과를 공유하는 세계 최고 수준의 학술 플랫폼이다. 국제 측지학 및 지구물리학 연맹(IUGG)이 주최하고, 산하 국제 기상학 및 대기과학협회(IAMAS), 국제 극지학협회(IACS), 국제 해양물리학협회(IAPSO)가 공동 주관한다.
행사기간 45개국 1천500여명의 국내외 기후과학 연구자와 산업계 관계자들이 한자리에 모여 기후위기와 환경문제의 과학적 해법을 모색하고, 해양·대기·극지 과학의 최첨단 연구 성과를 공유하였다.

2024년 8월에는 후쿠오카에서 개최하였고 2025년 8월에는 전라남도에서 개최하였는데, 기후위기 극복을 위한 지속가능성장을 위해 폐기물, 농수산, 건물 분야 등에서 다양한 논의가 이루어 졌다.

Participation in the Presidential Climate Commission (PCC): 

The idea for the PCC emerged at South Africa's 2018 Presidential Jobs Summit, when social partners agreed that a statutory body should be established under the Presidency to “maximise the opportunities for creating new and quality jobs in the context of a just transition to a low carbon economy and climate resilient society.” The PCC was formally created by the President of South Africa in December 2020 as a multi-stakeholder body tasked with advising on the country's climate change response, comprising at the time 13 government ministers and 27 representatives from major stakeholder groups in South Africa: business, labour, civil society, research and academic institutions, youth, and traditional leadership. The President is the chair of the PCC and is supported by a Secretariat that advances the agenda of the PCC, by commissioning research and policy work, arranging robust dialogue and consultation processes, and preparing strategic communications. 

The Commission meets on a quarterly basis; whilst ad hoc working groups on various thematic areas meet more frequently. The working groups include the following: Finance & Governance Committee of the PCC; Net-Zero Pathways; Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting and Climate Finance. In fulfilling this role the focus of the Commission include the following: •Create a social partnership around a just transition •Define a vision for a just transition, and means of achieving that vision, covering the necessary sectoral shifts, technological innovation, employment opportunities, and climate finance •Conduct independent analysis into climate change impacts on jobs, the economy, and policy •Monitor progress towards mitigation and adaptation goals, as well as the achievement of a just transition linked to broader development objectives •Engage with a wide range of stakeholders, including all spheres of government, business, labour, academia, communities, and civil society, with the aim of building social consensus around the complex and challenging decisions required to successfully navigate a just transition. 

City of Cape Town Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis served as one of two local government representative Commissioners on the PCC between early 2023 to March 2025. This appointment of local government representatives onto the Commission, which was facilitated by the South African Local Government Association (SALGA) was an important step towards recognising the crucial role that local governments play in the just transition. The City of Cape Town continues to plays an active role in the PCC through ongoing engagements between the relevant PCC and City technical teams, as well as SALGA. b. The immediate focus of the Commission's work has been the preparation of recommendations on the energy transition (specifically the electricity generation mix and governance), the development of a Just Energy Transition Investment Plan (JET-IP) and Implementation Plan, and consultation the updating of the country's NDC. For more see: https://www.climatecommission.org.za/

National Climate Change Act and associated requirements for local government: 

The South African Climate Change Bill was signed into law in July 2024, thereby becoming the Climate Change Act, which now serves as the country's statutory framework for responding to climate change. It was proclaimed into operation in March 2025, with the commencement of some provisions deferred to a later date. The Act stipulates the development a climate change response implementation plan as a future requirement for South African metropolitan and district municipalities. It further envisions the establishment of municipal forums on climate change, which will be intended to (a) coordinate climate change response actions for those activities within the operational control of the relevant municipality; and (b) provide a report on such actions to the relevant provincial forum on climate change.

The City actively participated in the public participation process of the Act - both by directly submitting comments as part of the formal public participation, as well as through joint advocacy processes via C40 and SALGA. Historically the City has participated in the Vertical Integration workshops with national and provincial government (hosted by C40). During these workshops the different levels of government shared the work they are doing in terms of climate action planning and identify opportunities for improved integration and coordination. These engagements are currently taking place as part of the Presidential Climate Commission (PCC) platform. . Although the structure of Municipal Forums on Climate Change for metropolitan municipalities is not currently prescribed by the Act, it is in the City's interest to have a structure in place which fulfils the purposes of such a forum. The City therefore established in 2024 an internal Climate Change Response Forum for co-ordination of climate change response activities, as well as monitoring and evaluation of the City's Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan and comprising cross-departmental membership of City officials. 
The Act is available here: https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202407/50966climatechangeact222024.pdf 

See more here: https://www.dffe.gov.za/mediarelease/george_climatechangeact#:~:text=The%20Act%20is%20intended%20to,provide%20for%20matters%20connected%20therewith

Western Cape Water Supply System: 

This relates to Goal 4 in the City's Climate Change Strategy, i.e. “Work to augment and increase water supplies to achieve 99,5% assurance of supply”. The national Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS) is the custodian of South Africa's water resources and responsible for the formulation and implementation of policy governing the water sector to ensure that the country's water resources are protected, managed, used, developed, conserved. DWS therefore also manages the Western Cape Water Supply System (WCWSS), of which the City of Cape Town is a major user of. The City therefore needs to partner, consult and get approval from DWS regarding any decisions, targets and goals with regard to the WCSSS. Engagements with other users of the WCWSS include district and local government.

Provincial Disaster Management Advisory Forum: 

The Provincial Disaster Management Advisory forum meets quarterly and consists of representatives from municipal Disaster Risk Management Centres across the Western Cape Province, including the City of Cape Town Disaster Risk Management Centre (DRMC). The City of Cape Town climate change planning team are not formally members of the Forum, however, climate change as a topic is discussed at Forum meetings and the City's climate change team usually presents on these if required or requested by the City's DRMC. Topics discussed during these sessions include discussions or feedback on the impact of climate related extreme events such as the impacts of storms, high rainfall events or flooding, energy security and resilience, which are risks outlined and addressed in the City's Climate Change Action Plan.

Western Cape Government (provincial government):
The City of Cape Town engages the provincial government of the region, the Western Cape Government (WCG) in a number of forums and platforms related to energy and climate change. 

In more recent years, this included: 
•Historically, the City has actively participated in the processes by the WCG to develop/update climate mitigation targets, such as the“2050 Emissions Pathway design” workshops in 2022 hosted by WCG to ensure alignment of mitigation targets between provincial government and the City..

•Participation in reviewing processes of provincial climate change strategy development, including the Western Cape Climate Change Response Strategy: Vision 2050 and Implementation Plan (2023). The Strategy is envisaged as a transversal strategy providing policy direction in response to climate-related risks and potential opportunities, through either creating or leveraging systemic innovative response programmes that tackle the region's vulnerability to droughts, heat and floods and take advantage of opportunities that will enable climate resilient development which fosters economic growth that is low-carbon and further creates an advanced green economy. 
To access the Western Cape Climate Change Response Strategy: Vision 2050, click the link: https://www.westerncape.gov.za/eadp/sites/eadp.westerncape.gov.za/files/atoms/files/WCCCRS%20Vision%202050%201st%20Revision%202023.pdf 
To access the Implementation Plan, click the link: https://www.westerncape.gov.za/eadp/sites/eadp.westerncape.gov.za/files/atoms/files/WCCCRS%20Implementation%20Plan%20March%202023.pdf 

•Engagement/consultation on relevant draft national strategies or plans related to climate change, via provincial government. Between 2024 to 2025 this included participation in commenting and stakeholder engagement processes facilitated by WCG on the South Africa Draft Climate Change Gender Action Plan, the national Climate Change Bill, the national draft Guideline for the Development of Emissions Targets for Provinces and Local Government and the development of Climate Change Adaptation Scenarios (as prescribed by the national Climate Change Act). 

•The City continues to collaborate closely with WCG under the Western Cape Energy Resilience Programme (WC ERP), which supports coordinated energy planning and resilience across the province. Through regular engagements - including monthly forums between the City's Energy Directorate and WCG's Core Energy Team in the Department of the Premier- the City contributes to key provincial initiatives that advance shared goals for decarbonisation, energy security, and a just, inclusive transition. The City also engages with various WCG departments, including Provincial Treasury, the Department of Economic Development and Tourism (DEDAT), the Department of Infrastructure, and the Department of Mobility, on matters such as IPP procurement and wheeling, energy poverty interventions, clean energy market development, EV infrastructure planning, and municipal financial sustainability in the energy transition.

South African Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reporting System: 

The City's operations triggers the annual national greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reporting threshold to report emissions of the following sectors: domestic wastewater discharge, landfill waste disposal and electricity generation to the South African Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reporting System (SAGERs) under the national GHG Emissions Reporting Regulations (2017, amended in 2020) under the National Environmental Management: Air Quality Act of 2004). 

The GHG Emissions Reporting Regulations is aimed at developing a standardised method to report GHG emissions that could aid the updating of the national GHG inventory and inform the formulation and implementation of legislation and policy. The SAGERs GHG emissions reports will be used to determine which entities are liable to pay carbon tax. In addition, each Party will regularly provide a national inventory report (NIR) of anthropogenic GHG emissions by sources and removal by sinks, as per Article 13, paragraph 7(a), of the Paris Agreement. City-level GHG emissions inventories can potentially feed this process. Finally, the City relies on key datasets from national government (e.g. Eskom supplied electricity areas and liquid fuels data) for the development of its GHG inventory and is in the process of undertaking a detailed updated analysis which the City undertakes every 5 years when publishing the Cape Town State of Energy and Carbon report (with the corresponding data product), which will be released towards the end of 2025 calendar year, based on 2023 data.

Participation in the in the South African Department of Forestry, Fisheries, and the Environment (DFFE), MINTECH and MINMEC forum:

The City of Cape Town via its Environmental Management department is actively involved as a participant in the national Department of Forestry, Fisheries & the Environment's (DFFE) intergovernmental meetings, namely Minmec, chaired by the DFFE Minister, and Mintech, chaired by DFFE Director-General. MINTECH, a technical forum, focuses on environmental management issues and provides recommendations to MINMEC. MINMEC, a ministerial forum, consists of the Minister of DFFE and the Members of the Executive Councils (MECs) of the nine provinces, who review and oversee the implementation of environmental policies and address related challenges. 

These interactions give provincial and local government entities (political and official level) the opportunity to respond on the outputs from key working groups (WG) within DFFE's portfolio. Critical to the City are: WG1(Biodiversity, Conservation & Forestry); WG2 (Air Quality Management); WG4 (Compliance & Enforcement); WG5 (Integrated Environmental Authorisations); WG6 (Sector Jobs) - specifically in terms of EPWP programmes; WG7 (Oceans, and Coasts & Inland Fisheries); WG8 (Chemicals & Waste Management); WG9 (Climate Change Management); and WG10 (Advisory Committee on Environmental Policy & Law Reform) - specifically giving the City a 'heads-up' on legislation currently in process. 

The City ensures that senior officials are present at all Minmec and Mintech meetings. Output from these meetings is used to determine key aspects that might impact how the City undertakes its mandated requirements. Senior political representation is attempted for all Minmec meetings, with this delegated by the Mayor to Deputy Mayor Alderman Andrews (Spatial Planning & Environment) or Alderman Twigg (Urban Waste Management) as his alternative. The majority of the meetings are virtual, with senior representation, often multiple staff, present at all meetings. In-person meetings usually happen February annually.

A key interaction in all Mintech/Minmec meetings is with the provincial government, Western Cape: Department of Environmental Affairs & Development Planning, in which provincial government will raise concerns on the City's behalf, or will facilitate meetings on specific topics between DFFE and the City.
The Mintech/Minmec meetings present the outputs from various Working Groups. The City has an open invitation to a number of these. Although these Working Groups are commonly DFFE officials, provincial technical officials, and national entities linked to DFFE (e.g. SANBI and SANParks), the City has been directly invited to participate and is often the only local government represented. Finally, as an adjunct to the Mintech/Minmec process, the City participates in the SALGA-hosted preparatory meetings, usually held before each Minmec, to discuss and raise key aspects, concerns, or nuances to note, in response to agenda items.

column17: Dallas County is one of ten counties that consistently do not meet the 2008 federal air quality criteria for ground-level ozone. Dallas-Fort Worth was ranked top 20 in the American Lung Association's 25 Most Ozone-Polluted Cities. Increases in temperature exacerbate poor air quality, putting city residents further at risk. Many of the actions in other CECAP sectors will contribute to improvements in air quality. Specific actions to monitor air quality at the neighborhood level, and that prevent the exposure of communities to sources of air pollution, are included in this sector. The Dallas Community Air Management Program (D-CAMP) is a collaboration between community, government, and academia to collect neighborhood air quality data using advanced low-cost sensor technology. This partnership is critical to the success of the program. Through participation, residents act as important partners. In D-CAMP, sensors will be placed throughout Dallas to measure levels of air pollutants where Dallas residents live, go to school, work, and play, particularly in communities with environmental justice concerns. The data will be shared with the community and academic partners, leading to a better understanding of how air pollutants impact daily lives. Data can also be used by City planners to ensure health of residents is protected when considering future development.

column17: The City of Dallas is a partner in Regional Integration of Sustainability Efforts (RISE) coalition that works to engage interested local governments in peer-exchange opportunities to support sustainability and environmental initiatives. This coalition is affiliated with the North Central Texas Council of Governments (NCTCOG). The NCTCOG covers the 16-county Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, and thus these efforts are important to implementing regional climate action. We are working with RISE to develop a regional GHG Inventory, and related climate plan. The City has also committed to the U.S. Department of Energy Better Climate Challenge (https://betterbuildingssolutioncenter.energy.gov/partners/dallas-tx) to reduce GHG emissions by 50% and improve energy efficiency by 20% across its portfolio of 140 facilities over the next 10 years. To achieve this goal, the City will maximize energy efficiency and decarbonize its buildings, transition its fleets to electric and low- or no-carbon fuels, and install renewable energy systems and other innovative technologies across its facilities.

column17: The Municipality's adaptation goal to implement the Transformative Riverine Management Programme (TRMP) across all 7,400 km of streams has been shared with national and provincial government. column17: The first ever city-wide GHG inventory for Ekurhuleni was completed in 2022 based on data from the 2018/19 financial year and was updated for the 2021/22 financial year. This citywide inventory was developed in accordance with the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories (the GPC) and is the first step towards understanding the emissions profile of the city. The inventory forms the basis for the subsequent emissions trajectory and scenario modelling used to identify mitigation strategies and quantify GHG reductions and formulate emissions goals. The City latest GHG inventory is for the 2022/23 Financial Year.

column17: Para desenvolvimento de uma análise da vulnerabilidade aos impactos das mudanças climáticas na cidade de Fortaleza e de um plano de adaptação que inclui medidas para responder às vulnerabilidades identificadas, foram acionados diversos atores sociais e governamentais. A construção dos documentos Índice de Vulnerabilidade às Mudanças Climáticas IVCC e Plano de Adaptação de Fortaleza ocorreu no âmbito da iniciativa Ciudades y Cambio Climático en América Latina, tem como objetivo a promoção do desenvolvimento de cidades com baixa emissão de carbono e resiliente às mudanças climáticas, viabilizado por um convênio de Facilitação de Investimentos para a América Latina LAIF firmado entre a União Européia, Agência Francesa de Desenvolvimento AFD e o Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina CAF. Para tal, foi contratada equipe técnica, em consórcio de 3 empresas, que viabilizou as análises e os processos participativos. Órgãos e concessionárias vinculadas ao governo do estado foram acionadas para disponibilização de informações, como dados meteorológicos e cobertura de esgoto na cidade. O debate e a priorização das ações foi validado por mesa técnica formada por especialistas, representantes dos órgãos direta e indiretamente relacionados à temática em diferentes níveis governamentais, representantes da comunidade acadêmica e oficinas envolvendo as comunidades de áreas distintas do território de Fortaleza como instância de participação da sociedade civil.

column17: A Política de Desenvolvimento Urbano de Baixo Carbono de Fortaleza, incorpora a sustentabilidade socioambiental aos processos de desenvolvimento da cidade, tendo por finalidades: Promover a inclusão social e a eficiência econômica e produtiva em harmonia com a proteção e recuperação dos recursos e ativos ambientais; Assegurar a manutenção de níveis de emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (GEE) condizentes com o impedimento de uma interferência antrópica perigosa no sistema climático; construir uma cidade resiliente aos efeitos inevitáveis das mudanças do clima nas dimensões institucional, social/comunitária, ambiental e de infraestrutura urbana, estimulando e fortalecendo a organização e integração entre os entes da Federação, as instituições públicas e da sociedade civil, e a população em geral, priorizando as comunidades mais vulneráveis aos efeitos das mudanças climáticas, de modo a desenvolver uma capacidade adaptativa e de redução dos riscos urbanos; Estimular a inovação tecnológica no planejamento e controle do desenvolvimento urbano de baixo carbono, a serviço da melhoria da qualidade de vida e da segurança e bem-estar da população; e garantir a continuidade da política para que seja uma Política de Cidade. Se relaciona com as instâncias superiores de governo, em especial ao governo Federal, por se adequar à Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima, assinada em Nova Iorque em 09 de maio de 1992, e cujo texto foi ratificado e promulgado por meio do Decreto Legislativo nº 01, de 03 de fevereiro de 1994; do Protocolo de Quioto, aprovado na Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas, realizada no Japão, em 1997; do Quadro de Ação de Hyogo, aprovado na Conferência Mundial de Redução de Desastres, realizada em 2005 no Japão; e de demais convenções, tratados, acordos e documentos sobre o tema, dos quais o Brasil for signatário; bem como das legislações pertinentes editadas em níveis federal, estadual e municipal, notadamente da Lei Federal nº 12.187, de 29 de dezembro de 2009, que institui a Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima e o Plano Estadual sobre Mudanças Climáticas. Foi regulamentada, inicialmente, pelo Plano Plano de Ações e Metas para a Redução dos Gases de Efeito Estufa, sendo guiada atualmente pelo Plano Local de Ação Climática de Fortaleza.

column17: Para elaboração e atualização dos instrumentos de planejamento da cidade frente às mudanças climáticas, foram necessárias articulações para obtenção de dados e definição de ações realistas, visto que as pautas são de responsabilidade de diferentes níveis de governo. As regionais, são essenciais para articular participação nos territórios Em 2015 foi lançado o Plano de Ações e Metas para a Redução dos Gases de Efeito Estufa, ligado ao Plano de Baixo Carbono de Fortaleza. Este documento passou por uma atualização que reflete uma evolução, tanto a nível de ambição proposta para as reduções de emissões, como à nível de estratégias de governança. As ações e propostas do plano também foram objeto do Sustainable Dialogue Lab (SD Lab - Laboratório de Diálogo Sustentável), sendo revistas por meio de uma ação conjunta com as universidades Northeastern University, da cidade de Boston, nos Estados Unidos e a Universidade de Fortaleza - UNIFOR, integrando assim academia, a juventude e o poder público. Esta atualização se concretiza em um novo Plano, denominado Plano de Ação Climática (PLAC) de Fortaleza, produzido em 2020 como parte do Projeto UrbanLEDS II. Sua elaboração partiu do alinhamento entre metas, ações planejadas e legislação existentes, utilizando a instância de participação social do FORCLIMA para debate das pautas e realizando diálogo com gestores de diferentes instituições e secretarias para validar e verificar possibilidades. Para fundamentação das metas são utilizadas informações dos estudos produzidos por Fortaleza, tendo como ponto de partida os Inventários de Emissão de Gases do Efeito Estufa (GEE), documentos nos quais se realiza o mapeamento, relato e monitoramento das fontes de emissão, e que são essenciais para o início do planejamento para a ação climática. Seguindo com o compromisso de se tornar carbono neutro e resiliente até 2050, o PLAC da cidade foi embasado em 3 princípios: Justiça Climática, Soluções baseadas na Natureza e Economia Verde. Já os objetivos, metas e ações do Plano estão divididos nos eixos Energia, Saneamento, Mobilidade, Resiliência. Tanto na manutenção destes princípios, como na execução das ações é necessária articulação com os diferentes níveis de governo nos quais as pautas perpassam. Há relação com as instâncias superiores de governo, também, no que diz respeito ao alinhamento com legislações ambientais e Contribuição Nacionalmente Determinadas.

column17: Fortaleza possui 5 Inventários de Emissão de Gases do Efeito Estufa (GEE), documentos nos quais se realiza o mapeamento, relato e monitoramento das fontes de emissão, e que são essenciais para o início do planejamento para a ação climática. Em 2014 a Secretaria de Urbanismo e Meio Ambiente de Fortaleza SEUMA junto ao ICLEI viabilizaram o 1º Inventário de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa GEE da cidade de Fortaleza com ano base 2012. Já em 2016 a PMF publicou o seu 2º Inventário de Emissões de GEE em parceria com o Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina CAF sob o nome Pegadas de Carbono e Hídrica da Cidade de Fortaleza, integrante do projeto Pegadas das Cidades realizado pela consultoria contratada Servicios Ambientales SA. Em conjunto ao Projeto foram também desenvolvidos os aplicativos 'Pegada de Água' e 'Pegada de Carbono' que possibilitam ao usuário calcular suas próprias pegadas ou de sua instituição. O 3° Inventário de Emissões de GEE, com ano base 2016, foi elaborado durante o ano de 2018, ano no qual a Cidade de Fortaleza, em parceria com o Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina CAF e Agência Francesa de Desenvolvimento AFD, participou do Projeto Ciudades e Cambio Climatico, que teve como objetivo elaborar o Estudo de Vulnerabilidade às Mudanças Climáticas e o Plano de Adaptação às Mudanças Climáticas de Fortaleza. O 4º Inventário de Emissões de GEE, com ano base 2018, utilizou as metodologias propostas no Protocolo Global para Inventários de Emissões de GEE na Escala da Comunidade GPC desenvolvido pelo ICLEI WRI World Resources Institute e o C40 Climate Leadership Group em 2014. O GPC fornece uma metodologia para padronização e realização dos cálculos de inventários de governos locais possibilitando fácil auditoria dos dados e comparação das emissões entre as cidades em diferentes âmbitos. O 5° Inventário de Emissões de GEE, para o ano base de 2020, foi elaborado segundo a mesma metodologia, pela Universidade Federal de Fortaleza e está em processo de revisão. A articulação intergovernamental, em especial com o Governo do Estado do Ceará, é essencial para a obtenção dos dados necessários ao preenchimento das ferramentas de cálculo, tendo em vista as responsabilidades administrativas relacionadas às temáticas.

No campo da gestão de riscos e vulnerabilidades, a Defesa Civil de Fortaleza atua em parceria com o Governo Federal e Estadual, tanto em ações preventivas quanto em situações de emergência. Em 2025, técnicos da Defesa Civil Nacional estiveram em campo em Fortaleza, junto às Defesas Civis estaduais e municipais, testando o novo sistema Defesa Civil Alerta, que envia mensagens por SMS e aplicativos móveis para avisar a população em casos de risco extremo. Após a capacitação, o envio de alertas passou a ser responsabilidade direta dos órgãos locais, fortalecendo a integração e a prontidão da cidade.

Além disso, em parceria com o Ministério das Cidades e o Serviço Geológico do Brasil (SGB), Fortaleza deu início ao Plano Municipal de Redução de Riscos (PMRR), com investimento de R$ 700 mil do Governo Federal. O plano terá duração de 18 meses e prevê a atualização completa do mapeamento de áreas de risco da cidade, abrangendo alagamentos, inundações, deslizamentos e outras ameaças, além da análise das vulnerabilidades sociais. A iniciativa permitirá diagnósticos atualizados em todas as Regionais, subsidiando soluções adequadas a cada território e possibilitando o planejamento de políticas públicas mais eficazes de prevenção e redução de desastres.

A articulação multiescalar também ocorre em outros componentes da agenda climática. No campo do saneamento e recursos hídricos, a Prefeitura coopera com órgãos estaduais como a CAGECE e a FUNCEME, que fornecem dados essenciais para inventários de emissões e análises de risco. Na área de energia, há integração com a CEGÁS e a ANEEL, possibilitando alinhamento regulatório e planejamento energético. Em nível federal e internacional, Fortaleza participa de projetos apoiados pelo Banco Mundial (como o programa Fortaleza Cidade Sustentável) e redes de cooperação climática, como ICLEI e C40, que aportam metodologias, recursos e auditorias técnicas, garantindo maior consistência e comparabilidade dos dados da cidade.

Essas conexões demonstram que a ação climática de Fortaleza é construída em cooperação horizontal e vertical, com apoio técnico e financeiro dos governos estadual e federal e validação por redes internacionais. Essa governança compartilhada amplia a capacidade de resposta do município, assegura maior qualidade dos diagnósticos e cria condições para transformar os compromissos climáticos em resultados concretos de adaptação, mitigação e justiça climática.

column17: La Comisión Interinstitucional para la acción ante el Cambio Climático (CICC) es el órgano responsable de coordinar y concretar la formulación e instrumentación de la Política Estatal de Cambio Climático y es presidida por el Gobernador del Estado. La CICC además busca alinearse las políticas climáticas de forma verticalmente y horizontalmente integradas y también atender agendas internacionales como los Objetivos del Desarrollo Sustentable (ODS).La Comisión es un mecanismo permanente de concurrencia, comunicación, colaboración, coordinación y concertación sobre la Política Estatal en materia de cambio climático.La CICC está activa desde 2015 y está conformada actualmente por 18 dependencias estatales, las tres coordinaciones estratégicas (Social, económica y gestión del territorio) seis dependencias federales y el Instituto Metropolitano de Planeación y Gestión del Desarrollo del Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara (IMEPLAN). Entre sus objetivos (Art. 40° Ley para la Acción ante el Cambio Climático del Estado de Jalisco - LACCJ) están: la aplicación transversal de cambio climático; la coordinación de esfuerzos de acciones para la adaptación, mitigación y reducción de la vulnerabilidad; la concurrencia, vinculación y congruencia de programas, acciones e inversiones; la evaluación de acciones, entre otras.https://semadet.jalisco.gob.mx/gobernanza-territorial/cambio-climatico2/comision-interinstitucional-de-accion-ante-el-cambio-climatico-cicc

column17: The Miami-Dade County Back Bay Coastal Storm Risk Management Feasibility Study is being conducted by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) that examines the impacts of and potential responses to storm surge damage in Miami-Dade County. The study area includes coastal and inland areas that are at risk from coastal storm flooding and sea level rise that includes City of Miami and surrounding municipalities within Miami-Dade County. The study authority for the Miami-Dade County Back Bay Coastal Storm Risk Management Feasibility Study is Public Law 84-71, June 15, 1955, which authorizes an examination and survey of the coastal and tidal areas of the eastern and southern United States, with reference to areas where severe damages have occurred from hurricane winds and tides. The purpose of the project is to reduce economic damage associated with coastal storms and improve human safety and coastal resiliency in the Miami-Dade County Back Bay. The Recommended Plan (RP) includes a combination of structural (such as surge barriers and floodwalls), non-structural (such as flood proofing, relocation, and elevation of structures) and natural and nature-based features (such as mangrove plantings). The project is funded under P.L. 115-123: Bi-Partisan Budget Act of 2018, Supplemental. This study was completed in August 2024.\n\nhttps://www.saj.usace.army.mil/MiamiDadeBackBayCSRMFeasibilityStudy/

column17: \nThe Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact - Unified Sea Level Rise Projections and the guidance report are key planning tools produced by the Compact and are intended to assist decision-makers at both the local and regional levels in Southeast Florida to plan for and make decisions about sea level rise and associated vulnerabilities based on best-available science. The projection is intended to inform adaptation strategies and policies and is offered to ensure that all major infrastructure projects throughout the Southeast Florida region have the same basis for design and construction relative to future sea level. The City adopted the 2019 Unified Sea Level Rise Projections as design standards for infrastructure projects in 2020 via Resolution R-20-0292. In the fourth quarter of 2024, the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact (the Compact) undertook a review of its 2019 Regionally Unified Sea Level Rise Projection (“2019 Projection”) vis-à-vis updates from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) 2022 Sea Level Rise Technical Report, as well as observational trends in the sea level in the region. Based on the review, the Compact recommended the continued use of the 2019 Regionally Unified Projection in Southeast Florida as a basis for resilience planning, design, and construction. In October 2022, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) upgraded the City Community Rating System (CRS) score to a 6, resulting in 20% discount on premium insurances to properties within the City. On March 13, 2024, the Commission adopted the 2021 Citywide Stormwater Master Plan under resolution R-23-0081. https://southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org/unified-sea-level-rise-projections https://miamifl.iqm2.com/Citizens/Detail_LegiFile.aspx?ID7674

column17: Vulnerability Assessments that identify or address risks of flooding and sea level rise are required for Florida municipalities per section 380.093, Florida Statutes. We collaborated with state and county entities to collect necessary data for the project. City of Miami received funding from Florida Department of Environmental Protection to develop a City of Miami Critical Facilities and Assets Vulnerability Assessment. The City completed its Flooding Vulnerability Assessment in September 2024. The Vulnerability Assessment evaluates the potential impact of existing and future flood conditions on the City's physical assets and facilities from rainfall, compound flooding, and storm surge. It provided insights into the timing, extent, and consequences of flood hazard impacts while also serving as a screening tool to prioritize assets most at risk to be considered for future mitigation projects. Additional community considerations addressed equity concerns, assigning higher priority to assets in Climate Justice Communities, and those identified as valued by the community through community engagement efforts. \n\nhttps://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2021/Chapter380/All

Dicha sección comprende el análisis de vulnerabilidad climática que permite la identificación de los sistemas vulnerables que serán atendidos con la implementación de las acciones propuestas en materia de adaptación y mitigación. 

Asimismo, este análisis permite identificar los principales fenómenos climáticos extremos que han afectado y afectarán a Monterrey para poder conocer las amenazas climáticas.

El Inventario de Emisiones de Gases y Compuestos de Efecto Invernadero (IMEGyCEI) desglosa la cuantificación de las emisiones y absorciones de gases y compuestos de efecto invernadero (GyCEI) por fuentes y sumideros para los cuatro sectores de emisión definidos por el IPCC: Energía; Procesos Industriales y Usos de Productos; Agricultura, Silvicultura y otros Usos de la Tierra, y; Residuos.

Se identificó que el sector Energía es el principal emisor de GEI con el 76.06% de las emisiones, seguido por el sector de Procesos Industriales y Uso de Productos con el 18.67%, y el sector Residuos con el 5.27%, siendo el sector Agricultura, Ganadería, Silvicultura y Otros Usos de la Tierra (ASOUT) el de menor contribución al inventario, este comportamiento se refleja de manera histórica a lo largo del periodo 2010 2020.

Su publicación permite definir y perfilar de mejor manera las acciones, estrategias y rutas de descarbonización que coadyuven en la mitigación del cambio climático y nos dirijan a la neutralidad en un largo plazo. Asimismo, estos resultados formaron parte del Inventario Estatal que se incluye en el Programa Estatal de Cambio Climático del Estado de Nuevo León y la Zona Metropolitana de Monterrey.

https://sostenible.monterrey.gob.mx/inventario-emisiones

El PAC, al ser un extracto del PECC NL y ZMM, es producto de la coordinación entre la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente del Gobierno del Estado de Nuevo León y de los enlaces en materia de acción climática de los gobiernos locales de la Zona Metropolitana de Monterrey (ZMM). 

El PAC coordina los esfuerzos conjuntos frente al cambio climático, asegurando un proceso participativo entre niveles de gobierno, la ciudadanía, el sector privado, sectores productivos, la academia y las organizaciones de la sociedad civil. Además, expande el liderazgo del Estado y los municipios en materia ambiental, económica y social, al alinear el desarrollo local con los esfuerzos internacionales en materia climática. 

Dicho programa, esta compuesto por ocho ejes que enmarcan 26 estrategias y 141 líneas de acción de mitigación, adaptación y programáticas, que atienden los problemas y oportunidades climáticas en los sectores y sistemas prioritarios identificados en los diagnósticos de emisiones y vulnerabilidad: seguridad hídrica, movilidad, edificaciones, el manejo de residuos, la industria, el sistema natural y la energía. 

Aunado a lo anterior responden a la visión de la política climática en el corto plazo (2026) , mediano plazo (2030) y largo plazo (2050). Cabe mencionar que su desarrollo e implementación han estado y estarán acompañados de un proceso de participación continua y un proceso de monitoreo, seguimiento y evaluación.

column17: Medellín hace parte del Nodo Regional de Cambio Climático de Antioquia (NRCC), constituido bajo directrices del gobierno nacional mediante decreto 298 de 2016 y conformado a través del Decreto departamental D2016070004161 de 2016. El NRCC es una instancia de coordinación entre diferentes niveles de gobierno que busca facilitar la consistencia entre políticas locales, regionales y nacionales. El NRCC hace una evaluación de las apuestas regionales y gestiona la coherencia entre los planes de acción, el desarrollo de medidas y el cumplimiento de las metas territoriales propuestas en la Contribución Nacionalmente Determinada de Colombia. Se adjunta Decreto Departamental 4161 de 2016 que conforma el NRCC de Antioquia.Medellín participa en la Contribución Nacionalmente Determinada de Colombia a través de siete medidas territoriales adoptadas en la Ley 2169 de 2021: Zona Urbana de aire Protegida, Densificación red ciclista, taxis eléctricos, buses eléctricos, construcción Metro de la 80, operación 4,5 km Tranvía de Ayacucho, Operación Metrocables Líneas M y H. column17: The City works closely with all other levels of government. Mayor Gallego continued her tenure on the Climate Mayor's leadership team as Chair highlighting three priority areas: 1) expanding city influence through private sector collaboration and philanthropy to supplement federal funding, 2) enhance regional work through the Western Water Security Cohort and address the challenges of extreme heat, and 3) align and support member cities of all sizes to ensure communities continue to access tools and resources to advance local climate action (https://azpbs.org/horizon/2025/01/phoenix-mayor-kate-gallego-climate-mayors/). The City of Phoenix works with many regional stakeholders and partners to address air quality, such as the Maricopa County Air Quality Department and their Clear Air Council, Arizona Department of Environmental Quality, and the Maricopa Association of Governments' Air Quality Technical Advisory Committee. The City is involved with various networks such as C40 cities, the Sustainable Cities Network, the Western Adaptation Alliance, the Arizona Center for a Carbon-Neutral Economy, and the Urban Sustainability Directors Network. ( C40.org, usdn.org, https://globalfutures.asu.edu/sustainable-cities/ https://www.azcarbonneutral.org/) . In March 2024, Phoenix Office of Environmental Programs was the lead applicant for the Climate Pollution Reduction Grant (CPRG) application as part of a coalition with the State of Arizona Office of Resiliency, Maricopa County, City of Mesa and City of Tempe. The application requested total funding of $453 million ($179 million for Phoenix) for measures that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve air quality in the region. Measures include microgrids, public fleet electrification, commercial lawn mower electrification, residential energy efficiency, fireplace electrification, food waste conversion, and workforce development. Our coalition CPRG application was not selected for funding. Phoenix also works with the Governor's Office of Resiliency on various climate projects. Additionally, the City of Phoenix regularly submits comments and information to the federal government to inform federal policy and grantmaking.

column17: Phoenix has a goal to reduce the amount of water consumed per person daily (GPCD) in the Phoenix service area to 155 GPCD by 2030. As of December 2024 our GPCD is 151 GPCD (https://cmpr-dashboard-phoenix.hub.arcgis.com/pages/wsd ). The City of Phoenix 2021 Water Resource Plan demonstrates that, for most foreseeable scenarios, Phoenix has sufficient water supplies for the next 50 years (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/waterservicessite/documents/2021%20city%20of%20phoenix%20water%20resource%20plan.pdf ). These projected supplies will likely be stretched further through planned conservation and infrastructure enhancements. The City also held Water Smart Teaching Workshops in early 2025 as a fun and interactive way for high school teachers to learn about water conservation in Phoenix and pass that knowledge on to students (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/supply-conservation/save-water/conservation-assistance/teacher-listening-workshops.html ). The City's “Save Water Pledge” was made permanent in May 2025, which underscores the City's commitment to sustainability and water resiliency in the face of ongoing drought and climate challenges (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/water-services-news/phoenix-mayor-kate-gallego-announces-continuation-of-the--save-w.html). The City's Water Services Department offered non-residential and residential turf replacement incentive programs that started in 2024 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/water-services-news/3259.html ). The City promotes the use of Green Stormwater Infrastructure (GSI) with the new Residential GSI Handbook released in November 2024 to help educate the public about how to capture and use stormwater for water conservation and ecosystem support (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/environmental-programs-news/3333.html). Phoenix also engages with other levels of government (county, state, and federal) for many activities, including: 1) Reporting on efforts to manage infrastructure capacity and adaptability to changing demands and climatic conditions, 2) Reporting on compliance with the Clean Water Act, NPDES, drinking water, and wastewater conveyance standards as climate changes, 3) Reporting on the quality and adaptability of conveyance and treatment technologies to climatic variability or extremes, 4) Reporting on stormwater management capacity, inundation, conveyance, and their relation to flooding and storm events, 5) Reporting on the planning process for water quality and treatment capacity, 6) Reporting on the planning process for projected population growth and management of wastewater, drinking water, pressure, and volume for collection, distribution, and treatment infrastructure.

column17: Phoenix completed a study in 2020 in partnership with RTI International and the US EPA to create an assessment regarding indicator-based community vulnerability from site and waste management facilities following extreme events. This assists decision makers in identifying vulnerable communities, tracking sites and facilities, and communicating how extreme events may affect these sites and facilities and the surrounding communities (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/UrbanVulnerability_R9_July2020_Clean_v2.pdf). The City's 2025 Heat Response Plan, updated annually, approved by city council in March of 2025. (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/cityclerksite/city-council-meeting-files/2025/3-25-25%20Policy%20Agenda%20-%20Final.pdf https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0Y2oIUz3TTg ). This Plan outlines 30 actions across eight strategy areas that the City leads and coordinates to protect the public from adverse heat health outcomes. Phoenix monitors drought and how it impacts our city and residents and through the City of Phoenix Drought Response Plan the city addresses long-term water conservation, planning, and diversified water supply (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/waterservicessite/documents/2021%20city%20of%20phoenix%20water%20resource%20plan.pdf ). Flood risks are assessed in the joint Maricopa County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan (MJHMP) (https://www.maricopa.gov/DocumentCenter/View/75143/Maricopa-County-MJMHMP-2021_MJPT-Final-2021-11-02). \nSeveral Phoenix-specific actions included in the MJHMP are: 1) Review building permits for compliance with Floodplain Ordinance and Nation Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) regulations, 2) Continue to include in the Phoenix General Plan policies that protect the natural flow regime of washes, designate areas for open space and preserves, and support the use of green stormwater infrastructure/low impact development to address multiple risks, 3) Storm Drain Capital Improvement Program - Construct drainage facilities to mitigate flooding hazard to residents of the city, 4) Coordinate review and approval of development projects located within flood hazard areas with Planning and Development and Floodplain Management, 5) Dam/Levee Safety Program - Operate and Maintain Dams/Levees to mitigate flooding hazard to the residents of the City, 6) Continue to provide links on the Phoenix.gov/Office of Emergency Management website to sources of hazard mitigation educational materials such as FEMA.gov and Ready.gov, 7) Address extreme heat through Summer Respite regional program to network with faith-based organizations to provide heat relief, hydration and respite with wellness checks. Program services are provided for the affected populations, 8) The “Take a Hike do it Right” Outreach Program aims to educate on hike/trail selection and hiking safety to avoid heat related illnesses, 9) Provide shade coverage at all City of Phoenix Bus Stops to shelter riders from excessive sunlight and extreme heat, and 10) Increase frequency of bus routes around vulnerable communities to minimize exposure to extreme heat while waiting for public transit.\n

column17: The Phoenix 2021 Climate Action Plan incorporates actions and goals that depend on multiple levels of government to accomplish. From national-level policy to state-level electricity generation regulations to regional planning agency plans. The Phoenix 2021 Climate Action Plan (CAP) includes the goals and commitments adopted by our Mayor and City Council. Additionally, the Phoenix Climate Action Plan considers and includes actions planned by our two local utilities, the Arizona Public Service (APS) and Salt River Project (SRP). Transportation modeling uses the Maricopa Association of Governments' Active Transportation Plan and Travel Demand Model information. Waste reduction modeling includes information from continuing efforts to reduce waste city-wide with a zero-waste goal by 2050; additionally, the Phoenix supports recycling efforts in neighboring jurisdictions which lack sufficient waste management infrastructure. Other waste-related goals include reducing food loss and food waste by 50% of 2010 values by 2030. Additional actions were created in the CAP, including increased deployment of solar and use of green biogas to substitute natural gas use and more use of transit, walking, biking, and micromobility. The City of Phoenix published the 2024 Climate Action Plan Progress Report in September 2024 to report to the community and City leaders about progress made in addressing our climate change challenge, and to inform the development of the complete Climate Action Plan update (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/COPHX_2024_2522_CAPReport_FullBook_C7.4.pdf). The Progress Report provides information on 1) Stationary energy: Phoenix renewable energy and energy efficiency, solar installation permit approval streamlining, and electric vehicle infrastructure requirements, 2) Transportation: active and alternate means of transportation, light rail expansion and walkable urban code update, fuel cell hydrogen/battery electric/hybrid electric buses, Transportation Electrification Action Plan, and alternatively fueled vehicles at airports, 3) Waste as a resource: organic waste and special event diversion, citywide recycling and organic waste diversion, building Adaptive Reuse Program, and brownfield redevelopment, 4) Air quality: overview of air quality progress, Phoenix as signatory to C40's Clean Air Accelerator, and Phoenix Travel Reduction Program, 5) Local food systems: integration of food goals into land use planning, local food production economic and workforce capacity development, partnerships for sustainable food practices, and increased access to healthy food and education, 6) Heat: actions that reduce heat health impact, tree planting, cool corridors and other shade implementation, and the Cool Pavement Program, and 7) Water: water infrastructure, City water conservation, community-wide water conservation, and green stormwater infrastructure.
