column17: Maricopa County along with twenty-four incorporated cities and towns, two tribes, and one other governmental organization participated in a cooperative effort to create and update the Maricopa County Multi-jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan. The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors officially adopted the Multi-jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan (MJHMP) (https://www.maricopa.gov/DocumentCenter/View/75143/Maricopa-County-MJMHMP-2021_MJPT-Final-2021-11-02. FEMA's approval of the Plan is for five years, effective April 30, 2010. The first 5-year update was officially adopted by the County of Maricopa, Arizona, on November 18, 2015. Due to the COVID-19 emergency, the next five-year update was delayed until 2022. The Maricopa County Board approved the next version of the MJHMP of Supervisors in February 2022. Hazard mitigation planning reduces the risk to people and property and reduces the cost of disaster recovery. A hazard mitigation plan can help communities become more sustainable and disaster-resistant by focusing efforts on the hazards and disaster-prone areas and identifying appropriate mitigation actions. The County and each participating community have an approved hazard mitigation plan intended to reduce the potential loss from natural hazards. This plan is a living document that requires adjustments to maintain its relevance and remain a useful tool and resource. The planning team members are committed to continuously monitoring and documenting any changes to the recommended actions in the Maricopa County Multi-jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan. This effort is essential for determining the progress made on each hazard mitigation initiative and in performing the annual evaluations of the plan.

column17: The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 provided tools to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) pollution through programs such as the Climate Pollution Reduction Grants (CPRG) Program. With funding from the IRA, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) coordinated the development and implementation of climate action plans to reduce GHGs for states, U.S. territories, municipalities, air pollution control agencies, tribes, and other regional organizations. CPRG is a dual-phase program: Phase One- Planning Phase: $1 million was provided to the 67 most populous MSAs to develop climate action plans to reduce GHGs and Phase Two- Implementation Phase: $4.3 billion for grants to implement GHG reduction measures developed through the phase one planning grants. Through Phase One, the Tampa Bay Regional Planning Council (TBRPC) received the $1 million planning grant funding from the EPA to lead the Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater MSA developed of a climate action plan. By participating in Phase One, the Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) jurisdictions, municipal agencies, departments, other municipal government offices, council of governments, metropolitan planning commissions, or other regional organizations comprised of multiple municipalities are eligible to apply for grant funding through Phase Two. The Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater MSA Priority Climate Action Plan (PCAP) analyzed high-priority, implementation ready projects in the largest GHG sectors in the MSA. The analysis showed that the energy and transportation and mobile combustion sectors as the largest emitters with 45.3% from the energy sector and 43.2% from the transportation sector. Jurisdictions and agency partners prioritized near-term, implementation ready projects in all sectors, but there was a large focus on the energy and transportation sectors. Projects that were identified were solar installation, deep energy efficiency retrofits, extend public, and converting on-road vehicles to electric vehicles. Using the identified projects in those sectors, a benefits and reduction measures analysis was completed. With a medium population growth in the MSA, implementing the prioritized projects in the energy and transportation sector is projected to decrease in GHG by 2.14% by 2030 and 51% by 2050. These projects could be focused on areas in the low-income and disadvantaged communities (LIDAC) that were identified, and engage with community stakeholders to establish community needs. Moving into the Comprehensive Climate Action Plan (CCAP), these areas will be expanded on to develop a robust plan that sets actionable goals and measures to help create a more resilient future. \n\nThe purpose of this Priority Climate Action Plan (PCAP) is to offer a strategic framework for measuring, planning, and reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and related climatic impacts within the Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater MSA. The approach involves designing and utilizing this climate action plan as a customized roadmap for making informed decisions and understanding where and how to achieve the largest, most costeffective GHG reductions that align with the region's goals. The plan will address the following objectives: GHG Inventory, GHG Emission Projections, GHG Reduction Measures, Benefits Analysis, Low Income/Disadvantaged Communities Benefits Analysis, Review of Authority to Implement, and Next Steps.

In recent years, several frameworks have been established at the national level to support the advancement of climate plans in local authorities. The Ministry of Energy' and the Ministry for Environmental Protection's guidelines and accelerator for developing adaptation plans is based on the methodology of Tel Aviv's adaptation plan, and core team members frequently share the city's knowledge and experience. The national guide for Local Climate Action Plans was compiled in collaboration with the Tel Aviv Yafo climate team, incorporating the C40 methodology for both adaptation and mitigation paths. 
The Climate Directorate of the Ministry of Environmental Protection leads the national climate crisis preparedness within government ministries, and the city often participates in learning and knowledge-sharing sessions.
The Climate Forum, headed by the President of Israel, is also a framework where the municipality helps shape policy, raise challenges, and city representatives participate regularly. Additionally, new laws and guidelines are referred to the city for strategic consideration in energy, planning, and transportation. The city's team together with leading experts from the Climate Forum are devising a new sustainable energy plan for the whole Metropolitan area.
In 2022, Tel Aviv Yao initiated a regional Nature Covenant together with the National Nature and National Parks Authority for the whole Dan region. The Covenant aims to cooperate in preserving and cultivating the natural environment in the face of climate change. The mayors recognized the need for collaboration due to the shared natural resources and ecology among the cities. The mayors emphasized the importance of combining environmental considerations with urban development, as seen in the example of Or Yehuda's Nahal Ayalon park.
Tel Aviv-Yafo's mayor highlighted the need for regional cooperation to protect the natural environment, as it crosses urban boundaries. He emphasized the importance of urgent action to address the ecological crisis. The agreement demonstrates the growing awareness and activity for nature preservation in Gush Dan. It signifies a proactive approach to addressing climate change and ensuring the sustainability of the region's natural resources. In 2025, the action plan is being updated in collaboration with the Regional Planning Committee and the National Parks and Nature Authority.
Tel Aviv-Yafo is a leading member of the Israeli Coastal Authorities Forum, actively participating in its various initiatives. The city is particularly focused on building capacity to address the impacts of climate change on the coastal area.
In April 2024, the municipality's climate task team organized a professional workshop on planning for sea-level rise and storm surges. The program was conducted in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment and UNPAPRAC. The workshop included roundtable discussions on coastal case studies prepared by participating cities. These case studies served as introductions to dedicated coastal adaptation plans. In 2025' Tel Aviv Yafo will host the Forum's annual conference, celebrating ten year of activities. 
The city is collaborating on a regular basis with the National Emergency Management Authority (NEMA), specifically leading the contingency planning on flooding and water management. In May, 2025, the city team took part participated in the 'Many Waters' national emergency drill, lled by NEMA in collaboration with the European Union's Prevention, Preparedness, and Response to Natural Disasters (PPRD) Directorate. The drill focused on a scenario of urban flooding and flash floods in the Tel Aviv-Yafo area. The main goal was to test the civil sector's readiness to cope with a major urban flood event, particularly the preparedness process following a 24-hour flood warning. Participants included the Israel Police, Israel Fire and Rescue Services, Magen David Adom, Ministries of Transportation, and Health, along with the Israel Meteorological Service and other agencies.
The drill highlighted the critical need for inter-organizational collaboration, as the city cannot handle an event of this magnitude alone. The event underscored the importance of building a new culvert from Ariel Sharon Park to the sea to significantly reduce the risk of flooding. This solution, combined with the park's retention basins, is considered essential for the city to manage extreme rainfall events.

Asimismo, en colaboración con la comunidad San José del cantón Santa Elena, se están desarrollando acciones de zonificación y planificación para la adaptación y mitigación climática, integrando actividades para el manejo sostenible de los productos no maderables como tagua y paja toquilla.

This includes 7 of the district Municipalities that fall with the UMDM. The key factor that will assist all local Municipalities, is that there will be a specific chapter on each municipality, which can be extrapolated and used by the Local Municipalities. This information can and will also be used to inform decision making around climate risks / hazards and vulnerabilities.

column17: O Instituto do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos (INEMA) é o órgão responsável pela execução da Política Ambiental do Estado da Bahia, promovendo a integração e o fortalecimento das políticas ambientais e de recursos hídricos, com foco na agilidade e qualidade dos processos. No contexto do Plano de Mitigação e Adaptação às Mudanças do Clima (PMAMC) de Salvador, a contribuição do INEMA concentra-se em ações voltadas à adaptação da zona costeira às mudanças climáticas, como a ampliação da Certificação Bandeira Azul. Esse selo internacional reconhece praias que cumprem rigorosos critérios socioambientais, garantindo condições adequadas para o banho e estimulando o turismo sustentável. A expansão dessa certificação está associada ao aumento da arborização e à preservação de áreas verdes, o que favorece a permeabilidade do solo, reduz os riscos de alagamentos, proporciona conforto térmico e minimiza a formação de ilhas de calor.\nJá a Empresa Baiana de Águas e Saneamento (EMBASA) é responsável pelos serviços de abastecimento de água e esgotamento sanitário, incluindo a captação, tratamento e distribuição de água, bem como a coleta, transporte, tratamento e destinação final dos esgotos domésticos. Conforme previsto no PMAMC, a EMBASA contribui por meio do fortalecimento da gestão dos recursos hídricos e da ampliação do tratamento de efluentes, com o objetivo de atender, prioritariamente, as áreas mais vulneráveis e deficitárias da cidade. Uma gestão eficiente assegura qualidade e regularidade no fornecimento de água, mesmo durante períodos de seca ou eventos críticos que possam comprometer o abastecimento.\nEntre as estratégias previstas estão: a redução do consumo por meio do combate às perdas, o incentivo ao reuso da água e à captação da água da chuva, a ampliação da captação por meio da proteção dos mananciais e da interligação entre sistemas. Além disso, destaca-se a expansão do saneamento básico em regiões com menor cobertura e infraestrutura precária, visando à preservação ambiental, à melhoria da qualidade de vida e à diminuição dos custos com saúde pública. Essas ações, aliadas a campanhas de conscientização, também evitam o despejo inadequado de esgotos e resíduos domésticos em rios e áreas públicas, contribuindo para a redução de doenças associadas à falta de saneamento.

column17: The City of Milwaukee Climate and Equity Plan will form the basis of broader Milwaukee-region Climate Action Planning through the Inflation Reduction Act's Climate Pollution Reduction Grant program. The City of Milwaukee, along with the Southeast Wisconsin Regional Planning Commission, applied for and received $1 million in formula funding for the Milwaukee Metropolitan Statistical Area to work in collaboration with officials in the 4-county region, including county-level and municipal-level managers to plan for implementation of many of the policy and program recommendations developed in Milwaukee's Climate and Equity Plan. There was agreement to apply for funding to (1) expand renewable capacity sufficiently so that communities in the Milwaukee MSA could run all operations from renewables (2) Collaborate regionally to expand electric vehicle charging infrastructure and (3) Fund a Commercial Buildings Resource Center to help building owners reduce energy use and GHG emissions from larger buildings and (4) Fund shared Sustainability Staff members to support the environmental sustainability efforts of smaller municipalities that do not have sufficient resources to fund their own sustainability staff person. The Milwaukee MSA also worked in close collaboration with the State of Wisconsin Office of Sustainability and Clean Energy, to ensure our various CRPG Implementation Grant funding requests were not duplicative and understand how there may be state resources available for GHG-reducing initiatives that would not be funded through the Milwaukee MSA application. Both the Milwaukee MSA and the State of Wisconsin CPRG Implementation Grant Applications were filed in the spring of 2024, though, unfortunately, neither application was granted. However, given the collaboration established through those CPRG planning processes, shared climate action planning is still taking place. For example, the City of Milwaukee is still seeking funding opportunities for shared Sustainability Staff members for suburban communities in the Milwaukee MSA that are most committed to climate action. In addition, the City of Milwaukee, SEWRPC, and the State of Wisconsin are collaborating on developing an improved Green Jobs guides and better clarify training and career pathways for green jobs.\n

column17: While we have strong goals to reduce GHG emissions by 90% by 2040 and to move to 100% renewable energy generation by 2050, there are several programs in place to move the needle on reducing emissions across the different pillars of our sustainability office. The City of Orlando committed, through its Community Sustainability Action Plan, to transition 100% of its fleet to alternative fuel or electric vehicles by 2030. Additionally, we aim to reduce single-occupancy vehicle travel through increased use of transit, micromobility, and active modes of travel; double the miles of complete streets; and eliminate pedestrian and bike fatalities. The advancement and adoption of electric mobility have become the prominent strategy to decarbonize transportation, and this is outlined in ORLANDO'S 2030 ELECTRIC MOBILITY ROADMAP. The city also has a goal to increase the local tree canopy by 40% through a \'one person, one tree\' giveaway program, which aims to increase shade to reduce surface and building temperatures, enhance resilience to flooding, and pull carbon from the atmosphere. Orlando's solid waste goals include striving to become a “zero waste” community and aiming to eliminate sending solid waste to landfills by 2040. The city of Orlando has established an ambitious municipal action plan aimed at achieving greenhouse gas (GHG) neutrality in its operations by 2030. To reach this goal, the city is committed to powering 100% of its municipal electricity from solar energy and transitioning its entire fleet to alternative fuel or electric vehicles by 2030.

To achieve these objectives, the city has implemented several strategies to reduce carbon emissions by the deadline. Key initiatives include, but are not limited to, installing solar panels and making energy efficiency upgrades across various facilities. In 2011, the city joined the Department of Energy's Better Buildings Challenge (BBC) initiative, which aims to reduce energy use by 20% over 10 years. By 2020 and 2021, the city successfully achieved energy savings of 23% and 18%, respectively, compared to the 2011 baseline. In 2024, onsite and offsite installed solar energy capacity across city-owned facilities accounted for about 30% of the city's total electricity consumption.

Furthermore, the city has joined the Department of Energy's Better Climate Challenge (BCC) initiative, committing to reducing its Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 90% within 10 years.

To track its progress toward carbon neutrality in municipal operations by 2030, the city develops and updates its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions data annually.

The development of a Climate Action Plan (CAP) is not legally mandated at the national level in Slovenia. However, municipalities are required to prepare a Local Energy Concept (LEK) in accordance with the Energy Act (EZ-1), which serves as a foundational document for energy-related aspects of the CAP.

In 2026, the City of Ljubljana will integrate several key climate-related documents—LEK, the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), the Climate City Contract (CCC), and the Climate Change Adaptation Strategy—into a single, consolidated Climate Action Plan. To avoid potential inconsistencies with the individual requirements of each document, the core content of each will be preserved in its prescribed legal or procedural format, while the operational measures will be merged into a unified plan.

This consolidated CAP will be structured around two main components:

A mitigation component, incorporating actions from the LEK, SECAP, and CCC (under the EU Mission 100), and an adaptation component, drawing from the LEK, SECAP, CCC, and the Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (in line with the EU Mission on Adaptation).

The plan will also include a vulnerability and risk assessment, dedicated sections on energy and transport poverty, as well as provisions on governance, stakeholder engagement, political commitment, and communication.

This approach will ensure greater transparency, consistent monitoring and reporting, and full alignment with European obligations and mission requirements, while also supporting the integration of local action with national strategies (NEPN, NDC, NAP) and EU policies (European Green Deal, Fit for 55).

Progress is currently tracked and reported through national requirements (e.g., LEK- reporting, City Council reports) and EU Mission platforms (NetZeroCities). Ljubljana cooperates closely with national ministries and agencies, the Ljubljana Urban Region, 17 district communities, and a wide range of stakeholders, ensuring a multilevel and inclusive governance approach.

In 2025, the City of Ljubljana prepared an updated Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment (CRVA). The assessment of vulnerabilities and risks was carried out in line with the IPCC AR5 methodology and the guidelines of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change. Although Slovenian national legislation does not require municipalities to prepare a CRVA, Ljubljana aligns its approach with the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) and contributes to national-level knowledge and coordination on climate risks.

The CRVA focuses on risks such as floods, droughts, heatwaves, forest fires, and landslides, many of which are also identified in the city's legally mandated Programme of Protection Against Natural and Other Disasters 2023-2030, prepared under the Protection Against Natural and Other Disasters Act (Official Gazette RS, No. 51/06 and amendments).

Although there is no formal national digital reporting platform for CRVAs, the City of Ljubljana shares progress and findings through city departments and public companies.

The CRVA namely serves as a basis for integrating climate risk into other municipal strategies and action plans, including spatial planning, civil protection, and resilience investments. It supports cross-sectoral collaboration and coordination with relevant national ministries and agencies, particularly in the field of water management and disaster preparedness.

In Daegu Metropolitan City, in accordance with South Korea's 'Basic Act on Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth for Response to Climate Crisis,' the city is pursuing carbon neutrality in conjunction with the national carbon neutrality and green growth master plan. This plan, which considers regional characteristics, is formulated for a 10-year period and updated every five years, with the most recent plan being established in April 2024. The main components include an analysis of the current status and future outlook of greenhouse gas emissions and absorption in Daegu Metropolitan City, and the development of 75 policy measures across eight major sectors with the goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. Furthermore, progress on greenhouse gas reduction initiatives will be reviewed, and annual action plans will be developed to address any deficiencies or necessary improvements, which will then be reflected in the following year's projects. All of these processes are subject to review and approval by the President's 2050 Carbon Neutrality Green Growth Committee and are made publicly available.
- The nine lower-level local governments under Daegu Metropolitan City must establish their own 'Carbon Neutral Green Growth Basic Plan' by April 2025.
- Daegu Metropolitan City will provide necessary information and budget support so that lower-level local governments can smoothly establish and implement their 'Carbon Neutral Green Growth Plan'.

According to the 'Basic Act on Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth for Response to Climate Crisis,' the Mayor of Daegu Metropolitan City and the nine local governments within Daegu's jurisdiction are required to develop and implement regional climate adaptation measures every five years, taking into account local characteristics. The goal is to minimize the negative impacts of climate change, protect vulnerable populations, formulate and implement practical measures suited to local conditions, and enhance climate change management capabilities. 
- The implementation evaluation of Daegu Metropolitan City's climate change adaptation project is conducted annually by experts and a citizen evaluation group.
- The results are reported to the central government and disclosed to the public.
- The evaluation is divided into four stages, and Daegu Metropolitan City has received the highest grade of 'Excellent' for eight consecutive years.

Here are several cases for explanation. Most of these cases are related to the business with the central government.

1. Carbon Neutral Incentive(Carbon Neutral Points) Program for households and car owners.
The Ministry of Environment operates the Carbon Neutrality Point System, a nationwide GHG reduction practice system that awards points to households, businesses, and others for reducing the use of electricity, water, and city gas. 
In addition, the Ministry of Environment operates an incentive system based on mileage reduction performance to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by reducing the mileage of vehicles. 

2. Renewable Energy Project and Green-Building Project
Based on the 2030 National Greenhouse Gas Reduction Roadmap, the aim is to reduce GHG emissions by 40%. New buildings are designated according to energy-saving design standards, with zero-energy buildings becoming mandatory and requiring certification. For new buildings, efficient energy management is promoted through energy-saving design standards, mandatory zero-energy buildings, and incentives for obtaining certification. To promote the creation of zero-energy buildings in the building sector, new and renewable energy installations are expanded, and zero-energy design support is provided for public and private housing complexes.
The main project contents include achieving energy independence for new buildings and zero-energy buildings by expanding the supply of new and renewable energy for new public housing districts in Goyang. Starting from 2025, in accordance with the government's 'Zero Energy Building Supply Plan' (June 2019), zero-energy construction of public housing with more than 30 households becomes compulsory, so a preemptive response is required.
Goyang is South Korea's first phased new town, where residential and commercial areas make up the majority of the development area. It has been 30 years since the new town was developed, and many of its buildings are aging. To improve the energy efficiency of old buildings, Goyang City went further than the government's initiatives, revising the Green Building Support Ordinance in 2021 and implementing the Green Building Support Project in the same year.

3. Small Business Energy Efficiency Improvement Project
The central government needs to promote energy efficiency and greenhouse gas reduction by identifying energy-saving opportunities in the commercial sector where greenhouse gas reduction is possible. Therefore, it is necessary to support the joint purchase of high-efficiency equipment and materials for small business stores and to promote energy efficiency through linked energy use rationalization projects. Goyang City improved energy efficiency in the commercial sector by replacing existing lighting equipment with LED lighting for wholesale and retail businesses that account for a high proportion of the industrial structure.

4. LED Replacement Project for Street Lights and Security Lights
Through the 'LED Lighting 2060 Plan', the central government presented a roadmap for distributing LED lighting to achieve 60% of the nation's total lighting by 2020, aiming for a 60% national LED lighting penetration rate and 100% in public institutions by 2020. The goal is to implement the LED lighting replacement plan in the public sector and promote the rational and efficient use of energy by supporting its expansion in the private sector. Goyang City assessed the current status of street lights and security lights and improved energy efficiency in stages by replacing sodium and metal lighting devices with LED lighting devices.

5. Household Low-NOx Boiler Installation Support Project
From April 2020, the central government implemented a mandate for eco-friendly boilers, promoting the mandatory production, supply, and sale of low-NOx (eco-friendly) boilers for home use certificate by the Ministry of Environment. This is because home-use low-NOx boilers absorb and recycle high-temperature heat that would otherwise be lost as exhaust gas, making them highly energy-efficient and reducing nitrogen oxide emissions to less than one-eighth compared to old boilers. In line with that, Goyang City expanded the supply by supporting the replacement of 6,000 low-NOx boilers for home use annually.
6. Goyang City, in cooperation with the central government, is also planning a resource-saving and carbon reduction project utilizing groundwater discharged from subway stations. With a budget of 4 billion KRW, the project aims to make use of more than 3,000 tons of groundwater discharged daily for nearby public facility water supply, roadside cooling roads, and river maintenance water. This project is expected not only to achieve water savings but also to provide convenience for nearby citizens suffering from the urban heat island effect.

The city is also coordinating with various private players to implement climate actions on PPP mode, i.e., 2000 TPD waste to energy plants, 500 TPD waste to bio-CNG plant, 1000 TPD C&D waste management plant etc. 

The city is also coordinating with local community to increase the green cover in the city from 6 m2 per capita in 2021 to 9 m2 per capita. The city, through public participation, has already planted 3 million trees in just three months in FY 2024-25

La Ley 4/2019, de 21 de febrero, de sostenibilidad energética de la Comunidad Autónoma Vasca, tiene por objeto el establecimiento, de acuerdo con la orientación general de la política energética, de los pilares normativos de la sostenibilidad energética en los ámbitos de las administraciones públicas vascas y del sector privado, articulando los deberes y obligaciones básicos que unas y otros deben cumplir y que se orientan fundamentalmente al impulso de medidas de ahorro y eficiencia energética, y de promoción e implantación de energías renovables. Entre sus objetivos está la reducción de las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero. El ámbito de aplicación de la ley incluye a las instituciones locales de la Comunidad Autónoma Vasca, entre ellas al Ayuntamiento de Vitoria-Gasteiz (AVG).La ley impone obligaciones a las diferentes administraciones públicas de elaboración de inventarios (de edificios, alumbrado público, y parque móvil), inventarios de consumos, auditorías y certificaciones energéticas, así como la elaboración de planes de actuación energética. Establece asimismo para las administraciones públicas objetivos cuantitativos de reducción de su consumo de energía y utilización de energía procedente de fuentes renovables, así como la renovación de instalaciones, equipos, flotas y vehículos.
Se puede acceder a esta normativa en el link:
https://www.boe.es/boe/dias/2019/03/15/pdfs/BOE-A-2019-3705.pdf
Asimismo, se han aprobado sendas leyes, estatal y autonómica, que imponen la obligación de elaborar planes de energía y clima. Se pueden consultar en los siguientes enlaces.
Ley 7/2021, de 20 de mayo, de cambio climático y transición energética. 
https://www.boe.es/buscar/pdf/2021/BOE-A-2021-8447-consolidado.pdf

Simultaneously, private stakeholders are encouraged to act (with tools such as the Environmental Index and the Municipal Master Plan). European union Mission on 100 Climate-neutral and Smart Cities in Europe by 2030 aims to support at least 100 cities to become carbon-neutral by the end of the decade. The City of Turku was selected as one of the 100 frontrunner cities.

Turku updated the Climate Plan that aims to year 2029 in 2022. Over 80 experts from both the City organization and other important stakeholder groups (e.g. local energy company, Universities, industry sector) participated in the process of updating the Climate Plan. Turku met its goal to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by 50 % from the 1990 level by 2021 already in year 2020. During the process of updating the Climate Plan the emission reduction targets were also updated and are now even more ambitious.
- By 2025, emissions will be reduced by at least 75 per cent compared to the level in 1990.
- By 2029, emissions will be reduced by at least 90 per cent compared to the level in 1990.
- By year 2029 at the latest, Turku will reach carbon neutrality. This means that the sum of Turku's emissions, carbon sinks and potential offsets is zero or below.
- From 2029 onwards, Turku strives towards an increasing climate positivity, which means that the sum of local emissions, carbon sinks and compensations is increasingly negative.

- In addition to reducing emissions in the Turku region, we also aim to reduce consumption-related emissions outside the area and to offer good climate solutions that can be used in an area wider than Turku. We will seek to reduce and monitor emissions caused by Turku residents that occur outside the area - the carbon footprint. Reaching the target of the Paris Climate Change Agreement requires significantly reducing consumption-related emissions and minimizing the carbon footprint per capita: adhering to the 1.5-degree lifestyle and strengthening circular economy. In accordance with the city strategy, a sustainable lifestyle and meaningful life go hand in hand in Turku.

As part of the climate plan, a comprehensive climate change risk and vulnerability assessment was carried out in Turku for the first time in 2018. The risk assessment was completed using the model of the Covenant of Mayors. In the analysis, a general view was gained of climate risks posing a threat to Turku. Climate risks refer to potential direct and indirect harm to people, businesses and environment caused by climate, weather and their development. In addition, the city's vulnerabilities i.e., areas in which the city is unable to respond or poorly prepared to respond to changes and extreme weather events caused by global warming, were identified. Both socio-economic factors and physical and environmental factors were identified among vulnerabilities. Finally, those sectors were mapped out that are considered most exposed to changes caused by global warming. 

During the update of the Climate Plan (9/2021-3/2022), the risk analysis has been updated based on new national data, local reports, and expert assessments.

Climate risks were assessed in terms of factors such as the following:
- Likelihood of occurrence (high, moderate, low)
- Level of risk and impact (high, moderate, low)- Expected change in the intensity of the risk (increasing, no change, decreasing)
- Expected change in frequency (increasing, no change, decreasing)
- Timeframe (short-term, mid-term, long-term)
- Sectors affected by the risks
- Vulnerable groups of the population. 

Adaptation measures have been outlined in line with the priorities of UN Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. Turku has joined the Mission Adaptation to Climate Change which aims at supporting regions and communities in Europe towards reaching climate resilience by fostering the development of innovative solutions. 

The consultations regarding risks, vulnerabilities, impacts and adaptation measures involved experts from the University of Turku, Turku University of Applied Sciences, the Centre for Economic Development, Transport and the Environment for Southwest Finland, the Regional Council of Southwest Finland, Valonia, the Natural Resources Institute Finland, the Finnish Environment Institute, the City of Turku and Sitowise Oy. 

More information can be found here: https://issuu.com/turunviestinta/docs/turku_climate_plan_2029/s/17470520

Finland's Climate Act has previously obligated municipalities to draw up a climate plan, and the government has issued guidelines for its implementation. However, the new government has repealed this obligation.

Turku Climate Plan 2029 adheres to the shared SECAP (Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan) model of the European Union. The plan also fulfills the government's recommendations for the content of municipal climate plans in Finland. Turku joined the Covenant of Mayors, a shared climate action movement of European cities and regions in 2010.

One international dimension in Turku's climate work is the EU Mission '100 Climate-neutral and Smart Cities', for which Turku was selected in 2022. The Commission approved the Turku Climate City Contract in March 2024. Turku has invited companies and other operators in the region to sign their own climate commitments as part of the Climate City Contract.

The adaptation component of the NDCs expands its scope by incorporating cross-cutting elements such as Nature-Based Solutions (NBS), Community-Based Adaptation (CBA), Ecosystem-Based Adaptation (EBA), and Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) focused on adaptation. It is divided into five subcomponents:
(a) Prevention and management of negative impacts on human populations and territories.
(b) Resilient production systems (including assessments and programs to address energy poverty) and food security.
(c) Conservation, restoration, and sustainable use of biodiversity and ecosystem services.
(d) Integrated water resource management with a focus on climate change.
(e) Protection of strategic infrastructure and tangible cultural heritage.

Based on the NDCs, climate mitigation targets prioritize the following sectors:
(a) Transport: Promoting clean transportation programs and implementing the National Electric Mobility Strategy.
(b) Power generation: Increasing clean energy integration into the national electric grid.
(c) Residential and commercial: Optimizing energy consumption in homes and businesses and promoting best practices in construction and renovation.
(d) Oil and gas: Enhancing efficiency in refining and processing systems.
(e) Industry: Promoting a circular economy across the entire production system.
(f) Agriculture and livestock: Encouraging best agricultural and conservation practices, agroforestry, agroecological systems, reducing agricultural fires, and adopting bio-digester technologies for livestock residues.
(g) Waste: Focusing on disposal, reuse, recycling, composting, and biodigestion (e.g., biogas from wastewater treatment plants).
(h) Land use, land use change, and forestry: Implementing ecological restoration projects to recover unused and degraded soils.

En el Plan Local de Acción Climática de Córdoba, se presentan las estrategias y acciones de mitigación y adaptación particulares para cada sector en función de la caracterización de impactos y riesgos. Estas estrategias y acciones se han desarrollado en base a un proceso participativo que ha involucrado a diversos actores de la ciudad y la región.
Las medidas de adaptación fueron pensadas y diagramadas en cuatro sectores, biodiversidad-sustentabilidad, transporte, energía y residuos. A continuación se detallan las acciones en cada uno de los sectores:
Sector biodiversidad - sustentabilidad
BS-1. Aumento del arbolado.
BS-2. Campañas de forestación.
BS-3. Promoción de la infraestructura verde urbana haciendo partícipe al ciudadano.
BS-4. Conservación de ecosistemas urbanos en situación vulnerable.
BS-5. Plazas de bolsillo o pequeñas plazas.
BS-6. Disminución de la deforestación.
BS-7. Prevención de incendios forestales.
BS-8. Reducción de pérdidas y desperdicios de alimentos y promoción de la alimentación sustentable y producción local.
BS-9. Incrementar superficies verdes y fuentes de agua para disminuir el efecto de isla de calor:
BS-10. Sensibilización sobre recursos turísticos.
BS-11. Programa Hoteles +Verdes. 
BS-12. Buenas prácticas en eventos municipales. 

Transporte
TP-1. Generar un transporte público cada vez más eficiente.
TP-2. Promover el uso de transporte no motorizado.
TP-3. Impulsar una ciudad policéntrica pensada para el peatón.
TP-4. Conducción eficiente.
TP-5. Incrementar el uso de biocombustibles en flotas municipales.
TP-6. Difusión de los beneficios y ventajas que presentan los biocombustibles. Incrementar los puntos de venta/surtidores de biodiesel y bioetanol.
TP-7. Red Urbana de Movilidad Activa (RUMA). 

Sector energía
EN-1. Aumento de la eficiencia energética en el sector residencial.
EN-2. Plan de eficiencia energética en establecimientos municipales.
EN-3. Etiquetado edilicio.
EN-4. Promoción de la generación de energía distribuida.
EN-5. Iluminación inteligente, luminarias LED y telegestión.
EN-6. Cambios de hábitos de consumo energético residencial.
EN-7. Estaciones solares en plazas, parques y paseos de la ciudad.
EN-8. Muros y techos verdes. 
EN-9. Presentación y difusión del manual de uso racional de energía.
Sector residuos
RS-1. Regulación de bolsas y plásticos de un solo uso.
RS-2. Separación en origen y recolección diferenciada por día.
RS-3. Promover el compostaje domiciliario. 
RS-4. Centros de compostaje y planta de lombricompuesto. 
RS-5. Centros de Transferencia de Residuos (CTR).
RS-6. Programa Sacate las pilas.
RS-7. Residuos de Aparatos Eléctricos y Electrónicos (RAEE).
RS-8. Recuperación de aceite usado.
RS-9. Incentivos para que el sector de la Industria recupere sus residuos.
RS-10. Centros Verdes.
RS-11. Programa Ecoaliados.
RS-12. Promoción de la economía circular. 
RS-13. Fortalecimiento de la cadena de valor de la Economía Circular.
RS-14 Recuperación de metano de enterramientos sanitarios.
RS-15. Generación de energía renovable a partir de biogás proveniente de la EDAR Bajo Grande.
RS-16. Ordenamiento de basurales a cielo abierto.
RS-17. Promover el uso racional del agua.
RS-18. Instalación y operación de una planta de residuos en el predio de piedras blancas. 
RS-19. “ALIMENTOS RESILIENTES” Programa de aprovechamiento y valorización de pérdidas y desperdicios alimentarios (PDA) provenientes de la comercialización de frutas, verduras y hortalizas en Mercados Municipales.

Las medidas de adaptación están basadas en tres ejes de acciones, que son soberanía alimentaria y huerta, enfriamiento urbano y gestión del riesgo de desastre. A continuación se detallan las acciones en cada uno de los ejes mencionados:

SA-2. Expansión de ferias agroecológicas.
SA-3. Proyecto Nuestra Huerta. 
Enfriamiento urbano (EU)

EU-2. Identificación y vigilancia de enfermedades asociadas al ambiente.
EU-3. Pulmones verdes.
Gestión del riesgo de desastre (GR)
GR-1. Elaboración del mapa de inundación y alerta temprana de inundaciones.
GR-2. Difusión de información sobre los efectos del cambio climático en la salud pública local. 
GR-3. Plan de contingencia para el manejo de residuos en caso de emergencias climáticas.
GR-4. Mejorar el mantenimiento de los sistemas de desagües de la ciudad.
GR-5. Recuperación integral del trayecto urbano del Río Suquía en la ciudad de Córdoba.

Cabe señalar que la vinculación del Municipio de Rosario con el gobierno provincial de Santa Fe en temas climáticos, son de colaboración y coordinación, en el marco de la implementación del PLAC y el sistema de monitoreo del PLAC. Se trata de trabajar en conjunto para alcanzar objetivos comunes de mitigación, adaptación y resiliencia. La Constitución Política Estatal establece en el artículo 83, fracción X, que los municipios, a través de sus Ayuntamientos y de conformidad con los acuerdos aprobados
por los mismos, en los términos de las leyes Federales y Estatales, tendrán, entre otras, la facultad de formular y conducir la política ambiental en el ámbito de su
competencia. En tanto que el artículo 85 Ter, fracción IX de dicha disposición constitucional, señala que los municipios, en el ámbito de sus respectivas jurisdicciones
concurrirán con las autoridades estatales y federales, de acuerdo con lo que establezcan las leyes respectivas en materia de protección al medio ambiente.
En ese sentido, para un mejor entendimiento de las atribuciones locales respecto de la elaboración y expedición de un inventario municipal de gases de efecto
invernadero, es necesario revisar el marco concurrente aplicable en materia de equilibrio ecológico y protección al ambiente relacionados con la materia de cambio
climático.
A lo anterior, a nivel nacional, la Ley General del Equilibrio Ecológico y la Protección al Ambiente, señala en el artículo 8, fracción XVI, que corresponden a los Municipios,
de conformidad con lo dispuesto en esta Ley y las leyes locales en la materia, entre otras, la facultad de formular y ejecutar acciones de mitigación y adaptación al cambio
climático.
Por su parte, según el artículo 9, fracciones I, VIII y X de la Ley General de Cambio Climático, corresponde a las entidades federativas, formular, conducir y evaluar la
política municipal en materia de cambio climático en concordancia con la política nacional y estatal; coadyuvar con las autoridades federales y estatales en la
instrumentación de la Estrategia Nacional, el programa y el programa estatal en la materia, así como también, elaborar e integrar, en colaboración con el INECC, la
información de las categorías de Fuentes Emisoras que se originan en su territorio, para su incorporación al Inventario Nacional de Emisiones, conforme a los criterios e
indicadores elaborados por la federación en la materia.
A lo anterior, los artículos 3 fracciones I y XVIII del Reglamento de Protección al Ambiente y del Equilibrio Ecológico del Municipio de Mérida, señalan que son facultades y
obligaciones del Ayuntamiento, por sí o a través del Presidente Municipal y demás dependencias municipales, la de formular, conducir y evaluar la política ambiental del
Municipio y vigilar su aplicación en los planes y programas que se establezcan en la materia, así como la atención de los demás asuntos que en materia de preservación
del equilibrio ecológico y protección al ambiente les concedan otros ordenamientos que no estén otorgados expresamente a la Federación o al Estado.
En el mismo tenor, el artículo 37 fracción III de dicha disposición reglamentaria municipal menciona que compete al Ayuntamiento, en el ámbito de su circunscripción
territorial aquellas funciones que determinen otros ordenamientos aplicables en materia ambiental.
Cabe mencionar que el artículo 2 del Reglamento de Protección al Ambiente y del Equilibrio Ecológico municipal citado, establece claramente que su aplicación
corresponde al Ayuntamiento de Mérida por conducto de:
● El Presidente Municipal.
● La Dirección de Desarrollo Urbano o área encargada.
● La Dirección de Servicios Públicos Municipales o área encargada.
● La Subdirección de Ecología y Residuos Sólidos o área encargada.
● A los demás servidores públicos que se indiquen en dicho reglamento y demás disposiciones legales aplicables en el ámbito de su competencia.
En esta lógica, el artículo 24 fracción XVIII de la Ley de Cambio Climático del Estado de Yucatán, determina que además de las atribuciones para los municipios señaladas
en el artículo 9 de la LGCC, le compete, entre otras, la de elaborar e integrar, en colaboración con el Gobierno del Estado de Yucatán, la información de las categorías de
fuentes emisoras que se originan en su territorio, para su incorporación al Inventario Estatal, conforme a los criterios e indicadores elaborados por la federación en la

Ayuntamiento de Mérida, a través de la Dirección de Desarrollo Sustentable, iniciaron las bases para la prevención del riesgo con la publicación del Atlas de Riesgos del Municipio de Mérida 2015-2018, particularmente enfocado a la identificación y análisis de riesgos físicos e hidrometeorológicos ante condiciones de cambio climático. En continuidad a estos trabajos, se presenta la actualización Atlas de Riesgos del municipio de Mérida, Yucatán, que incorpora la identificación de fenómenos no analizados en la edición anterior, particularmente en relación con el tema de inundaciones Estudio de Riesgos y Vulnerabilidad al Cambio Climático del Municipio de Mérida, Yucatán 2 pluviales, hundimientos, y otros fenómenos de origen antropogénico, como el almacenamiento y transporte de sustancias peligrosas, o las concentraciones masivas de población. De esta forma, se refuerza la política de gestión de riesgo en el municipio de Mérida, incorporando información más actualizada, y el análisis de fenómenos de reciente aparición o intensificación, derivado de las condiciones climáticas, el crecimiento y densificación de las zonas urbanas, y la construcción de nueva infraestructura. Por otro lado, la resiliencia se entiende como la “capacidad de un sistema, comunidad o sociedad expuestos a una amenaza para resistir, absorber, adaptarse y recuperarse de sus efectos de manera oportuna y eficaz, lo que incluye la preservación y la restauración de sus estructuras y funciones básicas” (UNDRR, 2023). Mientras que la Ley General de Protección Civil (LGPC) define la resiliencia como “la capacidad de un sistema, comunidad o sociedad potencialmente expuesta a un peligro para resistir, asimilar, adaptarse y recuperarse de sus efectos en un corto plazo y de manera eficiente, a través de la preservación y restauración de sus estructuras básicas y funcionales, logrando una mejor protección futura y mejorando las medidas de reducción de riesgos” (LGPC, 2021). Además, la LGPC resalta a la resiliencia de las comunidades como una prioridad, tanto de la reducción de riesgos como de la Gestión Integral de Riesgos.

El PACMUN es clave en la estrategia municipal para combatir el cambio climático y reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero. Se apoya en diversas políticas y marcos legales, que son fundamentales para coordinar acciones efectivas en los sectores público y privado.

Acuerdo de Escazú: Adoptado en 2018 por 24 países, este acuerdo busca garantizar derechos de acceso a información ambiental y participación pública en decisiones ambientales en América Latina y el Caribe. Es un hito al incluir protección específica para defensores de derechos humanos en temas ambientales. México, al ratificar el acuerdo en 2020, reafirma su compromiso con el multilateralismo y la protección del medio ambiente. Los principios que rigen el acuerdo incluyen igualdad, transparencia, y equidad intergeneracional.

Política de Cambio Climático en México: El país enfrenta un compromiso urgente para reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero y restaurar ecosistemas, considerando las vulnerabilidades sociales y económicas de su población. La Estrategia Nacional de Cambio Climático, actualizada para alinearse con el 
Acuerdo de París y la Agenda 2030: se centra en tres componentes: mitigación, adaptación y transversalidad.

Mitigación: Transformar la economía hacia bajas emisiones de carbono.
Adaptación: Fortalecer la resiliencia de sistemas sociales y productivos.
Transversalidad: Integrar la acción climática a través de coordinación y participación social.
El éxito de esta estrategia depende de la colaboración de todos los sectores de la sociedad, así como de la integración de las políticas climáticas en los diferentes niveles de gobierno.

Programa Especial de Acción ante el Cambio Climático (PECC) 2021-2024
El PECC establece un plan a seis años para adaptarse y mitigar los efectos del cambio climático, alineado con la Ley General de Cambio Climático. Presenta cuatro objetivos prioritarios:

1. Reducir la vulnerabilidad de la población y ecosistemas.
2. Disminuir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero.
3. Promover políticas que integren mitigación y adaptación.
4. Mejorar la coordinación y financiamiento entre niveles de gobierno.

column17:
En el marco de los compromisos asumidos por México en el Acuerdo de París del 2015 
para mitigar las emisiones de Gases y Compuestos de Efecto Invernadero, el desafío del cambio climático se erige como uno de los principales retos para los estados de la República y la economía mexicana en su conjunto. Estas acciones representan una valiosa oportunidad para impulsar la transición hacia un modelo de crecimiento sostenible, caracterizado por su baja emisión de carbono y la eficiente gestión de los recursos naturales. Mérida, comprometida a ser una ciudad neto cero para 2050, ejemplifica esta iniciativa con sus ambiciosos objetivos de descarbonización.

En virtud del artículo 9, fracción X, de la Ley General de Cambio Climático (LGCC) publicada en junio del 2012, se asigna a los estados y municipios la responsabilidad de elaborar y consolidar información sobre las Fuentes Emisoras presentes en su territorio. Para que estos puedan adoptar medidas de mitigación efectivas y económicamente beneficiosas, es necesario contar con herramientas que permitan cuantificar las emisiones de Gases y Compuestos de Efecto Invernadero (GYCEI), lo cual se logra mediante el desarrollo de inventarios específicos de estas emisiones. Este enfoque no solo facilita la identificación de áreas prioritarias para la mitigación, sino que también posibilita el establecimiento de indicadores y metas que faciliten el seguimiento y evaluación del progreso.

Las nuevas estrategias identificadas se desarrollaron utilizando la metodología SMART 
(Específica, Medible, Alcanzable, Realista y con un Tiempo definido). Esta metodología 
se eligió porque facilita un control detallado a través de un sistema de monitoreo, reporte 
y verificación (MRV), asegurando que los datos y resultados sean más confiables para 
los responsables de la implementación en cada área (ICLEI 2024). Las nuevas medidas 
se suman a las existentes, reflejando la necesidad de reforzar y continuar implementando las estrategias ya establecidas.

El resultado del análisis en conjunto fueron medidas para los cuatro sectores, residuos, movilidad, forestal y energía. Para el sector residuos se identificaron 4 estrategias y 14 líneas de acción. Del sector movilidad se identificaron 4 estrategias y 14 líneas de acción. En el sector forestal se identificaron 3 estrategias y 10 líneas de acción. Por último, del sector de energía se identificaron 4 estrategias y 8 líneas de acción.

El Módulo de Adaptación al Cambio Climático de Mérida detalla las medidas y acciones 
específicas, medibles y alineadas a las atribuciones municipales. Involucra a los tres 
niveles de gobierno y otros actores clave para la implementación y evaluación de las 
medidas de adaptación. La metodología utilizada incluye (GIZ, 2024) :
1.Revisión Bibliográfica : Se analizaron documentos normativos, de planeación y métodos 
de adaptación al cambio climático. 
2. Diagnóstico Previo : Se utilizó información del diagnóstico previo sobre adaptación 
al cambio climático en Mérida conjunto a la elaboración del Estudio de Riesgos y 
Vulnerabilidad de Mérida. 
3. Entrevistas Semiestructuradas : Se realizaron entrevistas que abordan conocimientos 
sobre adaptación al cambio climático, marco legal, coordinación interinstitucional, 
evaluación y monitoreo de políticas públicas. Se identificaron cuatro actores principales: 
departamentos gubernamentales estatal y municipal, academia y organizaciones no 
gubernamentales.
4. Taller Participativo : Se facilitó un taller participativo con actores clave identificados, 
utilizando el análisis multicriterio (Dirección de Cambio Climático; Ministerio de Medio 
Ambiente y Energía, 2021) para identificar y priorizar medidas de adaptación basadas en 
el ERVCC. Este enfoque promueve la transparencia, equidad y legitimidad.
5. Identificación y Priorización de Medidas : Durante el taller, se priorizaron 12 medidas 
de adaptación para Mérida, basadas en seis criterios: Eficiencia (18%), Solidez (15%), 
Practicidad (16%), Legitimidad (15%), Sinergia (11%) y el estatus en el ERVCC (25%). La 
atribución del municipio en cada medida se verificó con el Reglamento de la Administración 
Pública Municipal.

Los resultados del taller participativo sobre adaptación al Cambio Climático han destacado 
la priorización y desarrollo de 10 nuevas medidas de adaptación para el Municipio de 
Mérida. Actualmente, contamos con 15 medidas de adaptación en fase de implementación 
(ver Anexo), las cuales se están reforzando cada año con evaluaciones y mejoras 
continuas. Además, se están planteando nuevas propuestas en fase de planeación para 
garantizar que Mérida no solo se adapte de manera efectiva al cambio climático, sino 
que también lidere con ejemplo en la creación de una ciudad más resiliente y sostenible.

Medidas de Adaptación:
1. Resiliencia de infraestructura
2. Gestión sostenible del agua
3. Adaptación agrícola y seguridad alimentaria
4. Conservación y restauración de ecosistemas
5. Desarrollo de infraestructura verde y planificación urbana resiliente
6. Fortalecimiento de sistemas de alerta temprana y gestión del riesgo de desastres
7. Promoción de tecnologías limpias y energías renovables
8. Educación, sensibilización y capacitación
9. Género y grupos vulnerables en la adaptación al Cambio Climático
10. Financiamiento para la Adaptación al Cambio Climático.

Durante 2024, el Municipio de Saltillo se adhirió al Programa Feral de Acciones de Infraestructura, Operación y Mejoramiento de Eficiencia de Saneamiento (PROSANEAR), cuyo objetivo es la asignación de recursos federales provenientes del pago de derechos por el uso o aprovechamiento de bienes del dominio público de la Nación como cuerpos receptores de las descargas de aguas residuales con las siguientes acciones:
1. Infraestructura de saneamiento: 
-Construcción, ampliación y rehabilitación de infraestructura para la recolección, conducción, saneamiento y disposición de las aguas residuales generadas en los centros de población.
-Recolección, saneamiento y disposición de lodos producidos durante el proceso de tratamiento.
-Producción y captación de biogás, y a partir de éste, la cogeneración de energía eléctrica para autoconsumo.
-Reúso, reutilización e intercambio del agua residual tratada.

2. Operación de saneamiento:
-Acciones necesarias para que el saneamiento de aguas residuales cumpla con los parámetros establecidos en el permiso de descarga, en las Normas Oficiales Mexicanas aplicables o con el estudio de clasificación de corrientes, en lo concerniente a DQO y SST.

column17: The City actively engages with regional partners in southern Nevada and across the state. The All-In Regional Climate Collaborative of Southern Nevada (RCC) was initiated in January 2024 to identify as a priority action in the All-In Clark County Sustainability and Climate Action Plan. The primary goals of the RCC are to: Foster Convening and Capacity Building; Deliver Regional Public Education and Outreach; Take Action on Climate Solutions; Share and Leverage Regional Climate Collaborative participating entities including Clark County, the five cities within Clark County (Boulder City, Henderson, Las Vegas, North Las Vegas, and Mesquite), the Southern Nevada Water Authority (SNWA), and the Regional Transportation Commission (RTC) of Southern Nevada. Other recent collaborations with key stakeholders include the Southern Nevada Clean Cities Coalition, Nevada Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, Nevada Department of Environmental Protection, Nevada Department of Wildlife, Nevada Department of Agriculture, Nevada Department of Transportation, Colorado River Commission, Public Utilities Commission of Nevada, NV Clinicians for Climate Action, Las Vegas Valley Water District (LVVWD), NV Energy, Southwest Gas, Republic Services, NV Clean Energy Fund (NCEF), NV Conservation League, University of Reno & Northern NV Coalition. Since January 2024, the RCC hosted 14 working sessions to review the Climate Pollution Reduction Grants (CPRG) requirements, discuss updated data and analyses for the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) inventory, identify high impact strategies for the Priority Climate Action Plan (PCAP), and develop and implement a communications and engagement strategy. The City of Henderson chairs several groups with All-In Clark County, including the Legislative and Local Policy Watch Working Group and as the advisory chair for the Southern Nevada Clean Cities Coalition.

column17: In 2016 The City of Saint Paul and Ramsey County collaborated on the development of the Saint Paul - Ramsey County Public Health Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment. https://www.ramseycounty.us/sites/default/files/Departments/Public%20Health/ccva_final.pdfIn accordance with its 2014-2018 Strategic Plan, Saint Paul- Ramsey County Public Health (SPRCPH) conducted a climate change vulnerability assessment (CCVA) to identify populations and geographic areas that may be especially susceptible to the negative effects of climate change at the local level.The goals of this report are to:- communicate climate change trends in Ramsey County;- explain how these trends directly and indirectly affect human health;- identify characteristics that increase individual vulnerability to the effects of climate change; and- demonstrate geographic regions of vulnerability in the county using a variety of maps.The purpose of this report is to serve as an informational resource to aid in the conversation regarding the development of climate change adaptation measures in Ramsey County.- Adaptation refers to strategies to promote risk communication, community and infrastructure planning, and emergency preparedness in order to prepare for the effects of climate change.- Vulnerability refers to the characteristics and situation of a person or group that negatively affect their ability to anticipate, adapt to, and recover from the effects of a climate hazard (e.g., low socioeconomic status, limited education, pre-existing physical or mental health illnesses, barriers in communication, and very old or very young age).- Environmental risk factors refer to aspects of the environment that increase the negative impact of a climate hazard; they are independent of population characteristics.Vulnerability is combined with environmental risk factors to describe the overall impact of a climate hazard.VULNERABILITY + ENVIRONMENTAL RISK FACTORS = IMPACTThe assessment focused on six topics related to climate change and vulnerability in Ramsey County:- Extreme heat events- Poor Air Quality- Changes in Precipitation- Changing Ecologies- Changing Demographics- Psychological Impacts. The County has completed and is preparing to release an update of the Vulnerability Assessment.

Em 2019 o Município de Matosinhos renovou o seu compromisso nomeadamente em relação ao Pacto dos Autarcas para o Clima e Energia adicionando à vertente de mitigação a componente de adaptação às alterações climáticas. 
Desta forma, o Município de Matosinhos desenvolveu em 2018 a sua Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMAAC). 
No âmbito da elaboração da EMAAC foi realizado um levantamento das vulnerabilidades climáticas locais, para perceber como estes eventos adversos afetaram as atividades, as pessoas e as infraestruturas do concelho. 
Em 2021, e no âmbito do desenvolvimento Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e Clima (PAESC) foram identificados os riscos previamente destacados na EMAAC, estando definida como uma das opções de adaptação (AO) deste novo plano a atualização periódica da análise de riscos e objetivos/opções de adaptação (OA1). 
Esta avaliação requer o envolvimento de diferentes departamentos e unidades municipais, bem como entidades locais com atuação em diferentes setores.

O Plano Municipal de Ação Climática constitui-se como um instrumento de política local em matéria de mitigação, adaptação, erradicação da pobreza energética e promoção da qualidade de vida e bem-estar dos matosinhenses - matérias que, na sua maioria, já integravam o Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e Clima (PAESC) - dando resposta simultaneamente aos requisitos da Lei de Bases do Clima (Lei n.º 98/2021, de 31 de dezembro) e antecipando as suas metas, guiando o caminho de Matosinhos rumo à neutralidade carbónica em 2030.
O seu desenvolvimento contou com diferentes iniciativas de participação multinível e cocriação, nomeadamente com envolvimento dos representantes das quatro Uniões de Freguesia, vários serviços municipais, empresas municipais, a Agência de Energia do Porto (AdEPorto), a Presidente da Câmara Municipal e um conjunto de Vereadores dos pelouros mais pertinentes para a ação climática. 
Também a sua implementação e monitorização é baseada num modelo multinível, integrado e colaborativo. A concretização do cenário da neutralidade carbónica em 2030 depende de uma relevante articulação entre diferentes entidades públicas e privadas.

A Câmara Municipal de Matosinhos traçou como objetivo reduzir em 85% as emissões de carbono até 2030, antecipando a meta de descarbonização prevista a nível nacional para 2045. 
Esta ambição supera as metas estabelecidas pela Lei de Bases do Clima (Lei n.º 98/2021, de 31 de dezembro), no qual se estabelece a necessidade de redução de emissões de gases de efeito de estufa em, pelo menos, 55%, até 2030, entre 65% e 75% até 2040 e, pelo menos, 90% até 2050, face aos níveis de 2005. 
Este compromisso é firmado no Roteiro para a Neutralidade Carbónica Matosinhos 2030/Plano Municipal de Ação Climática.
O seu desenvolvimento contou com diferentes iniciativas de participação multinível e cocriação, nomeadamente com envolvimento dos representantes das quatro Uniões de Freguesia, vários serviços municipais, empresas municipais, a Agência de Energia do Porto (AdEPorto), a Presidente da Câmara Municipal e um conjunto de Vereadores dos pelouros mais pertinentes para a ação climática.

column17: The City of Fort Lauderdale participates in the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact which was founded by the four counties in Southeast Florida. The Compact generates regional sea level rise projections every five years which Fort Lauderdale officially adopts. The Compact also hosts an annual summit and multiple education events throughout the year for local governments. Broward County conducted the 2014 vulnerability assessment for multiple cities in the region including Fort Lauderdale. The City also collaborates with the State of Florida, such as through grant opportunities which will fund an updated citywide vulnerability assessment. The City works with the regional South Florida Water Management District on monitoring the saltwater intrusion line movement toward our potable water wellfields. The City also completes annual surveys for the Compact summarizing its climate mitigation and adaptation actions. In addition, in September 2024, the City completed a citywide Vulnerability Assessment incorporating over 30 models for sea level rise, storm surge and precipitation events addressing potential impacts on critical assets such as vital stormwater and transportation infrastructure consistent with state requirements. The results show flood risk is significantly elevated in low-lying areas and local economy and vulnerable populations can be adversely affected due to sea level rise, storm surges, and high tides, so implementation of adaptation strategies is crucial for the City of Fort Lauderdale to become a more resilient community.

One key aspect of their collaboration includes the integration of regional transportation and infrastructure planning with Fayetteville's climate objectives, such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing community resilience against climate impacts. The NWARPC's involvement helps Fayetteville to develop comprehensive strategies that address both local and regional needs, making climate action more effective and wide-reaching.

In addition to regional coordination, the City of Fayetteville actively engages the public and gathers input through various events and online platforms to shape its Climate Action Plan, which emphasizes clean energy, waste reduction, and nature-based solutions. Fayetteville, Arkansas, has played a pivotal role in helping the Northwest Arkansas Regional Planning Commission (NWARPC) develop its Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions inventory by providing critical data, technical expertise, and support in the inventory process. As a city that has been actively involved in sustainability efforts, Fayetteville has a well-established system for tracking and reducing GHG emissions, which has served as a model for other communities within the NWARPC.

Data Sharing and Methodology: Fayetteville has shared its methodologies for calculating GHG emissions with the NWARPC. This includes data collection techniques, emission factor selection, and best practices for accuracy and consistency. The city's experience with developing its own GHG inventory, as part of its Climate Action Plan, has provided a framework that the NWARPC could adapt for broader regional use.

Technical Expertise: The city's Sustainability Department, led by experts such as Peter Nierengarten, has collaborated with the NWARPC to ensure the technical aspects of the GHG inventory are robust. Fayetteville's expertise in areas such as energy consumption, waste management, and transportation emissions has been crucial in helping the NWARPC develop a comprehensive inventory that covers multiple sectors across the region.

Regional Coordination: Fayetteville's active participation in regional sustainability efforts, including its work with the NWARPC, has helped align the GHG inventory process with broader regional goals. The city's involvement ensures that the inventory reflects not only the emissions within Fayetteville but also contributes to a cohesive strategy across Northwest Arkansas, which is essential for regional planning and policy-making.

Public Engagement and Transparency: Fayetteville has also emphasized the importance of public engagement and transparency in the GHG inventory process. By sharing its approach to involving residents and stakeholders in understanding and reducing GHG emissions, Fayetteville has helped the NWARPC incorporate similar strategies, making the regional inventory more inclusive and effective.

Overall, Fayetteville's contributions have been instrumental in shaping the NWARPC's GHG emissions inventory, providing a strong foundation for ongoing regional climate action efforts.

column17: The City of St. John's collaborated with both the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador and Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) on the Atlantic Canada Storm Surge and Wave Modelling Climate Impact Study. Funded through NRCan's Climate Resilient Coastal Communities Program, this study focused on assessing the impacts of climate change on coastal communities across the Northern Avalon Peninsula, including St. John's Harbour, Portugal Cove-St. Philip's, and Conception Bay South. The City of Knoxville collaborates with Knox County and the Town of Farragut to produce a Multi-Jurisdictional Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (HMP). The HMP identifies and profiles 12 natural hazards (dam failure, drought, earthquake, expansive soils, extreme temperatures, flood, land subsidence/sinkholes, landslide, severe storms, tornadoes, wildfire, and winter storms) across the County. The risk assessment also estimates the
exposure of lives, property, and infrastructure to these hazards.

The planning process followed a methodology prescribed by FEMA, which included a Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee that identified and profiled hazards that pose a risk to the planning area, assessed the vulnerability to these hazards, and examined the capabilities in place to mitigate them. The HMPC identified goals for reducing hazard risks, recommended mitigation actions to meet those goals, and developed an implementation plan for each action. The participating jurisdictions developed this
plan pursuant to the requirements of the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 (Public Law 106-390) and the implementing regulations set forth by the Interim Final Rule published in the Federal Register in 2002 (44 CFR §201.6) and finalized in 2007 to achieve eligibility for the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Hazard Mitigation Assistance (HMA) programs.

The Plan was formally adopted by City and County Commissions in 2018 and was updated in 2025. Progress reports are also published periodically. Details can be found at https://www.knoxcounty.org/stormwater/fema_mitigation.php.

In 2020, Mayor Kincannon convened the Mayor's Climate Council to identify and evaluate strategies to achieve the community-wide emission reduction goal established by Council in 2019. The cross-sector group of over 65 members included clean energy experts, conservation activists, advocates for equity, neighborhood representatives, developers, business leaders, utility representatives, and more. Representatives from Knox County, University of Tennessee, Tennessee Valley Authority, and Oak Ridge National Lab actively participated.

Council members and working groups (transportation, buildings/energy, waste, and equity) evaluated dozens of proven high-impact strategies for their impact to climate,
economy, and community. Specifically, strategies were ranked based not only on emission reduction but also impact on equity and other societal benefits (air quality, public
health, mobility and access, housing affordability, human services, and civic engagement). The strategies ranked highest by the Council across transportation, buildings/energy, and waste formed the basis for the City's 2021 Energy & Sustainability Work Plan, which directs the Office of Sustainability's work and more.

Even after the Work Plan was adopted, the Office of Sustainability continues to engage external experts from state (TN Department of Environment and Conservation, TN Department of Transportation) and federal (TN Valley Authority, Oak Ridge National Lab) agencies on climate activities.

The City of Sunnyvale develops community-wide greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions inventories to measure progress toward its climate mitigation goals. These inventories are not only a local planning tool but also align with and support goals of higher levels of government. California mandates ongoing emissions tracking (at the state level) to evaluate progress toward statewide reduction targets established under AB32 and AB1279. To ensure consistency, Sunnyvale follows state-recommended methodologies, and its inventories are integrated into regional and federal climate programs.

Sunnyvale has published GHG inventories for 2021 and 2022, which demonstrate measurable reductions in emissions compared to the City's 1990 baseline. These inventories are also a core component of Sunnyvale's Climate Action Playbook (CAP), providing the data foundation for setting priorities, evaluating effectiveness, and reporting progress to the community and state authorities. More details are available on the City's Sustainability webpage:
https://www.sunnyvale.ca.gov/your-government/city-initiatives/sustainability

In addition, Santa Clara County's Community Climate Roadmap 2035 provides county-wide GHG inventories and long-range emissions forecasts. Sunnyvale contributes data to this effort, which allows the City's local actions to be integrated into a broader regional framework. The Climate Roadmap coordinates climate strategies across all cities in the county, aligning them with California's statewide climate goals and ensuring that individual city plans are part of a larger, coherent regional response. More details can be found on the County's sustainability website:

column17: As Boulder has continued to pursue its locally based climate activities, it's become clear that federal, state, and local energy and environmental policies do not occur in isolation. Instead, they frequently involve the sharing of responsibility. In 2021, the state released its Greenhouse Gas Pollution Reduction Roadmap. The roadmap represents the most action-oriented, ambitious, and substantive planning process that Colorado has ever undertaken on climate leadership, pollution reduction and a clean energy transition. It lays out an achievable pathway to meet the state's science-based climate targets of 26% by 2025, 50% by 2030 and 90% by 2050 from 2005 levels that were part of House Bill 19-1261 Climate Action Plan to Reduce Pollution. The release of the Roadmap in Colorado recognizes that rather than taking a backseat, state leadership must continue alongside a more supportive federal government, allowing the United States to achieve deeper emissions reductions through a framework that leverages comparative strengths at different levels of governance. Beyond working at the State level, Boulder has also been a national leader in exploring the use of the legal system in pushing for larger systems-level change. Both through its active participation in multi-jurisdiction efforts — like the Clean Power Plan Plaintiffs group — or its climate liability lawsuit with Boulder and San Miguel Counties against ExxonMobil and Suncor, Boulder has demonstrated that there are a range of different levers cities can take hold of to drive more fundamental systems change. The city was a founding member of CC4CA, which advocates for stronger state and federal climate policy. Annually, Boulder's City Council adopts a formal Policy Statement on Regional, State and Federal Issues, which informs the city's position and lobbying efforts at both the state and federal legislature. Climate-specific policy positions are prominently featured.

column17: Through the Environmental Protection Agency's Climate Pollution Reduction Grant program, the Denver-Aurora-Lakewood Metropolitan Statistical Area received a $1 million planning grant to develop climate action plans in coordination with stakeholders throughout the region, including the City of Boulder. In March 2024, the Denver Regional Council of Governments (DRCOG) Priority Climate Action Plan, the first deliverable for the Climate Pollution Reduction Grants program, was completed. It includes a greenhouse gas inventory, a workforce planning analysis and climate pollution reduction measures, including an assessment of the positive effects the measures will have on low-income and disadvantaged communities and a review of the authority to implement the measures. In July 2024, DRCOG was awarded a $199.7 million implementation grant through the CPRG program that will improve 60,000 homes and businesses across the region with a particular focus on low-income and disadvantaged communities, leading to a nearly 150 million metric ton reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. The initiative will replace fossil fuel-burning appliances in homes and businesses and foster a future-forward workforce, enhancing public health, spurring innovation and invigorating the economy. Boulder served as a principal in developing the grant and is contributing cost share in the form of both staff support and rebate funding.

Keterlibatan Kota Medan dalam Program ProKlim

1. Pencapaian Wilayah ProKlim
Kota Medan memiliki beberapa kelurahan yang telah terdaftar dan aktif dalam Program ProKlim, di antaranya:
a. Kelurahan PB Selayang I, Kecamatan Medan Selayang
b. Kelurahan Sidomulyo, Kecamatan Medan Tuntungan
c. Kelurahan Terjun, Kecamatan Medan Marelan
Wilayah-wilayah ini telah melaksanakan berbagai aksi seperti pengelolaan sampah terpadu, penanaman pohon, konservasi air, dan edukasi iklim kepada masyarakat.

2. Pengakuan Tingkat Nasional
Kelurahan Belawan Sicanang Kecamatan Medan Belawab telah menerima penghargaan dari Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup untuk kategori Lokasi Proklim Kategori Utama pada tanggal 11 Agustus 2024, yang menandakan pengakuan terhadap upaya adaptasi dan mitigasi berbasis komunitas yang dijalankan secara konsisten dan inovatif.

3. Sosialisasi & Pendampingan oleh DLH Medan
Dinas Lingkungan Hidup Kota Medan aktif menyosialisasikan dan membina kelurahan-kelurahan untuk mengikuti ProKlim, termasuk dengan memberikan pelatihan, bantuan teknis, serta memfasilitasi proses pendaftaran ke sistem nasional Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup.
DLH juga mendorong pelibatan warga, kelompok PKK, karang taruna, sekolah, dan tokoh masyarakat agar semua elemen ikut terlibat dalam aksi iklim lokal.

4. Jenis Aksi Iklim yang Dilakukan
Aksi adaptasi: seperti biopori, sumur resapan, pengendalian banjir lokal, pemanenan air hujan.
Aksi mitigasi: komposting, bank sampah, urban farming, dan penanaman pohon penyerap karbon.

5. Rencana Perluasan
Pemerintah Kota Medan menargetkan lebih banyak kelurahan masuk dalam daftar ProKlim setiap tahunnya.
ProKlim dijadikan sebagai indikator kinerja lingkungan hidup daerah, serta diintegrasikan ke dalam program kegiatan OPD lain seperti ketahanan pangan, kesehatan lingkungan, dan sanitasi.
