Keterlibatan Kota Medan melalui Pelaporan ke SIPSN

SIPSN (https://sipsn.menlhk.go.id/) adalah sistem daring nasional yang dikembangkan oleh Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup untuk memantau dan mengevaluasi data pengelolaan sampah dari seluruh kota/kabupaten di Indonesia. Data ini digunakan untuk merumuskan kebijakan nasional, menghitung capaian target pengurangan sampah 30% dan penanganan 70% pada tahun 2025 sesuai amanat Perpres No. 97 Tahun 2017.

Setiap tahun, Pemerintah Kota Medan melaporkan data meliputi:
a. Jumlah timbulan sampah harian	: Berapa ton sampah dihasilkan per hari
b. Komposisi jenis sampah : Organik, plastik, logam, kertas, B3 rumah tangga, dll
c. Jumlah sampah terangkut dan tertangani :	Termasuk yang masuk ke TPA, bank sampah, kompos, dll 
d. Jumlah TPS, TPS3R, Bank Sampah : Fasilitas pengelolaan berbasis masyarakat
e. Data pengangkutan dan daur ulang : Volume yang dikelola dan diolah kembali

Tahun 2024, volume timbulan sampah Kota Medan mencapai ±2.000 ton per hari, yang dibuang ke TPA Terjun.

Manfaat Pelaporan ini:
1. Mendukung pengambilan keputusan nasional dan daerah terkait kebijakan pengelolaan sampah.
2. Menjadi dasar evaluasi kinerja daerah, termasuk insentif untuk program seperti Adipura.
3. Menghubungkan Kota Medan dengan pemerintah pusat dalam program dukungan seperti bantuan alat, pelatihan teknis, dan pendanaan sanitasi.
4. Meningkatkan transparansi dan akuntabilitas, karena data dapat diakses publik melalui dashboard SIPSN.

市域を超えた広域連携
CO2は市域内の活動だけで排出されるものではなく、国外も含む市域外でのあらゆる活動において排出されます。
脱炭素社会の実現に向けては、市域を超えて広域的に取組を進めていくことも重要となるため、近隣都市や再エネポテンシャルを有している地域等と連携した広域的な取組を推進します。
特に九都県市（埼玉県、千葉県、東京都、神奈川県、横浜市、千葉市、さいたま市、相模原市、川崎市）の首長で構成される九都県市首脳会議の「九都県市地球温暖化対策特別部会」では、地球環境の保全に係る国際協力及び普及啓発等の調査・検討に関すること、省資源、省エネルギー等に配慮した環境保全型の都市づくりの調査・検討に関することなどについて、九都県市で連携し、さまざまな取組を進めています。

column17: The Amman City Climate Change Risk Assessment has been executed following the structured methodologies of C40 CCRA and IPCC. These methodologies offer a systematic framework for cities to evaluate their susceptibility and exposure to climate-related hazards while pinpointing adaptive measures. Ensuring an all-encompassing approach, this assessment is grounded in gender inclusivity and leaves no individual or locale overlooked, contingent upon data availability. This comprehensive approach ensures a holistic understanding of Amman's climate change risks, reinforcing the city's ability to forge informed and effective strategies for a more resilient future. The assessment employs an intricate blend of qualitative and quantitative strategies, encompassing the following methodologies: •\tDesk Review: Thorough analysis of Amman City's institutional strategies, policies, and ongoing projects. •\tStakeholder Interviews: Engaging with key stakeholders including the Greater Amman Municipality, Miyahuna (Water Company), and pertinent units within the Ministry of Health. •\tFocus Group Discussions: Collaborative interactions with technical and managerial personnel from the Greater Amman Municipality. (see Annex I for list of attendees) •\tGIS Mapping: Harnessing remote sensing data—especially climatic projections from Jordan's Fourth National Communication Report—to facilitate climate impact assessments across diverse sectors. Furthermore, spatial indicators encompassing demographics, socioeconomics, urban planning, infrastructure, health, and more are meticulously mapped using GIS tools. Data sources for this assessment encompass a diverse range of entities, including: •\tVarious departments within the Greater Amman Municipality, such as Geographic Information System (GIS), Amman Urban Observatory, Comprehensive Planning, Highways, Public Transportation, Engineering, and Sustainability, among others. •\tJordan Water Company L.L.C - MIYAHUNA, with inputs from the Operations Directorate and GIS Department. •\tProjects affiliated with UN agencies, like the Sustainable Urbanization and Resource Efficiency in Greater Amman Municipality (SURE) Project by UNDP, and initiatives by UN-Habitat focused on enhancing social stability and resilience against flash floods. •\tNon-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) involved in endeavours like the Green Infrastructure (ILCA) project aimed at improving living conditions in disadvantaged areas, the Ghabawi Municipal Solid Waste Management Landfill Project backed by EBRD and the World Bank, and the Jordan Biogas Project. CLIMATE CHANGE RISK ASSESSMENT PROCESS: Climate Hazard Identification: The initial phase entails the recognition and examination of various climate hazard categories that a city is anticipated to encounter as a result of climate change. These hazards encompass, but are not limited to, exceptionally high temperatures, water scarcity, flooding, and biological risks. Therefore, ACCRA Coordination and management team have identified Heat waves, Flash floods, Drought, and Borne diseases as four priority climate hazards to be explored in this risk assessment. Spatial Indicators Analysis: Building upon the existing dataset, a panel of experts curated and ratified a set of specific indicators, precisely reviewed and approved by the GAM resilience unit. These indicators span a range of domains, including demographics, socioeconomics, urban planning, infrastructure, water and wastewater systems, energy, solid waste management, health, and emergency response. Climate Hazard Assessment: A practical evaluation grounded in scientific evidence, this phase delves into historical climate data, climate model projections, and comprehension of anticipated climate scenarios. This assessment gauges the gravity and recurrence of hazard types over three distinct timeframes: short-term (up to 2050), medium-term (2050-2070), and long-term (2070-2100). These evaluations are conducted under both moderate and high greenhouse gas emissions scenarios (RCP4.5 and RCP8.5), encompassing all 22 districts of Amman. Projected climatic data originates from Jordan's Fourth National Communication Report, and each data point is subjected to expert-driven scoring and weighting. These evaluations are further informed by expert deliberations, consultations, and a discerning assessment of the impact of various hazard types, considering historical trends and the city's present circumstances. Climate Vulnerability Assessment: This phase appraises the susceptibility and resilience of a system in the face of adverse climate impacts, spanning climate variability and extremes. It employs an indicator-based analysis to gauge the exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity of individuals, urban systems, and services.

column17: Jordan's Economic Modernisation Vision centers on the slogan of “A Better Future”, and is based on two strategic pillars:- accelerated growth through unleashing Jordan's full economic potential;- improved quality of life for all citizens, while sustainability is a cornerstone of this future vision.The vision will be implemented through eight economic growth drivers, covering 35 main sectors and sub-sectors and more than 360 initiatives. One of the strategic drivers is \'Green Jordan\' which aims at Supporting sustainable practices as a pillar of Jordan's future economic growth and enhancing quality of life.The Economic Modernisation Vision seeks to:1. Ensure transparency in providing information related to national goals and priorities.2. Determine comparative and competitive advantages that Jordan can capitalise on to stimulate growth and create economic opportunities.3. Unify efforts of ministries and public institutions to support the achievement of the national strategic goals within a clear roadmap.4. Direct national planning towards strategic thinking to ensure the delivery of national goals in a better and sustainable manner than being achieved through tactical actions.5. Enhance decision-making and policy development to make it data-driven and evidence-based to minimise changes and populist decisions to ensure more strategic decisions.6. Strengthen the capacity for accountability and follow-up, and enable necessary interventions to improve the implementation process and performance measurement.7. Propose a roadmap for political parties to interact with when developing their programmes or suggest alternatives that are in line with the vision priorities.8. Enrich the cooperation agenda with Jordan's development partners to direct support towards the priorities set by the vision.As the main challenge lies in implementation, particular focus was placed on developing a mechanism responsible for rigorous follow-up on vision execution across all sectors, and enable taking the required steps to ensure continuity of implementation and overcoming any obstacles thereof. This necessitates strengthening the roles of the Prime Ministry Delivery Unit (PMDU) and deliveryunits in ministries and public institutions (including Greater Amman Municipality), as well as support extended by the Ministry of Planning and International Cooperation to line ministries through the coordination of strategic planning, while the Royal Hashemite Court will monitor progress in accordance with the tasks assigned to the government in Letters of Designation.Sustainability:Through the Vision and its Roadmap, Jordan will continue its efforts to tackle needs related climate change (including delivering on the Paris Agreement), food security and water, and availability of clean energy. The Davao City Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) 2024-2026 was developed through close coordination with the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), as mandated by the Climate Change Act of 2009 (RA 9729). Technical guidance and capacity support were provided by DENR-EMB XI, DILG XI, and NEDA XI, ensuring the plan's alignment with national climate policies and the National Adaptation Plan (NAP).

The City Planning and Development Office (CPDO) and City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) led the formulation process, engaging regional and barangay governments for data collection, validation, and prioritization of adaptation and mitigation strategies. The city also coordinated with NCIP XI and local Indigenous councils to ensure inclusivity and recognition of ancestral domains in climate and land-use planning.

This multi-level engagement enabled Davao City to develop a science-based, participatory, and locally responsive climate action plan that aligns with both the Philippine Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), while strengthening the city's resilience to climate hazards such as flooding, drought, and extreme heat.

With the climate warming, the active period of vector mosquitoes is gradually prolonged, the epidemic period of Dengue fever is increased, and the interval is shortened, which causes a great threat to people's health. In order to effectively prevent the local Dengue fever epidemic, the city continues to promote four major epidemic prevention measures with the goal of \'no local confirmed cases of Dengue fever\':(1) Prevent overseas epidemic: Through the infectious disease notification management system, fever screening of inbound passengers at international airports and people's active notification, timely and quickly grasp the Dengue epidemic imported from abroad, and promote the reward mechanism for people and doctors to actively notify. (2) Community epidemic prevention: A \'Taichung City Dengue Fever Prevention and Control Center Meeting\' was held to integrate the dengue fever prevention and control capabilities and division of labor of various departments, and announce the dengue fever prevention measures of Taichung City. If there is a confirmed case of dengue fever, the district-level prevention and control center will be activated immediately, and the district office, cleaning team, and health center will jointly carry out relevant prevention and control work. Epidemic prevention personnel from each district health center will conduct mosquito density surveys and strengthen breeding clearance in quarantine hotels in high-risk areas, and supervise the quarantine hotels under their jurisdiction to implement environmental inspections and remove stagnant water containers to reduce the chances of mosquito breeding and the risk of dengue fever epidemics. A mosquito density survey will be conducted in each district of the city every month to monitor and understand the ecology of mosquitoes. In 2024, a total of 73,487 households were surveyed, and 326,647 stagnant water containers were found, including 1,770 positive stagnant water containers. The stagnant water containers were immediately cleared on site, and breeding source investigations were carried out to prevent mosquito breeding. (3) Medical integration: Encourage grassroots hospitals to join the public-funded dengue fever NS1 rapid screening test institutions. By 2024, a total of 169 hospitals will be able to provide rapid screening services, and each administrative district will have a rapid screening base; conduct clinic visits, strengthen the promotion of clinic suspected case consultation and reporting, and complete a total of 2,281 visits. (4) Epidemic prevention education: A total of 3 education and training for medical care, epidemic prevention, agriculture, animal husbandry and veterinary medicine, tourism operators and relevant bureaus of the city. On October 12, 2023, Taiwan promulgated the 'Regulations on the Administration of Voluntary Greenhouse Gas Reduction Programs.' On August 29, 2024, three sub-laws were enacted regarding the carbon fee collection system: the 'Carbon Fee Collection Regulations,' the 'Voluntary Reduction Plan Management Regulations,' and the 'Greenhouse Gas Reduction Targets for Carbon Fee Subjects,' officially marking the country's entry into the era of carbon pricing. Furthermore, according to Article 26 of the Climate Change Response Act, voluntary reduction credits can be used to offset greenhouse gas emissions, reduce carbon fee payments, and reduce the difference in carbon emissions from imported products. This provides a legal basis for achieving the 2050 net-zero emissions target and other carbon reduction policies. The government provides assistance and guidance to businesses to understand the relevant policies. Currently, there are 47 regulated businesses in Taipei, 45 of which are subject to carbon fees. To mitigate the impact of the carbon fee system on local businesses, in addition to continuing to provide voluntary reduction project guidance to help businesses develop carbon credits and enhance their carbon asset management capabilities, briefing sessions on voluntary reduction plans will be held starting in 2025 to assist businesses in securing preferential carbon fee rates, promote industry and policy alignment, and jointly advance toward net-zero emissions goals in line with international standards.

As of August 26, 2025, the Ministry of Environment has reviewed the voluntary reduction plans of nine businesses within Taichung City.

An initial science-based Climate Change Risk Assessment has been developed for Sunderland, aligned with the UK Climate Risk Independent Assessment (CCRA3). The Risk Assessment has been considered by the Council's Chief Officer Group in September 2024, with agreement that it will form the basis of our Adaptation Plan. The risk assessment identifies climate risks across: infrastructure; health, communities, and the built environment; business and industry; natural environments and assets. Existing levels of deprivation and inequalities including health inequalities, and the associated implications are factored into the risk assessment in addition to consideration being given to the potential for these to increase as a result of climate change. The risk assessment will be a working document, updated regularly with input from service area experts across the Council as well as from partners on the 2030 Shadow Board and beyond as appropriate. It will enable us, for example, to highlight particularly vulnerable areas specific to Sunderland. The risk assessment will then inform our Climate Change Adaptation Plan to mitigate these risks, Priority actions to reduce the risks identified and their impact will be taken forward as part of a strategic and co-ordinated approach to adaptation, working both locally and regionally as appropriate. 
Sunderland's Level 1 Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (SFRA - published in November 2020) was carried out in accordance with the central Government's latest development planning guidance at the time. 

The Northumbria Community Risk Register, which covers the whole of Northumbria including Sunderland, is based on the National Risk Register produced by central Government. This covers all climate hazards for the region e.g. flooding, adverse weather and wildfires. 
The Community Risk Register details some of the key emergencies that might happen in the Northumbria Local Resilience Forum (LRF) area and aims to summarise Risks in a format for residents and communities. It does not include every risk only the ones that are likely to happen.
If there are any risks such as flooding, partners (including the EA, Met office, Emergency Services..etc) in the LRF will come together to discuss any planning required to respond to this type of event, but not to discuss climate change as a specific subject

More detail on these risk assessments, including links and attachments, can be found in section 2.

Sunderland is also working with neighbouring local authorities to develop and deliver wider regional level climate related plans and projects. This includes a Bus Service Improvement Plan, the North East Transport Plan, and the North East Community Forest all at a whole region (seven local authorities) level (LA7&NECA level) as well as the sub-regional the South Tyne and Wear Joint Municipal Waste Strategy.

In addition, Sunderland is working with the UK government to deploy numerous funding streams in line with the key priorities of the citywide Low Carbon Framework and the Council's Low Carbon Action Plan. For example, The Levelling Up Fund is being deployed for several low carbon developments in Sunderland, such as the Housing Innovation Construction Skills Academy (HICSA), Vaux Housing and at the Nile + Villiers community housing scheme in Sunniside. HICSA, which is scheduled to open in September 2025, will upskill and train people in low carbon technology and Modern Methods of Construction (MMC) to support the delivery of Sunderland's low carbon ambitions for new build and retrofitting. Education Partnership NE (Sunderland College) have recently been granted a license from the Retrofitting Academy to deliver qualifications from HICSA. Aside HICSA, Vaux Housing is providing 135 new homes to Future Homes Standard and is utilising solar PV, air source heat pumps and battery technology. Vaux housing will also be connected to a smart energy network to effectively manage consumption, reduce waste and mitigate impact of rising energy costs. Sunderland aims to work with the UK government to implement MMC, as such Sunniside, as well as the other sites, will utilise MMC solutions for homes, with low embodied carbon, renewable energy technology, and promotion of the circular economy.

Through a separate project, the Levelling Up Fund supported the delivery of 20 buses operating in Sunderland to be converted to electric and three rapid charging hubs which are awaiting installation in 2025. In addition to the Levelling Up Fund, Sunderland City Council has used Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme Funding to help decarbonise municipal operational buildings and will continue to work with partner organisation Gentoo to enable Warm Homes Social Housing Fund resources to decarbonise social housing in Sunderland among other examples.
In 2023 Sunderland became part of a 3-year Destination Development Partnership (DDP) with the seven local authorities across the North East (LA7&NECA) which is focused on the visitor economy within the context of destination management. This is a pilot approach with Visit England, the first of its kind in the UK. As part of the DDP, early discussions have taken place on the need to increase knowledge and awareness of sustainability issues in relation to tourism in the region's cities, with a range of actions now incorporated into the new Sunderland Tourism Strategy, which was launched in May 2025.

Sunderland was one of 3 North East English cities invited to submit a return to the Global Destination Survey as part of the work through the DDP, which seeks to measure cities' approach to tourism across four broad categories aligned to the Global Sustainable Development goals. These are: Environmental Performance; Social Performance; Supplier Performance; and Destination Management. In 2024 there were 69 qualitative and quantitative metrics on which Sunderland submitted its return and for which it received an overall score of 38.7, scoring particularly highly for Environmental performance (69.4 and in line with the GDS international average of 69.97). Following feedback from GDS, Sunderland has begun work on the gaps identified, and this work is now incorporated into the delivery plan for the NECA LA7 group which is attended by the Sunderland Council Low Carbon and Sustainable Regeneration Senior Manager. This group are working regionally to maximise opportunities from the Devolution White Paper which brings additional powers to the region in relation to decarbonisation, retrofitting and climate adaptation.

The UK has a target of being net zero as a nation by 2050 and it is widely acknowledged that cities are key to this. It is also widely acknowledged that local partnerships, such as the Sunderland City Partnership, are in a unique position to help reduce citywide greenhouse gas emissions. As well as knowing the detail, geography, demographics and needs of their local areas well, cities, local authorities and city partnerships have a strong influence over a proportion of the emissions in their area. The Local Government Association predicted in 2021 that Local Authorities alone have a direct or strong influence over 35% of area-wide emissions, and some impact over 80% (2024).

In 2020, with the national target of 2050 in mind, Sunderland set an ambitious goal to become a carbon neutral city by 2040. Achievement of this target will contribute to the UK's 2050 goal.

In addition to the above, Sunderland City Council reaffirmed its commitments to UK100 in February 2022, by signing their new Net Zero pledge, continuing with an annual membership thereafter. Signatories are working collaboratively to ensure net-zero targets are reached as soon as possible, committing the city to net-zero greenhouse gases by 2045 at the latest. The signature also broadens the council's ambition from carbon neutral to net zero by 2030.

An initial science-based Climate Change Risk Assessment has been developed for Sunderland, aligned with the UK Climate Risk Independent Assessment (CCRA3). The Risk Assessment has been considered by the Council's Chief Officer Group in September 2024, with agreement that it will form the basis of our Adaptation Plan. The risk assessment identifies climate risks across: infrastructure; health, communities, and the built environment; business and industry; natural environments and assets. Existing levels of deprivation and inequalities including health inequalities, and the associated implications are factored into the risk assessment in addition to consideration being given to the potential for these to increase as a result of climate change. The risk assessment will be a working document, updated regularly with input from service area experts across the Council as well as from partners on the 2030 Shadow Board and beyond as appropriate. It will enable us, for example, to highlight particularly vulnerable areas specific to Sunderland. The risk assessment will then inform our Climate Change Adaptation Plan to mitigate these risks, Priority actions to reduce the risks identified and their impact will be taken forward as part of a strategic and co-ordinated approach to adaptation, working both locally and regionally as appropriate. 
Under the Flood and Water Management Act 2010 (FWMA), Sunderland City Council became a Lead Local Flood Authority (LLFA). As a LLFA, Sunderland City Council has key responsibilities to manage flood risk from localised sources across the city and a duty to develop, maintain, apply and monitor a Local Flood Risk Management Strategy.

Sunderland's Local Flood Risk Management Strategy (LFRMS), last updated in 2016, has been developed with strategic objectives and guiding principles which are consistent with the Environment Agency's (EA) National Strategy. Furthermore, the LFRMS has been prepared with reference to the Local Government Group Framework and is also consistent with the National Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management (FCERM) Strategy.

In addition to the above, under the Coastal Protection Act 1949, Sunderland City Council also has a legal duty to monitor and manage the coastline and coastal erosion.

Sunderland is also part of the North East Community Forest (NECF) Partnership who aim to plant 500 hectares of trees by 2025, doubling canopy cover in the region by 2050 (Sunderland's share of this hectare target is 45 hectares). 
The NECF was launched in February 2022 and in four planting seasons Sunderland has planted a total of 19,887 whips, 1273 standard trees, 413 orchard trees and 4.3km of hedgerow (22876 hedgerow plants and 38 hedgerow trees), complemented by the planting of 190,600 bulbs and 11 hectares of wildflowers. Sites have included 12 schools 12 park and 20 community greenspaces. 
Between 2022 and 2024 173 volunteers took part in five community planting events. 
In 2025, 45 volunteers took part in three community planting events at Copt Hill and Flint Mill, planted as part of the Links with Nature project. 
 
To date, Sunderland has delivered 66 hectares of tree planting over 48 sites, 20 hectares more than the city's 4 year target. 

In relation to Public Health, Sunderland City Council also aims to reduce mortality due to air pollution each year. This is a common national goal through Public Health England. More information can be found at Fingertips | Department of Health and Social Care (phe.org.uk).

Finally, to tackle inequalities, Sunderland City Council aims to reduce the number of residents within the city who are fuel poor. This reflects existing fuel poverty levels and potential for these to increase. This is also a common national goal through Public Health England. More information can be found at Fingertips | Department of Health and Social Care (phe.org.uk).

As propostas construídas com a sociedade civil foram consolidadas e enviadas formalmente como a contribuição oficial de Palmas para a etapa estadual e, subsequentemente, para a Conferência Nacional de Meio Ambiente.

A elaboração do Inventário de GEEs de Palmas é um processo colaborativo que utiliza parcerias e ferramentas para garantir a precisão, a transparência e o alinhamento das informações. O município fortalece sua capacidade técnica através da parceria com o ICLEI - Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade. Essa colaboração nos dá acesso a metodologias globais e a ferramentas inovadoras. Um exemplo central é a utilização da plataforma Google Environmental Insights Explorer (EIE), que nos fornece dados e estimativas de alta qualidade para setores-chave, como as emissões do setor de transportes e de edificações, além do potencial de geração de energia solar nos telhados da cidade. O uso dessa ferramenta complementa os dados coletados localmente, aumentando a precisão do inventário municipal.
A base para um inventário completo é o processo de colaboração interna. Há um fluxo de trabalho que envolve a troca de dados de atividade entre múltiplas secretarias municipais (como Planejamento, Infraestrutura, Transporte e Meio Ambiente). Essa governança interna assegura a qualidade e a confiabilidade das informações que são, subsequentemente, compartilhadas externamente.
Esse engajamento visa alinhar as bases de dados e permitir que as emissões de Palmas contribuam de forma correta para o balanço de GEEs regional.

A jurisdição está em um momento estratégico de avanço em sua política climática. Com base na Política Municipal de Mudanças Climáticas já existente (Lei Nº 2.373/2018), estamos atualmente trabalhando na sua atualização e na elaboração do Plano Municipal de Ação Climática (PAC).
O engajamento com outros níveis de governo é um pilar central deste processo de elaboração. A colaboração com a Secretaria de Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos do Tocantins é crucial para garantir que a atualização da nossa política e o novo PAC estejam em total sinergia com as diretrizes climáticas estaduais. O objetivo é alinhar metas e compartilhar dados para ações conjuntas, especialmente na gestão do bioma Cerrado e dos recursos hídricos. 
Buscamos o alinhamento estratégico com o Plano Clima Nacional e a NDC do Brasil. A colaboração com o Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima e com instituições como o INPE é fundamental para incorporar cenários climáticos oficiais e as melhores práticas técnicas na elaboração do nosso plano, garantindo sua robustez e credibilidade.

By connecting the “points” of each station along the “lines” of development, and further extending into “surfaces” of large-scale development zones, New Taipei City is gradually evolving into a Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) model. Since 2014, the central government (Environmental Protection Administration) has worked with local governments to promote the “Certification Program for Low Carbon Sustainable Homeland,” aiming to build residents' capacity for climate change mitigation and adaptation and to foster low-carbon lifestyles at the village and neighborhood level. This initiative promotes both bottom-up achievement and top-down support, helping residents adopt sustainable habits while raising awareness of energy conservation and environmental protection.

Modeled after the Sustainable Jersey certification in the U.S., Taiwan's version adopts a unique “compete with yourself” approach, in which participating communities select suitable low-carbon actions, implement them, and report outcomes. Based on scores reviewed by the central government, they receive bronze or silver certification.

The program raises public awareness of environmental protection and promotes both bottom-up participation and top-down guidance to support low-carbon lifestyles. New Taipei City has seen strong results in indoor lighting upgrades, wetland and pond conservation, rainwater reuse, community gardens, and vertical greening, with these efforts gradually replicated citywide.

1. Policy Promotion 
In alignment with the Environmental Protection Administration's “Low Carbon Sustainable Homeland” initiative, the New Taipei City Government encourages communities and schools to adopt low-carbon features and practices. Public spaces such as community centers, state-owned land, libraries, and parks are being upgraded with low-carbon infrastructure to boost energy efficiency and environmental protection, laying the foundation for a citywide culture of sustainability.

2. Setting up a Project Team
In addition to staff from relevant government departments, the project team includes experts and scholars from both industry and academia, who offer professional advice and policy recommendations to support the implementation of climate-related initiatives.

3. Establishment of Demonstration Sites and Support Mechanisms
(1) Low-Carbon Communities
In apartment and residential communities, energy-saving actions often begin with replacing lighting fixtures. However, carbon reduction can go beyond this, incorporating water conservation, resource recycling, the use of green transportation, building insulation, and community-based environmental education.
(2) Power-Saving Clinics
New Taipei City has launched the “Power-Saving Clinic” initiative, where expert “Power Doctors” provide free on-site assessments for communities, public institutions, and schools. The team identifies potential areas for energy conservation and offers tailored solutions related to electricity, air-conditioning, lighting systems, water resource management, recycling, and building greening or insulation.
(3) Low-Carbon Campus
To promote low-carbon awareness through education, New Taipei City launched Taiwan's first “Low-Carbon School Certification” in 2009, with Gold Bear and Silver Goose levels. Since 2013, the “Little Environmental Leader” program has supported student-led environmental governance and campus-wide sustainability efforts. Schools retrofit facilities based on six low-carbon aspects: green buildings, green energy, recycling, green transport, sustainable living, and innovation. By 2024, over 90% of schools (309 total) were certified—195 Silver Goose and 114 Gold Bear.
(4)Since 2010, the Environmental Protection Administration launched the “Low Carbon Sustainable Homeland” project and, in 2014, began the “Certification and Rating Program” to promote low-carbon actions through bottom-up participation and top-down guidance. New Taipei City was the first municipality to earn the highest-level Silver certification at the city level. The city supports villages and districts based on local needs to obtain certification. By March 2025, 415 units had registered, including 190 certified villages (177 Bronze, 13 Silver) and 15 certified districts (9 Bronze, 6 Silver), totaling 205 certified entities.

4. Establishment of Regional Low Carbon Promotion Centers
(1) New Taipei City offers 'Building Low Carbon Communities' courses to promote low-carbon lifestyle concepts through environmental education. These courses aim to instill energy-saving and carbon-reduction practices in everyday life across general communities, neighborhoods, and households.
(2) The city has cultivated 'Low Carbon Community Planners,' who are trained professionals responsible for assisting communities in designing and implementing low-carbon renovation plans, helping shape model low-carbon communities across the city.
(3) The 'New Taipei City Regional Low Carbon Promotion Center' was established to manage training courses and workshops on energy saving and carbon reduction, while also serving as a hub for public outreach on environmental protection policies and promoting environmental education throughout the city.

Since 2014, New Taipei City has promoted its public bicycle system to provide citizens with effective first- and last-mile transportation solutions. The system has since evolved into YouBike. As of the end of 2024, the city has built 691.1 kilometers of bike paths and installed 14,420 bike racks. As of August 2024, New Taipei City has fully upgraded from YouBike 1.0 to YouBike 2.0. The city now offers 1,384 YouBike 2.0 stations with a total of 22,759 bicycles operating throughout its neighborhoods.

The aim is to encourage the public to use bicycles as a short-distance transport mode that connects seamlessly to public transportation hubs. By promoting low-cost, zero-emission, and energy-free transportation options, the city hopes to strengthen its green mobility system, reduce reliance on private motor vehicles, and alleviate urban congestion, environmental pollution, and energy consumption. Surveys and literature reviews will be conducted to assess current issues, identify future directions, and further improve the public bicycle service.

In 2021, the 'New Taipei Safe Business Epidemic Prevention and Energy-Saving Measures Subsidy' program was launched to provide subsidies to local businesses and service providers for installing PVC door curtains and ceiling-mounted circulation fans. PVC door curtains help separate indoor and outdoor areas or front and back counters, effectively blocking droplet transmission and reducing air conditioning loss. Ceiling fans enhance indoor air circulation and improve energy efficiency, resulting in an estimated 18% savings in air conditioning energy consumption. A total of 95 applications were subsidized under this program, with an estimated annual electricity saving of 999,470 kWh.

In 2022, the 'New Taipei Service Industry Insulation Equipment Subsidy' program was introduced to support local service industry operators in purchasing air curtains, ceiling-mounted circulation fans, and glass insulation improvements. The subsidy covered up to 50% of the total equipment cost, with a maximum of NT$100,000 per application. The total subsidy budget for the year was NT$5.5 million, and a total of 133 applications were received. The estimated annual electricity saving from these projects is 1.44 million kWh.

In 2023, the 'Net-Zero Carbon Demonstration Site Subsidy Program' was launched to assist multiple enterprises in setting up solar photovoltaic power generation systems, energy storage systems, and energy management systems at designated demonstration sites. These installations were supplemented by expert-led energy efficiency diagnostics. Eligible applicants included companies, factories, legal entities, organizations, and public or private universities registered in New Taipei City with a contract electricity capacity of at least 51 kW. The program provided subsidies for up to 49% of the total installation cost, with a maximum subsidy of NT$1.5 million per project.

Serves as the foundational document for all climate-related efforts in the city.

Facilitates coordinated action with public institutions, NGOs, and academia.

Ensures alignment between national targets and local strategies.

Acts as a strategic reference when applying for climate finance and international networks like C40, EU funding, or UNDP.

Municipality-to-Municipality Collaboration:

Çanakkale engages in knowledge sharing with other Turkish cities, exchanging best practices in sustainable transport, waste management, and renewable energy implementation.

column17: In addition to York's own Climate Change Action Plan and Climate Change Strategy, York has engaged with York and North Yorkshire Combined Authority's Routemap to Carbon Negative. This document sets out the region's ambitious plans to be net zero carbon by 2034 and carbon negative by 2040. As such, it both combines a Climate Change Action Plan and Climate mitigation target. The objectives of the Routemap are to: provide strategic direction and a coordinated approach to decarbonisation; catalyse collaborative action at pace and scale; build confidence that reaching net zero and beyond to carbon negative is feasible; harness the economic opportunities of net zero, leveraging public and private sector investment; position York and North Yorkshire at the forefront of national climate action and provide a platform to influence Government policy and funding. In York and North Yorkshire we have a critical contribution to make to national and global efforts we have the potential to go beyond net zero and become Englands first carbon negative region This Routemap provides an ambitious pathway for local authorities businesses charities academia and communities to come together to deliver carbon reduction at the necessary pace and scale to reach net zero by 2034 and net negative by 2040 The series of targets and actions set out in this routemap have been informed by comprehensive stakeholder engagement and a growing evidence base including York and North Yorkshires Carbon Abatement Pathways study York has been involved as a key stakeholder in the development of the York and North Yorkshire routemap to carbon negative Yorks contribution to helping the region reach this goal is set out in our climate change strategy and climate action plan. The routemap to Carbon Negative is currently undergoing a refresh process, however further information on the topic can be found here: https://yorknorthyorks-ca.gov.uk/project/routemap-to-carbon-negative/ and a summary of the previous iteration of the routemap can be found here: https://yorknorthyorks-ca.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Routemap-to-Carbon-Negative-Summary-290125.pdf

column17: In December 2014, the City produced its first Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment and Adaptation Plan (CDM Smith).1 The Plan focused on six sectors - critical building infrastructure, water, energy, stormwater, transportation, and vulnerable populations, outlined 17 prioritized vulnerabilities and listed 46 general adaptation strategies. Putting this designation to work2 , Salem received the following MVP grants:  Salem Sanitary Sewer Trunk Line Relocation Assessment - FY18, design to relocate a hundred year old sewer trunk line suspended over Willow Ave Beach to avoid a rupture due to increasing storms and surge that would cause catastrophic damage to Salem Harbor, homes and businesses that rely on municipal sewage removal - $ 345,000  Green Infrastructure for Stormwater Management in City Projects - FY19, incorporates green infrastructure into existing City projects, including the renovations of Bertram Field and Gallows Hill Park and the filling of empty tree pits in downtown Salem with replacement street trees and pervious pavement - $320,861

column17: In 2022, the City of Denton as well as other municipalities in the DFW region collaborated with the North Central Texas Council of Governments to complete the first regional greenhouse gas inventory in the state of Texas. This project includes the 16 county region of the NCTCOG as well as 12 individual cities many of whom are completing their first greenhouse gas inventory. As a city that has been completing community inventories periodically since 2011, the City of Denton was able to not only participate but assist other cities in the region with data collection and understanding of scope. The regional project will provide a baseline for the DFW area as whole, and allow for the comparison of community inventories across the many cities in the region. It will also allow for a better understanding of large scale emission sources such as transportation and energy. The results will be used by all participants not only for climate planning purposes, but for air quality, transportation, and infrastructure planning as well.

Dundee City Council engages actively with the Scottish Climate Intelligence Service (SCIS), a national capacity-building programme funded jointly by the Scottish Government and all 32 Scottish local authorities through COSLA. SCIS is delivered through a partnership between the Edinburgh Climate Change Institute (ECCI) and the Improvement Service, with technical support from ClimateView and additional guidance from the Sustainable Scotland Network.
SCIS supports area-wide emissions reduction across all Scottish local authorities. Local authority carbon emissions are calculated using standardised methods to create robust baseline figures, which are then used within the ClimateView platform as a planning and communication tool for emissions reduction. Through this platform, Dundee can model interventions, track progress against national and local targets, and communicate results in a consistent and transparent way.
Dundee's engagement with SCIS also includes participation in learning sessions and capacity-building activities with other local authorities, ensuring that city-wide climate action is informed by national-level expertise, aligns with Scottish Government targets, and is supported by standardised, evidence-based data. This collaboration strengthens Dundee's ability to plan, monitor, and report climate actions while contributing to Scotland's collective emissions reduction goals.

Public awareness campaigns about energy efficiency and the benefits of renewable technologies.

Expansion of cycling infrastructure and the implementation of Park & Ride systems to reduce car dependency.

Redesigning public transport ticketing systems to make them more user-friendly and integrated.
3. Community Involvement
Launch of the Rzeszów Climate Panel, where residents identify priorities such as investing in green energy and enhancing public transport. Recommendations with at least 80% support from participants are set to be implemented.
Education campaigns to inform citizens about climate action benefits, such as home energy upgrades and cleaner heating systems.
4. International Climate Programs
Rzeszów is part of the European Union's “100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities by 2030” initiative, positioning it as a leader in climate action in Europe.

column17:
La acción climática de la comuna de Punta Arenas se encuentra estrechamente vinculada con otros niveles de gobierno, en particular con el nivel nacional, a través del marco establecido por la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático (Ley N.º 21.455). Esta ley establece que todos los municipios del país deben desarrollar e implementar un Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), asegurando la coherencia entre las políticas locales y los lineamientos nacionales de mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático.

En este contexto, el PACCC de Punta Arenas se articula con las estrategias y programas definidos por el Ministerio del Medio Ambiente, recibiendo supervisión técnica y metodológica para garantizar la correcta identificación de riesgos y oportunidades, la priorización de acciones y la medición de resultados. Esta vinculación permite que las iniciativas locales se alineen con los objetivos nacionales de reducción de emisiones, resiliencia territorial y sostenibilidad, al tiempo que facilitan el acceso a recursos, capacitación y programas de financiamiento del Estado.

Asimismo, la interacción con otros niveles de gobierno asegura que las acciones comunales no operen de manera aislada, sino que contribuyan al cumplimiento de metas nacionales, al fortalecimiento de la gobernanza ambiental y a la integración de la planificación climática en los distintos instrumentos de desarrollo territorial y planificación urbana de la comuna.

Además, esta información se vincula con otros instrumentos de planificación y gestión, como los planes de emergencia, los planes de gestión de riesgos de desastres y otros programas de resiliencia territorial, asegurando que la acción climática comunal sea coherente, integral y alineada con las políticas nacionales.\n\nDe esta forma, Punta Arenas asegura que las medidas locales de mitigación y adaptación no solo respondan a necesidades comunales, sino que también contribuyan al cumplimiento de metas nacionales y fortalezcan la coordinación intergubernamental, optimizando la prevención de riesgos y la resiliencia frente a los efectos del cambio climático.

Este inventario se articula con los inventarios regionales y nacionales, asegurando la coherencia de los datos, la estandarización de metodologías y la integración de la información local en los reportes nacionales de emisiones. Esta coordinación permite que las acciones de mitigación identificadas en el PACCC estén alineadas con los objetivos nacionales de reducción de emisiones y las estrategias regionales de sostenibilidad, facilitando además el acceso a recursos, asistencia técnica y programas de financiamiento a nivel central.

De esta manera, Punta Arenas asegura que la planificación y ejecución de medidas de mitigación climática no solo respondan a las necesidades locales, sino que también contribuyan al cumplimiento de metas regionales y nacionales, fortaleciendo la gobernanza climática y la articulación intergubernamental.

column17: Le Plan climat air énergie territorial (PCAET) est une obligation réglementaire pour les établissements publics de coopération intercommunale de plus de 20 000 habitants. La réglementation impose un suivi annuel, un bilan à 3 ans et une révision à 6 ans. Ce PCAET comprend des objectifs d'atténuation et d'adaptation pour le territoire. Ces objectifs sont repris par les communes du territoire qui sont labellisées Territoires Engagées pour la Transition Ecologique (label de l'ADEME), qui s'engagent à les respecter dans le cadre de leur politique climat-air-énergie. En décembre 2022, la Métropole a publié le bilan à mi-parcours du PCAET qui décrit l'état d'avancement des actions réalisées et des objectifs à atteindre. Le même mois a été votée la fusion du PCAET avec le Schéma de Cohérence Territorial (SCOT) d'ici 2026.

column17: We provide funding for and are a lead member of the Western Sydney Regional Organisation of Councils Ltd (WSROC). WSROC leads coordination and resource development for a number of different projects related to climate change and energy. For example, Turn Down the Heat is a WSROC-led initiative that takes a collaborative, multi-sector approach to building a cooler, more resilient future for Western Sydney. The initiative is guided by the Turn Down the Heat Strategy and Action Plan (2018) which was co-designed by over 55 stakeholders who recognise that the response to extreme heat and heatwaves is a shared responsibility. Projects guided by this Strategy and Action Plan include: - an Urban Heat Planning Toolkit (2020 - 2021) developed to help local government strengthen their planning provisions to reduce the impacts of heat. The Toolkit outlines a clear evidence base to support a resilience approach to addressing heat and provides recommendations for other parts of the planning system (state and national) to be addressed- Cool Suburbs Tool (2020 - 2022) a rating and assessment tool for building heat resilience in urban planning and development- Heat Smart Western Sydney (2020 - 2021) which conducted a review of heatwave management across the city, and through extensive stakeholder engagement developed a resources for engagement and a framework for Heatwave Management - Climate resilient street trees (2020 - 2022) a project that set up a number of demonstration sites to test how species selection and passive irrigation influence successful outcomes- Future Proofing Residential Development (2022) a project seeking to to understand how current building design regulations will perform in future climates. The study reviews the performance of NSW BASIX-compliant homes and apartments under future climate scenarios in Greater Western Sydney- Greater Sydney Heat Taskforce (2023-2024) a program seeks to address this gap, bringing together state, local, industry and community stakeholders towards a long-term vision where people living in Greater Sydney can survive and thrive in a warming climate and during extreme heat events.

Last year, the Florida Legislature amended state law, through Senate Bill CS/SB 1122, to provide for a definition of Adaptation Action Areas (AAA) as an optional component of Local Comprehensive Plans for those low-lying coastal zones that are experiencing coastal flooding due to extreme high tides and storm surge, and which are more vulnerable to the impacts of rising sea level. It further specifies that local governments which adopt an AAA designation may consider policies within the Local Comprehensive Plan to improve resilience to coastal flooding resulting from high-tide events, storm surge, flash floods, storm water runoff, and related impacts of sea level rise. Subsequent to state legislative action, the concept of AAA designations moved to the federal level and members of Congress have since requested the definition of AAA in federal law to provide for appropriations for adaptation planning and infrastructure needs in designated areas.

In the fourth quarter of 2024, the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact (the Compact) undertook a review of its 2019 Regionally Unified Sea Level Rise Projection (“2019 Projection”) vis-à-vis updates from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) 2022 Sea Level Rise Technical Report, as well as observational trends in the sea level in the region. Based on the review, the Compact provides this 2024 statement as guidance for the continued use of the 2019 Regionally Unified Projection in Southeast Florida as a basis for resilience planning, design, and construction. The Compact intends to revisit this guidance in the future as new science and modeling become available.

Unified Sea Level Rise Projection 2019: https://southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/Sea-Level-Rise-Projection-Guidance-Report_FINAL_02212020.pdf Executive SummaryEarly in the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact's (“the Compact”) work together, Broward, Miami-Dade, Monroe, and Palm Beach counties recognized the need to unify a diversity of local sea level rise projections to create a single, regionally unified projection, ensuring consistency in adaptation planning and policy, and infrastructure siting and design in the Southeast Florida four-county region. The Compact published the first Regionally Unified Sea Level Rise Projection for Southeast Florida in 2011, and updated the projection in 2015. This document, the Compact's third Regionally Unified Sea Level Rise Projection, provides an update to the amount of anticipated sea level rise in Southeast Florida through 2120. These projections represent a consensus from a technical Work Group consisting of members from the academic community and federal agencies, with support from local government staff, and incorporates the most up-to-date, peer-reviewed literature, and climate modeling data. The Projection supports local government, regional entities, and other partners in understanding vulnerabilities associated with sea level rise and informs the development of science-based adaptation strategies, policies, and infrastructure design.

column17: The Resilient 305 Strategy was developed by Greater Miami & the Beaches (GM&B), a unique partnership of Miami-Dade County, the City of Miami and the City of Miami Beach with support from the 100 Resilient Cities, an organization pioneered by the Rockefeller Foundation, and The Miami Foundation. The Strategy is a living document created to address resilience challenges prioritized through intergovernmental and community collaboration. Resilient305 is deeply interconnected with the County's Climate Action and Sea Level Rise strategies. In particular, in the climate action strategy we detail a related municipal collaboration, Resilient35 (which represents all lower municipalities within Miami-Dade County). Utilizing information from the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact Climate Assessment Tool and insights obtained during informational sessions on the County's Sea Level Rise Strategy and draft Climate Action Strategy, the County will work collaboratively with municipalities on helping accelerate implementation of the bold actions outlined in the climate action strategy while also helping celebrating successes along the way. Uniting as a \'Resilient35\', representing the 35 municipalities in the 305 coalition, also helps accelerate the pace and impact of our collective efforts in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Having a plan and being prepared also better positions the work for future State and Federal funding opportunities as both levels of government begin prioritization of climate related activities. Advancing action on climate is difficult both politically and financially, but, similar to storm recovery, multi-jurisdictional collaboration will help make the journey a little less burdensome in our Miami-Dade County community.

In 2020 Dane County issued a Climate Action Plan, outlining strategies to cut countywide emissions in half by 2030. We worked closely with local governments to develop the CAP and now, in implementing the CAP, we convene a collaborative (Sustainable Leaders Collaborative or SLC) of the 61 cities, villages and townships in Dane County as well as the 17 school districts. We convene the SLC group regularly to share ideas and strategize about collaborative approaches for reducing emissions within local government operations and across our communities.

Examples of SLC work include hands-on meetings about converting fleets to clean fuels and webinars on accelerating solar adoption both within local governments and across communities. In addition to these educational efforts, the SLC framework has facilitated cross-community partnerships where communities are doing joint clean energy planning. In early 2023, for example, SLC members successfully collaborated on a proposal for electric vehicle charging infrastructure to address equity in charging access across our region.

SLC members also worked collaboratively to achieve SolSmart designations, going from 2 local designations to six with two more pending.

In 2021 Dane County helped to establish the Wisconsin Local Government Climate Coalition, which brings together Wisconsin counties and local municipalities with climate and clean energy goals. Through WLGCC local governments have a coordinated voice on state policy issues; the coalition makes it easier for local governments with ambitious climate goals to advocate for state policies that will support (rather than thwart) those local ambitions.

One example is building codes. Under Wisconsin law, building codes are set at the state level and local governments are not allowed to set higher local building codes. In 2022 WLGCC members collaborated to influence the ongoing update to Wisconsin's building codes, influencing the state to pursue stronger codes than would have occurred otherwise. Similarly, WLGCC is actively influencing various utility regulations at the Public Service Commission. All of this work aims to enhance the abilities of each local government to achieve its climate goals. For Dane County, being part of this coalition means our progressive voice is coupled with more perspectives from more areas of the state, expanding our ability to influence state officials.

Another important benefit of the WLGCC is that it creates a forum where we can exchange ideas and lessons learned with other local governments across Wisconsin. WLGCC enables us to do more faster because we can leverage insights from other local governments facing the same state policies.

column17: The City of Boynton Beach was awarded a $150,000 Resilient Florida Program Planning Grant to update the comprehensive Climate Vulnerability Assessment that was conducted for the CRP of Southeast Palm Beach County in 2021. The previous study identified the following core systems within each jurisdiction: Critical Facilities, Water Infrastructure, Economic Factors, Natural Resources, People and Socioeconomics, Property, and Transportation and Mobility. These factors were compared to other various climate threats, such as extreme heat and flooding, and were evaluated to determine which areas are most vulnerable to a warmer climate. The assessment identified the following regional issues:- Residential properties are vulnerable to all types of flooding: rainfall-induced, tidal, and storm surge. The vulnerability is driven by many factors, including but not limited to coastal proximity, density of development/imperviousness, whether it was built before base flood elevation (BFE) requirements were in place, and impacts to floodplains/native hydrology.- Critical facilities are often vulnerable to multiple threats (e.g., high winds and flooding).- Road access is the most widespread vulnerability associated with future tidal flooding.- Socioeconomic disparities within the region indicate people in certain areas will be disproportionately impacted by climate threats (especially by extreme heat, high winds, and rainfall-induced flooding).- Sea level rise and climate change will exacerbate existing threats and present new challenges to the region.- Most climate threats are interconnected The main vulnerabilities in this region include rainfall-induced flooding, extreme heat, and tidal flooding in the near-term and mid-term, as well as enhanced impacts to long-term rainfall-induced flooding, storm surge, and high winds.

The development and reporting of this component are shaped by multiple levels of government engagement and in certain cases, mandated by the national government. For example, the preparation of the State of the Environment Report is a legal requirement, coordinated under national regulations and submitted annually for the province. Beyond this mandatory obligation, Antalya Metropolitan Municipality aligns its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) with national policy frameworks, including the National Climate Change Strategy, National Adaptation Plan (NAP), and relevant sectoral strategies.
The municipality collaborates with national institutions such as the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change, the General Directorate of Meteorology, AFAD, and the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry to collect data, receive technical guidance, and integrate national climate priorities into local planning. This includes risk and vulnerability assessment inputs, greenhouse gas inventory alignment, and adaptation measure harmonization.
At the regional and lower levels, Antalya Metropolitan Municipality maintains regular cooperation with district municipalities, the governorship, and other public agencies to ensure coherent implementation of climate actions. Mechanisms such as the Environmental Board—established by municipal council decision—facilitate multi-stakeholder engagement, bringing together representatives from different levels of government, academia, NGOs, and the private sector.
Information sharing and capacity building are key elements of this engagement. Data from local climate monitoring projects (e.g., smart agriculture, renewable energy initiatives, and climate risk assessments-CLIMAAX) are communicated to higher levels of government, while feedback and technical advice are integrated into local action plans. The municipality also participates in workshops, training programs, and joint projects supported by higher-level institutions to strengthen technical capacity and ensure the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action benefits across the province.

column17: The undertaking of a community-wide greenhouse gas emissions inventory is a legal necessity and a strategic need. At the national level, Türkiye's Climate Change Mitigation Strategy and Action Plan, Türkiye's Nationally Determined Contribution and Green Deal Action Plan call for establishing credible GHG inventories in line with IPCC standards. At the regional and metropolitan level, the inventory will be undertaken in collaboration with the Antalya Provincial Directorate of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change, and various municipal institutions to achieve good alignment of data sources, calculation methods and sectoral boundaries.\nThe inventory process will ultimately be integrated into the potential future national MRV (Monitoring, Reporting and Verification) system, where progress updates and results can be shared through the digital spaces. This facilitates integration with Türkiye's national GHG reporting obligations under the UNFCCC, and underpins integration to the NDC.\nThe inventory process will also involve communication across all levels to synchronize emission factors, activity data and sectoral boundaries, to help ensure comparability and quality of data. Local inventory data directly informs the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) of Antalya Metropolitan Municipality, and also plays a role in regional climate planning, as well as becoming part of national datasets.

Para além disto, dados referentes a consumos de transportes públicos e de quantidades de resíduos encaminhadas para os vários destinos finais de eliminação/tratamento destes são fornecidos através de relatórios anuais emitidos pelas respetivas entidades responsáveis, isto é, a Sociedade Transportes Coletivos do Porto (STCP) e Associação de Municípios para a Gestão Sustentável de Resíduos do Grande Porto (LIPOR), respetivamente.
Por fim, estes inventários permitem ao Município delinear estratégias para mitigação das suas emissões de forma a estar em conformidade com diretrizes europeias e nacionais.

A adesão ao Pacto dos Autarcas em dezembro de 2017, a adoção de uma Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMAAC) em fevereiro de 2019 e a subsequente elaboração do Plano Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (PMAAC) em novembro de 2020 evidenciam a necessidade sentida pelo Município de promover, em todo o território municipal, uma resposta coerente às problemáticas relacionadas com as alterações climáticas, através de ações de gestão preventiva e adaptativa, definidas num quadro de operacionalização da estratégia definida.
No que se refere à transição energética, a estratégia municipal para se alcançar o desígnio da energia sustentável encontra-se plasmada no Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável da Maia 2030 (PAES), sendo que a meta de mitigação será reforçada e integrará o futuro Plano Municipal de Ação Climática da Maia (PMAC).
No sentido da operacionalização das medidas definidas no âmbito dos processos em curso e no quadro legislativo nacional, de acordo com o determinado na alínea 2, do artigo 14º da Lei de Bases do Clima - Lei nº 98/2021, de 31 de dezembro, devem os Municípios portugueses elaborar um Plano Municipal de Ação Climática (PMAC) que defina a estratégia local de mitigação e adaptação às Alterações Climáticas, acelerando a descarbonização e potenciando a resiliência do Concelho às Alterações Climáticas.
Pretende-se dar continuidade ao trabalho já desenvolvido, refletindo a preocupação do Município no âmbito da proteção do Ambiente e do desenvolvimento sustentável local, identificando um conjunto de ações definidas de acordo com as especificidades e necessidades do território que visam a adaptação e a mitigação às Alterações Climáticas, de modo a alcançar uma redução de GEE, redução da pobreza energética e neutralidade climática.
Por outro lado, a articulação do PMAC com os Instrumentos de Gestão Territorial (IGT) reforçará a estratégia climática definida para o Município da Maia. Com efeito, a mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas devem ser consideradas no planeamento, execução e avaliação das diversas políticas setoriais e no desenvolvimento das atividades económicas, sociais e políticas, assegurando a sua integração, coerência e complementaridade.
Assim, o Plano a elaborar deverá ser articulado com as estratégias e planos em vigor, considerando-se a informação dos referenciais municipais já existentes, devendo ainda estar alinhado com os objetivos e metas estabelecidas a nível nacional, nomeadamente a própria Lei de Bases do Clima, o Roteiro para a Neutralidade Carbónica (RNC 2050), o Plano Nacional de Energia e Clima (PNEC 2030), a Estratégia Nacional de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (ENAAC) e o Programa de Ação para a Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (P3-AC).
As medidas e ações a contemplar no PMAC deverão considerar ainda os elementos disponíveis no âmbito das ações-piloto enquadradas no Laboratório Vivo para a descarbonização - Baze, Living Lab e do Roteiro de Neutralidade Carbónica, em elaboração.

Mediante o exposto, considera-se que o desenvolvimento do Plano Municipal de Ação Climática do Município da Maia deverá integrar as seguintes componentes:
	Elaboração e operacionalização do Plano de Ação Climática do Município da Maia (suportado nos documentos existentes)
	Integração das opções de descarbonização nos planos e instrumentos municipais
	Plano de monitorização das medidas definidas 
	Plano de financiamento das medidas definidas
	Plano de Comunicação 
	Acompanhamento da implementação das medidas adotadas
Complementarmente, será necessário que as ações previstas contemplem a capacitação dos técnicos que acompanharão o desenvolvimento do processo, bem como os mecanismos necessários para o envolvimento dos cidadãos em todas as fases do processo.

A Câmara Municipal da Maia traçou como objetivo reduzir em 85% as emissões de carbono até 2030, antecipando a meta de descarbonização prevista a nível nacional para 2045. 
Esta ambição supera as metas estabelecidas pela Lei de Bases do Clima (Lei n.º 98/2021, de 31 de dezembro), no qual se estabelece a necessidade de redução de emissões de gases de efeito de estufa em, pelo menos, 55%, até 2030, entre 65% e 75% até 2040 e, pelo menos, 90% até 2050, face aos níveis de 2005. Este compromisso estará contemplado no futuro Plano Municipal de Ação Climática da Maia, atualmente em fase de inicial de arranque.
O seu desenvolvimento contou com diferentes iniciativas de participação multinível e cocriação, nomeadamente com envolvimento dos representantes das diversas Freguesias, vários serviços municipais, empresas municipais, a Agência de Energia do Porto (AdEPorto), o Presidente da Câmara Municipal e um conjunto de Vereadores dos pelouros mais pertinentes para a ação climática.

1. The Climate Action Plan (CAP) for Bradford District aligns with West Yorkshire Combined Authority's (WYCA) approved 2025-28 Climate & Environment Plan - in terms of the 2038 net zero target and key mitigation and adaptation priorities around energy, transport, nature, housing and the economy. WYCA is a key stakeholder and consultee for the development and implementation of the CAP.

2. Bradford's CAP supports and contributes to the four aims of Yorkshire & Humber Climate Commission (YHCC). YHCC is an independent co-funded advisory body who share a regional 2038 net zero target. The 4 aims include rapid emissions reduction, climate adaptation and resilience, nature restoration and just transition.

3. Development of the Bradford CAP was achieved through the engagement of elected members, Town and Parish Councillors (90 Councillors and 20 Town/Parish Councils). 

4. The development, implementation, priority areas and impact of the CAP will be embedded in new policy areas, such as Bradford's new Local Plan and Transport Plan. 

5. Bradford's CAP framework supports the development of school climate action plans to meet the government's DfE 2025 targets to reduce emissions, improve energy efficiency and develop climate-related learning. This is supported through UK government-funded advisory sister organisations such as Let's Go Zero, National Education Nature Park scheme and Climate Ambassadors.
 
6. Other public bodies that were involved in the development and consultation process of Bradford's CAP include University of Bradford, Bradford District Care NHS Foundation Trust, and local colleges (including Shipley and Bradford).

7. A collaborative project involving the Health Determinants Research Collaboration (HDRC), Bradford Council and University of York is conducting focussed community-based climate-related research to better understand and support an inclusive and just approach to a net zero transition. 

Examples of community led manifestos can be found using the following link:
https://heyzine.com/shelf/ClimateManifestos


8. The CAP has been co-developed with external partners such as West & North Yorkshire Chamber of Commerce, local Business Improvement Districts, utility/energy providers, housing providers, Fairtrade Yorkshire and multiple groups and organisations from the Voluntary, Community & Social Enterprise (VCSE) sector. VCSE organisations who have been involved in the consultation and engagement stages include:

-Environment and nature based groups such as Trees for Cities, Aire Rivers Trust, Canal Rivers Trust, YorGreen CIC, Keighley Creative, Yorkshire Wildlife Trust, Natural England, Groundwork UK.

-Social inclusion/community based groups such as Community Action Bradford & District (CABAD), City of Nature, local climate action groups, Race Equality Network (REN), Bradford & District Community Empowerment Network (CNet), Bradford Trident, Global Justice Bradford, Women's Health Network.

-Faith-based organisations, such as Airedale Methodists, Shipley Christians Together, Faith Partnership, Singh Sabha Gurdwara, Muslim Women's Council, Council for Mosques.

-Local Active Travel organisations, such as Capital of Cycling and Active Travel Hubs.
 
9. Implementation of the CAP is supported through collaborative working with neighbouring authorities - Leeds, Calderdale, Kirklees and Wakefield, and through the wider WYCA relationship.

GHG baseline emissions data collation, analysis and reduction pathway modelling has been developed through the appointment of specialist environmental consultants, Ricardo, to support Bradford's Climate Action Plan and net zero target. The emissions data has been collated from numerous sources. 

The core dataset is from the Local Authority Greenhouse Gas emissions inventory from the UK Government's Department of Energy Security and Net Zero. This includes GHG emissions from stationary energy combustion, transport, waste, agriculture, forestry and other land use which are presented in CO2 equivalent (CO2e), using warming potentials (GWPs) from the IPCC Fourth Assessment Report: Climate Change 2007 (AR4) over a 100-year timeframe. 

The council continues to effectively lead on Air Quality monitoring and improvement in the District through it's Clean Air Zone monitoring stations and via input to planning applications. The Council's Sustainability Service is working closely with the Central Government's Joint Air Quality Unit (JAQU) to ensure that statutory Air Quality obligations are met. 

Industrial emissions collated, analysed and modelled through the Innovate-UK funded Local Industrial Decarbonisation Programme was fed into the district-wide GHG emissions inventory.

The Council is supporting the work of the Yorkshire & Humber Climate Commission which looks at regional collaborations, including a climate adaptation action to help realise the opportunities for improving health, wellbeing and quality of life and building long-term resilience in the face of a changing climate.

Across the district, the Council promotes Property Flood Resilience advice and support, such as Protecting Your Property to help householders, businesses and communities to 'Be Flood Ready'.

https://www.befloodready.uk/bradford
https://www.bradford.gov.uk/emergencies/flooding/protecting-your-property/
https://www.bradford.gov.uk/emergencies/flooding/flood-risk-management/

Under the Flood and Water Management Act 2010 the Bradford Council is the Lead Local Flood Authority (LLFA) and maintains council owned watercourses, clears grilles of debris at hotspots, advises on flood risk, designs drainage schemes, inspects and maintains council owned culverts, pumping stations and reservoir inspections. 

Through the planning process we provide consultation responses to mitigate flood risk due to development and we work closely with partners during flood events.

The Local Flood Risk Management Strategy outlines the Council's approach to managing flood risk from all water sources throughout the district, and has been developed to align with current legislation, guidance and Council policy, such as the Local Plan. 

It highlights the importance of working in partnership with all agencies and stakeholders, including farmers and infrastructure providers, in planning and adaptation to ensure Bradford is a flood resilient district. The strategy aims to:

1.	Improve the understanding and communication of flood risk and flood risk management responsibilities in Bradford District and amongst partners, stakeholders, communities and the media.
2.	Promote the role of individuals and communities in managing flood risk.
3.	Ensure sustainable and appropriate development.
4.	Improve knowledge of local watercourse network and drainage infrastructure.
5.	Undertake targeted maintenance and deliver flood risk management measures, including nature-based solutions, that provide social, economic and environmental benefits.

An example of a key nature-based solution is the restoration work which began on Ilkley Moor in 2020. This collaborative project (involving the Council, Friends of Ilkley Moor, Rebel Energy-Rebel Restoration and Moors for the Future) is on track to:
•	Plant 56,000 sphagnum moss plugs which hold water and form peat.
•	Create 494 leaky stone dams and 9 large timber dams to 'slow the flow' of water to reduce flood risk, reduce sediment run-off and stop peat being washed away.
•	Improve footpaths and drainage to reduce erosion and run-off.
•	Manage a hectare of bracken.
•	Manage 25 hectares of heather to create more diverse moorland vegetation. 
•	Build 65 heather bale dams.
•	Remove 25 hectares of Sitka spruce.
•	Plant 200 new trees.

As part of the City Centre Walking and Cycling Improvement scheme, new green spaces, such as Norfolk Gardens include Sustainable Urban Drainage (SUDS) to help manage rainwater and prevent flooding, as well as improve biodiversity.
https://www.future-bradford.co.uk/project/bradford-city-centre-cycling-and-walking-improvements/

column17: Cornwall level inventory of emissions for 2022 (Cornwall level data is always 2 years in arrears due to Government National Datasets) is produced, following the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories (GPC), by the Centre for Energy and Environment at University of Exeter. The inventory provides a comprehensive overview of Cornwall's GHG emissions broken down by sectors. The inventories have been recalculated for the years 2008 to 2021 to reflect revisions to source data and methodologies. The report provides the evidence base to underpin the activity that Cornwall Council and Cornwall are required to undertake to reach our ambitious target as well as inform the decision-making process for adaptation, resilience, mitigation and decarbonisation across our communities.
