column17: The Good Growth investment plan, facilitating the £186.6m Shared Prosperity Fund (2022 - March 2026) including £7.2m of Rural England Prosperity Funding (2022-March 2026), has been shaped around the requirement to deliver on Cornwall's net zero and nature recovery commitments and to this end deliver an overarching 'Good Growth' policy, which all projects must contribute towards. Supporting businesses and organisations across all sectors to achieve net zero, as well as investing in infrastructure and skills to assist Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly in becoming a net zero economy, has been a central component of the Shared Prosperity Fund (SPF) programme and is being achieved in multiple ways. At a programme level, the net zero agenda is an underpinning principle in our skills provision: from entry level Green Skills in Construction, to embedding circularity and nature recovery into our business and entrepreneurial support programmes, with bespoke support for the agricultural industry due to the specific requirements of the sector. In addition, the programme is investing in key infrastructure projects such as Floating Offshore Wind (FLOW), both at feasibility and construction stages, increasing the production of zero carbon energy across the region as well as positioning Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly to play a key role in the Green Industrial Revolution. With a focus on skills and infrastructure, the results of these investments will be indirect; however, they will lay the foundation for the growth of a new workforce that is equipped with the appropriate skills to fill the employment opportunities that will arise from the development of the net zero carbon energy sector. At a project level, it is being achieved more directly through the installation of low carbon, energy efficient technology in homes and businesses that will yield high impact and tangible CO2e reductions. Additionally, all projects are required to demonstrate how they are delivering towards the Good Growth Principles, including CO2e reduction and the circular economy (for reference the Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly Good Growth Policy document can be found at this link www.ciosgoodgrowth.com). These measures are being used to shift behaviour and support organisations to prepare for operating in a net-zero economy. From 2022-2025 SPF projects have saved 18,325t CO2e.

column17: Cornwall wide risk assessment developed in consultation with Cornwall Climate Risk Management to 1. Model climate drivers and their potential impacts on Cornwall 2. Establish a Climate Risk Profile for Cornwall 3. Provide an evidence-based report that helps inform environmental resilience and adaptation within Cornwall 4. Better understand the risks and opportunities presented by climate change to Cornwall both internally & externally 5. Support Cornwall Councils commitments to the Carbon Disclosure Project and provision of transparent climate change data management 6. Developed using the National Evidence Base to utilise published evidence to produce a baseline Cornwall Climate Profile, detailed scenario modelling and mapping for climate risks, review of Cornwall specific risks against Cornwall Climate scenarios and prioritise further activities for cascading risks and strategies for adaptation. Through the development of the climate change risk assessment, we have prepared a new information base about the very specific 'local risks' of climate change. This information will ultimately inform the Council's cross service decision making in relation to resilience, adaptation and further support the case for decarbonisation amongst our communities.

2024-25 represents the seventh consecutive year that Cornwall Council has undertaken an inventory of its operational greenhouse gas emissions, with 2018-19 representing a baseline year. The inventory is conducted in line with the GHG Protocols, a comprehensive, standardised, globally recognised framework to manage and measure greenhouse gas emissions that is used by private and public sector organisations alike. All scope 1 and 2 emissions are included in this inventory along with those scope 3 emissions where the council has a level of operational or financial control over them. 
In addition to this, Cornwall Council also contains a separate section with wider scope 3 emissions where there is sufficient data to analyse. This includes, but is not limited to, entities within the Group of Companies (GOC), tenanted assets and the broader supply chain. These figures are kept separate from the operational emissions inventory as they are outside of the council's direct control and subject to their own delivery plans.

The authority has been engaging with government to secure Salix Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme grant. PSDS grant scheme was made available for capital energy efficiency and the heat decarbonisation projects within the public sector for non-domestic buildings. The schemes that were successfully awarded grant in Round 1 of the scheme were to supplement existing gas boilers with less polluting energy efficient electric heating systems by way of air source heap pumps, thereby reducing the carbon output of the four buildings identified. This project supports the work of the Climate Emergency Board and the Climate Emergency Action Plan, specifically the strategic aims of improving Energy Efficiency & Decarbonising heat. The grant scheme will deliver stimulus to the energy efficiency and low carbon heat sector and deliver significant carbon savings. The grant of £3.289m was awarded to the Authority. The Authority subsequently bid into the Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) Phase 3c to reduce carbon emissions within the Authorities public buildings estate. The objective of the Phase 3c application was to support the transition to low carbon heating in public sector buildings, in addition to improving energy efficiency. It aims to achieve this by providing funding to replace end-of-life fossil fuel systems (gas boilers) with low carbon heat sources as a requirement and bundled with energy efficiency measures to facilitate a 'whole building' approach to heat decarbonisation. In 2023/24 the Authority was successful in its submission and are in receipt of a grant offer of £1,128,557.00 with the match contribution for projects being met by the Authority. An opportunity has now arisen to bid to the Salix Low Carbon Skills Fund to enable survey work to be undertaken to provide information on options that may be available to reduce carbon emissions within the Authority public buildings and schools estate. On 20 March 2024, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero announced a £16 million of funding for public sector organisations to engage specialist and expert advice and skills to develop detailed project proposals to help applications for future grant funding for capital decarbonisation measures, or alternative sources of finance. Undertaking additional upfront design work should mean future applications represent improved Value For Money and put the Authority in a strong position for future funding opportunities. The LCSF scheme is 100% funded with no match funding required. The Authority is currently awaiting the outcome on this.

In 2024/25 the Authority was awarded £2.912m of PSDS grant which will be used to replace existing gas fired boilers in two buildings with air source heat pumps. In addition to the air source heat pumps, a range of ancillary systems and equipment will be upgraded to ensure the building management systems are fully optimised. Solar PV will feature on one building to reduce the requirement of grid electricity to power the heat pumps. The works are expected to save 252 tCO2e across both sites.

The assessment sets out the risks and opportunities facing the UK from climate change, the most recent of which is CCRA3: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1047003/climate-change-risk-assessment-2022.pdf\nThere is now a call for evidence out which will inform the CCRA4

column17: The Flood and Water Management Act 2010 addresses the threats of flooding and water scarcity. Under the Flood Risk Regulations 2009, the Environment Agency is responsible for managing flood risk from main rivers, the sea, and reservoirs.Lead local flood authorities (LLFAs) are responsible for local sources of flood risk, in particular surface water run-off, groundwater, and ordinary watercourses. LLFAs are statutory consultees on major development. Local authorities are responsible for ensuring that requirements for preliminary flood risk assessments are met. As an LLFA, North Tyneside Council has published its Local Flood Risk Management Strategy which can be found here https://my.northtyneside.gov.uk/sites/default/files/web-page-related-files/North%20Tyneside%20Local%20Flood%20Risk%20Management%20Strategy-Appendix%201.pdf.

column17: The UK has set ambitious targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and in all four UK nations there is law or policy requiring local planning authorities to consider and take action on mitigating and adapting to climate change. The Climate Change Act 2008 includes a statutory target of reducing carbon dioxide emissions to at least 100% below 1990 levels by 2050, with interim targets, set through five-yearly carbon budgets. The Act also created a framework for climate change adaptation. North Tyneside Council has its own target of achieving net zero carbon emissions and has set out ambitions to significantly reduce carbon emissions, as set out in our Action Plan which can be found here - https://my.northtyneside.gov.uk/sites/default/files/web-page-related-files/CNZ2030_Action%20Plan%202024.pdf. The Authority will also be consulting on the UK Government's potential data reporting change to an aligned Greenhouse Gas Protocol for Cites and the Global Covenant of Mayors Common Reporting Framework

column17:
The authority participated in Defra's Local Authority Pilot as part of the 4th round of Adaptation Reporting Power. On 17th July 2023, the government published their third National Adaptation Programme. The National Adaptation Programme sets the actions that government and others will take to adapt to the impacts of climate change in the UK. The NAP3 sets out the key actions for 2023 to 2028, forming part of the 5-yearly cycle of requirements laid down in the Climate Change Act 2008 (CCA 2008). Previously, the government had asked key infrastructure and utilities companies to report such as water, energy and road and rail firms. However, as part of the fourth round of climate adaptation reporting, the government invited c.40 local authorities (LAs) to be included in the scope of reporting as part of a pilot scheme. NTC was part of that co-hort. Based on our historical work around climate adaptation and more recent positive and successful steps of managing the overall Net Zero agenda both for the authority and the borough, the Authority agreed to participate in the pilot. This enabled the Authority to continue to develop its profile within the new combined authority as well as sharing best practice. It is also very likely that local authorities will be required undertake this work in the near future. Our participation can help shape the national process as well as inform our own climate adaptation strategy, risk assessment, and action plan. The Authority's ARP4 submission has now been published at https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/climate-adaption-reporting-fourth-round-local-authority. 1.Following the completion of the DEFRA Pilot, the authority fully participated in the subsequent 'lessons learned' workshops. Further to this, the Authority was interviewed on two separate occasions with DEFRA appointed consultants to evaluate a range of Value for Money aspects associated with the pilot reporting process.

2.The MET Office Local Authority Climate Service (LACS) has been designed to help Local Authorities with their adaptation planning. North Tyneside Council has been interviewed by MET Office senior staff on the use of this service. This has now resulted in the Authority being now cited in the 2025 MET Office Annual Report as a case study related to its use.

The Authority was invited to participate in a pilot study to test the use of the Local Authority risk and adaptation (LARA) toolkit. The toolkit has been developed by the Centre for Climate and Health Security within the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). 
The LARA toolkit is intended to support those who work in a local authority within the UK. The purpose of the LARA toolkit is to provide a framework to support local authorities to understand the health risks posed by heat, to consider the implications of their local context, and to identify a range of options for action. The LARA toolkit provides a structured approach to identify areas of good practice already in place, and to guide local authorities to consider further steps, using national guidance, such as the Adverse Weather and Health Plan, to protect communities and vulnerable groups from inequitable and preventable harm from heat. 
The tool kit was successfully tested within the Authority and had contributions from 10 key Services. Detailed feedback was provided to the UKHSA on finding s and those will be used to refine the product before it is formally launched for national public sector organisations to use in late Autumn.

Warm Homes: Local Grant is a government-funded scheme that will be delivered by local authorities to provide access to grants for energy performance upgrades and low carbon heating for low-income households living in the worst quality, privately owned homes in England.

The scheme aims to deliver both energy costs and carbon savings for eligible households and will cover all fuel types. To be eligible for the scheme residents will need to be a homeowner or private sector landlord whose property has an Energy Performance Certificate D or below.

On the 29 November 2024, the Authority submitted an Expression of Interest to the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) for the allocation of funding from the Warm Homes Local Grant Scheme (WHLG). The funding will provide energy performance upgrades and low carbon heating for low-income households living in the worst quality, privately owned homes in the Borough. 

On the 28 February 2025 the Authority received notification that an award of £4,281,163 over the next three years (2025-2028).

column17: The WMCA convene a Local Authority Climate Adaptation group (made up of officers from their seven constituent authorities) to discuss respective climate risks, adaptation actions and capacity building opportunities. The resources available to support climate adaptation work is relatively sparse in respective local authorities. This group offers a space to share learnings and gain feedback on the regional adaptation programme to ensure that it aligns with and supports our local authority's adaptation ambitions. The WMCA also convenes an informal Mayoral Combined Authority Adaptation group which brings together the adaptation officers (where they exist) from Combined Authorities across the country. The purpose of the group is for Combined Authorities who face similar barriers and opportunities in terms of climate adaptation, to meet quarterly to share learnings, ideas and opportunities for collaboration. Both the Local Authority Climate Adaptation group and the MCA Adaptation group have collaborated on the development of Climate Adaptation Guidance for integration adaptation considerations across project life cycle stages. This collaborative work will be published imminently and available to group members.\n\nVia the UKRI-funded West Midlands-Adapt project, the WMCA now convene a Regional Adaptation Network (RAN), which brings together organisations from across the public and third sector wo have a role in managing climate risks. The RAN meets quarterly and is comprised of over 140 members from a range of organisations including utility providers, local authority departments and the third sector.

column17: As part of the region's shared Net Zero goal -WM2041- the WMCA has a role in supporting the local authorities in the region to meet this goal. column17: The WMCA has been in conversation with Defra around devolution adaptation asks to seek to formalise regional and local authorities responsibilities in national adaptation governance. In 2025 the WMCA launched its first Integrated Settlement and in 2026, there are plans to introduce an Environment and Climate pillar to this settlement. The WMCA are in ongoing negotiations with Defra on the potential to pilot a regional approach to climate risk management and adaptation planning. Through the WMCA's statutory role as Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) responsible authority, it is ensuring that adaptation is both an outcome of nature recovery and that nature recovery itself is adapted to future climate scenarios.

column17:
The WMCA is a trailblazer combined authority, meaning it is one of two combined authorities who are in discussions with central government around a 'deeper devolution' deal for the region. The Trailblazer Devolution Deal, and following Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for the Trailblazing Single Settlements for WMCA and GMCA (late 2023) documents, set out the framework for devolving energy, net zero and retrofit activities. The first devolved Integrated Settlement was agreed to begin on 1st April 2025.
£167m of retrofit funding for domestic and public sector buildings was included in the first three-year Integrated Settlement period. The targeted outcomes of this funding have been agreed as 14,000 social or low-income private homes upgraded to EPC C and an annual carbon emissions reductions from public buildings of 3.6ktCO2.
Ongoing negotiations are seeking to extend the existing funding devolution arrangements and expand the Integrated Settlement's remit to other areas of spending - in particular, heat networks development funding.

Further negotiations will continue and there is hope that the devolution deal will broaden to include funding and powers for other programme areas, such as circular economy, climate adaptation, heat networks and air quality.

column17: The Mayor of the West Midlands, Richard Parker, has set about establishing strong relationships with key government departments in relation to net zero and the environment. This has been done in a number of ways, including attendance at the Mayoral meeting at 10 Downing Street. The Mayor also wrote a letter to the following people (and more): Ed Miliband MP, Minister for DESNZ. Parker outlined the leading role the WMCA can play in the transition to a greener, more sustainable future and accelerating towards net zero. This includes through retrofit and regional energy planning. Steve Reed MP, Minister for Defra. Parker outlined the importance of the region's biodiversity and natural environment and the role that the WMCA can play in key areas of delivery around nature and climate adaptation (noted that in the latest reshuffle, Steve Reed has left Defra. The Mayor has also met Mary Creagh MP, another Defra minister to discuss climate actions). As well as letters and discussions with senior ministers, the WMCA has also engaged directly with government departments, which has included writing letters to the following people: Jeremy Pocklington, Permanent Secretary, DESNZ. Parker again outlined the role that the WMCA can play in net zero, asking for devolved powers and money to deliver, as well as key legislation change to support the WMCA's ambition. Tamara Finkelstein, Permanent Secretary, Defra. Parker again outlined the role that the WMCA can play in improving the environment and reducing emissions, highlighting the value of devolved power and funding on nature recovery, climate adaptation, air quality and circular economy. The Mayor continues to work with government and other regional mayors to call for further devolution of power and money, beyond the initial Integrated Settlement (April 2025) for the West Midlands to lead on the environment and climate action. \n

column17: Şanlıurfa Metropolitan Municipality Greenhouse Gas Inventory has been prepared in line with the GPC -Global Protocol For Community-Scale GreenHouse Gas Inventory. The inventory covers emissions from Stationary Energy, Transportation, Waste, Industrial Processes and Product Use (IPPU) and Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sectors. The process followed in greenhouse gas inventory studies consists of the following steps: • Establishment of Inventory Principles • Defining Inventory boundry • Identification of Emission Sources • Calculation and Reporting of Emissions • Inventory Results and Evaluation The international CIRIS (City Inventory Reporting and Information System) program was used for inventory calculations. Within the scope of this repor, inventories for years 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021 have been prepared. In terms of future targets, because it best reflects the current emission level and climatic conditions, the inventory period of 01.01.2021-31.12.2021 was chosen as the “BaseYear”. In the medium and long-term climate change action planning, the mitigation target will be set according to the 2021 base year. Due to very few reduction opportunities, less control power of the city administration over the sectors of Industrial Processes and Product Use (IPPU) and Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) (which are included in BASIC +); mitigation target has been set according to GPC-BASIC reporting level.

column17: The Republic of Korea enacted the “Framework Act on Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth for Coping with Climate Crisis” in September 2021, followed by the adoption and enforcement of its Enforcement Decree in March 2022. Under this law, the national mid- to long-term greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction target is set at a 40% reduction by 2030 compared to 2018 levels. In line with this requirement, Nowon-gu formulated its First Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Basic Plan in 2025.

column17: The purpose of the Durham Community Climate Adaptation Plan (DCCAP) is to provide a state-of-the-science projection of key climate parameters for a relevant future period for purposes of planning: - Infrastructure upgrades and new design criteria; - Extreme weather and emergency response programs; - Business continuity programs; - Improved urban and rural design for resilience; and - Programs and measures to protect human health and property. DCCAP provides detailed climate projections for all eight local municipalities in the Region of Durham: Ajax, Brock (Beaverton), Clarington (Bowmanville), Oshawa, Pickering, Scugog (Port Perry), Uxbridge (Town of Uxbridge), and Whitby. The development of the Whitby CERP Phase 1: Resilience is identified as the primary mechanism to respond to a changing climate across the community. CERP Phase 1: Resilience uses the ensemble model climate projections developed in DCCAP by the Region of Durham in partnership with the local municipalities and conservation authorities in 2019 to determine future climate projections. A Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) is a greenhouse gas concentration (not emissions) trajectory adopted by the International Panel on Climate Change. Two scenarios were leveraged through this model (RCP 4.5 & RCP 8.5) to identify climate projections to the year 2100. The Technical Advisory Group that informed the development of CERP included, but was not limited to, representatives of the Town of Whitby's internal departments, the Region of Durham's internal departments, conservation authorities such as Central Lake Ontario Conservation Authority (CLOCA), developers, utilities, educational institutions, researchers, health authorities, and transit organizations. Representatives from these groups attended two stakeholder workshops. Strategic documents, planning initiatives, and climate modelling for The Town of Whitby, as well as the Region of Durham and other nearby municipalities, have been compiled and reviewed to develop a plan and modelling method for CERP. Drawing examples, principles and approaches from these documents will increase CERP's alignment with these other plans, and help to integrate all of these different but related initiatives, in turn improving the chances of success for all of them.

column17: In June 2019, Whitby Council became the first Durham municipality to declare climate change an emergency to reduce the local and global impacts of climate change and the need to strive for a deep reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The Durham Community Energy Plan (DCEP) adopted by Council in 2019, is a joint initiative led by the Region of Durham, in conjunction with the area municipalities and five utilities. The purpose of DCEP is to seek to accelerate the transition to a clean energy economy in Durham, while simultaneously achieving multiple economic, environmental, and social benefits. This is achieved by examining opportunities across the Region of Durham to: • improve energy efficiency; • increase energy security; and, • reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In March 2021, the Town of Whitby Council endorsed “Zero Carbon Whitby” which defines short, medium, and long-term targets for greenhouse gas reduction to enable the Corporation to eliminate greenhouse gas emissions by 2045. This target aligns with the recommended research from the International Panel on Climate Change. These targets include: • 20 percent GHG emissions reduction by 2025, below 2019 levels • 40 percent GHG emissions reduction by 2030, below 2019 levels • 100 percent GHG emissions reduction by 2045, below 2019 levels Zero Carbon Whitby is the Town's corporate Climate Mitigation Plan that outlines a management system to embed climate considerations within decision-making in Whitby with a particular focus on emissions derived from municipal buildings, fleet, lighting, and waste. The management system has two objectives: 1. Systematically integrate consideration of climate change into the decision-making processes of the Town; and, 2. Provide a carbon management framework, identifying a Carbon Budget that aligns with the existing Business Planning Cycle to enable the Town to substantively address the climate emergency for its corporate operations. On a community scale, the development of the Whitby Climate Emergency Response Plan (CERP) is the primary mechanism to respond to a changing climate across the town. Due to the complexity and different approaches necessary to fully understand the response needed to address climate change, CERP has been developed in two phases: • Phase 1: Resilience - to address the climate changes we already experience and expect to experience in the future even with the adoption of greenhouse gas emissions mitigation measures. Phase 1 was approved by Council and is in the process of implementation. • Phase 2: Mitigation - to help prevent climate change from occurring in the future through the elimination of greenhouse gas emissions. Baseline GHG Inventory The first step to the development of the CERP Phase 2: Mitigation that is currently underway with technical advise from Whitby, Durham Region and Elexicon Energy is to undertake a baseline greenhouse gas inventory. This inventory helps to understand how and where energy is consumed within the community and the associated greenhouse gas emissions. For CERP Phase 2: Mitigation, the baseline greenhouse gas inventory encompasses both Scope 1 & 2. To model the greenhouse gas emissions inventory, the City Insight Model is being used. This model allows Whitby to generate a community energy and emissions model with integrated spatially explicit land-use and transportation components, and stocks-and-flows accounting and actual energy consumption data. To understand what emissions could look like in the future, three scenarios will be developed: 1. Business as Usual (BAU): Through the BAU scenario, a greenhouse gas pathway to the year 2050 is developed considering current patterns of energy consumption, while accounting for population growth, fuel efficiency standards and the impacts of climate change on heating and cooling requirements in buildings. 2. Business as Planned (BAP): The BAP scenario projects emissions based on an anticipated increase in provincial building codes, building retrofits in the residential and commercial sectors (considering current policy directives such as the Whitby Green Standard), adoption of building scale solar photovoltaic systems, electric vehicles and a modest increase in local large-scale solar and wind generation. 3. Low Carbon Pathway (LCP): The LCP scenario will be developed to achieve Whitby's community greenhouse gas reduction targets. This model will evaluate different actions such as building efficiency standards, building retrofits, renewable energy, technological advancement, electrification of transportation, land-use changes, and industrial efficiencies to determine which actions will need to be implemented to reach the community's targets. The development, endorsement and implementation of the CERP fulfils the commitments made through the Climate Emergency Declaration and DECP to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. column17: The UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (CCRA3) was completed in 2021. A report summarising the implications for Wales of the evidence for the third and latest UK climate change risk assessment (CCRA3) Technical Report has been published outlining the key risks for Wales (attached). The Independent Assessment used to help inform the third UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (CCRA3) assesses 61 risks and opportunities from climate change to Wales, including to business, infrastructure, housing, the natural environment, our health and risks from the impacts of climate change internationally. Risks categorised as “More action needed” and “Further investigation” are more urgent than “Watching brief” and “Sustain current action.” Of these 61 risks and opportunities, more action is needed in Wales now to address 32 of them, with sustaining current action only deemed appropriate in five cases. Of the 61, six issues are deemed to be both a risk and opportunity, four of which are associated with the natural environment and each of these require more action or further investigation. There are also eight opportunities that could arise from climate change in Wales, with half of these also related to the natural environment. In total, 26 risks from climate change in Wales have increased in urgency score since the previous CCRA five years ago; these are summarised at the start of each section of this report. Only one risk has decreased in urgency score since the previous CCRA. There are also some new risks that were not covered in CCRA2. In summary, risks in Wales that have a high future magnitude score and where more action is required now to address them, after considering any existing adaptation responses, include the following: • The impacts of climate change on the natural environment, including terrestrial, freshwater, coastal and marine species, forests and agriculture. • An increase in the range, quantities and consequences of pests, pathogens and invasive species, negatively affecting terrestrial, freshwater and marine priority habitats species, forestry and agriculture. • The risk of climate change impacts, especially more frequent flooding and coastal erosion, causing damage to our infrastructure services, including energy, transport, water and Information and Communication Technologies (ICT). • The impact of extreme temperatures, high winds and lightning on the transport network. • The impact of increasing high temperatures on people's health and wellbeing. • Increased severity and frequency of flooding of homes, communities and businesses. • The impact on coastal businesses due to sea level rise, coastal flooding and erosion. • Disruption to the delivery of health and social care services due to a greater frequency of extreme weather. • Damage to our cultural heritage assets as a result of temperature, precipitation, groundwater and landscape changes. • Impacts internationally that may affect the UK, such as risks to food availability, safety and security, risks to international law and governance from climate change that will affect the UK, international trade routes, public health and the multiplication of risks across systems and geographies. Wales level guidance is available to support adaptation across the region including Adapting to Climate Change: Guidance for Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk for Management Authorities in Wales published in August 2021. The guidance is provided as supplementary information to the Welsh Government's Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management (FCERM) Business Case Guidance, published June 2019. It supports the National Strategy for Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management (2020) and should be used to consider the impact of climate change within the development of all FCERM projects or strategies.

Keterlibatan Pemerintah dan Pemangku Kepentingan dalam Penyusunan Climate Action Plan Kabupaten Sumbawa

Penyusunan Climate Action Plan Kabupaten Sumbawa melibatkan berbagai tingkatan pemerintahan serta pemangku kepentingan untuk memastikan bahwa dokumen yang dihasilkan komprehensif, berbasis data, inklusif, dan dapat diimplementasikan secara efektif. Keterlibatan tersebut meliputi:

1. Pemerintah Nasional

Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup dan Kehutanan, Kementerian PUPR, BNPB, dan kementerian terkait lainnya memberikan:

Pedoman, kerangka kebijakan nasional, dan standar metodologi

Data iklim, risiko bencana, dan inventarisasi GRK

Dukungan teknis serta sinkronisasi dengan komitmen nasional (NDC, SRN)

2. Pemerintah Provinsi Nusa Tenggara Barat

Pemerintah Provinsi NTB terlibat dalam:

Penyelarasan rencana aksi iklim kabupaten dengan dokumen provinsi (RAD-PI, Dokumen Hijau NTB)

Pendampingan teknis serta fasilitasi lintas sektor

Penyediaan data spasial, kebencanaan, dan lingkungan

3. Organisasi Perangkat Daerah (OPD) Lintas Kabupaten

OPD di kabupaten dan OPD dari kabupaten tetangga terlibat untuk:

Integrasi data sektor-sektor kunci seperti energi, transportasi, pertanian, kehutanan, pesisir, dan persampahan

Penyusunan program mitigasi dan adaptasi berbasis wilayah dan DAS lintas kabupaten

Kolaborasi implementasi program berbasis ekosistem

4. Pemerintah Kecamatan dan Desa

Perangkat kecamatan dan desa berperan penting dalam:

Penyediaan data lapangan dan informasi kerentanan lokal

Identifikasi masyarakat dan sektor paling terdampak

Integrasi rencana aksi iklim ke dalam perencanaan tingkat desa (RPJMDes/RKPDes)

5. Masyarakat dan Kelompok Rentan

Keterlibatan masyarakat dilakukan melalui forum konsultasi publik, FGD, dan musyawarah desa untuk:

Memastikan masukan dari kelompok rentan (petani kecil, nelayan, perempuan, komunitas miskin)

Validasi data kerentanan dan identifikasi kebutuhan prioritas

Memperkuat penerimaan dan keberlanjutan program

6. NGO/LSM

NGO lokal maupun nasional berkontribusi pada:

Pendampingan teknis dan metodologi penilaian risiko

Program konservasi, restorasi ekosistem, dan edukasi iklim

Penguatan kapasitas kelembagaan desa dan kelompok masyarakat

7. Akademisi dan Lembaga Penelitian

Perguruan tinggi dan lembaga riset berperan dalam:

Analisis ilmiah, pemodelan iklim, dan evaluasi dampak

Penyusunan baseline data emisi dan risiko

Kajian adaptasi dan mitigasi berbasis sains

Keterlibatan Berbagai Tingkatan Pemerintahan dan Pemangku Kepentingan dalam Penyusunan Climate Mitigation Target Kabupaten Sumbawa

Penyusunan Climate Mitigation Target Kabupaten Sumbawa dilakukan melalui proses kolaboratif dan partisipatif yang melibatkan berbagai level pemerintahan serta pemangku kepentingan utama. Pendekatan ini memastikan bahwa target pengurangan emisi yang ditetapkan akurat, realistis, selaras dengan kebijakan nasional, dan dapat diimplementasikan secara efektif. Keterlibatan tersebut meliputi:

1. Pemerintah Nasional

Melalui Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup dan Kehutanan (KLHK), Kementerian ESDM, dan kementerian terkait lainnya, pemerintah pusat berkontribusi dalam:

Penyediaan pedoman inventarisasi Gas Rumah Kaca (GRK) dan standar penetapan target mitigasi.

Penyelarasan target kabupaten dengan komitmen nasional (NDC, FOLU Net Sink 2030, transisi energi bersih).

Dukungan data energi, kehutanan, transportasi, dan limbah yang diperlukan untuk menghitung baseline emisi.

2. Pemerintah Provinsi Nusa Tenggara Barat

Provinsi NTB berperan sebagai penghubung antara kebijakan nasional dan kabupaten, dengan dukungan berupa:

Sinkronisasi target mitigasi dengan Rencana Aksi Daerah Penurunan Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca (RAD-GRK) provinsi.

Fasilitasi koordinasi lintas sektor dan lintas kabupaten.

Penyediaan data spasial dan kebijakan energi terbarukan provinsi.

3. OPD Kabupaten Sumbawa

Organisasi Perangkat Daerah (OPD) sektor kunci terlibat dalam penyusunan target mitigasi melalui:

Penyediaan data sektoral (energi, transportasi, pertanian, kehutanan, persampahan, industri).

Identifikasi potensi penurunan emisi dan tindakan mitigasi yang dapat diterapkan pada sektor masing-masing.

Penyusunan proyeksi, baseline, dan skenario penurunan emisi.

Sektor yang terlibat meliputi:
DLH, Dinas Perhubungan, Dinas Pertanian, Dinas Kehutanan/UPT KPH, Dinas Pekerjaan Umum, BPBD, Dinas Perindustrian, dan Bappeda.

4. Pemerintah Kecamatan dan Desa

Kontribusi wilayah kecamatan dan desa mencakup:

Penyediaan data aktivitas lokal seperti pola penggunaan energi, kondisi tutupan lahan, dan pengelolaan sampah.

Identifikasi potensi aksi mitigasi berbasis komunitas (pohon desa, bank sampah, energi biogas, pengurangan pembakaran lahan).

Validasi data di lapangan yang digunakan dalam penyusunan baseline.

5. Masyarakat dan Komunitas Lokal

Masyarakat, melalui kegiatan diskusi kelompok (FGD) dan survei lapangan, berperan dalam:

Memberikan informasi terkait praktik yang mempengaruhi emisi (transportasi, pertanian, bahan bakar rumah tangga).

Mengidentifikasi peluang mitigasi berbasis komunitas seperti agroforestri, konservasi energi, atau pengurangan sampah.

Mendukung keberterimaan sosial dari target mitigasi yang ditetapkan.

6. NGO/LSM

Organisasi non-pemerintah memberikan dukungan berupa:

Pendampingan teknis terkait pengembangan strategi mitigasi rendah karbon.

Program demonstrasi (pilot project) seperti rehabilitasi mangrove, pengelolaan sampah terpadu, dan energi terbarukan.

Edukasi masyarakat dalam mendorong perubahan perilaku ramah lingkungan.

7. Akademisi dan Lembaga Riset

Perguruan tinggi dan lembaga penelitian berperan penting dalam:

Analisis ilmiah untuk penyusunan baseline emisi, proyeksi, dan skenario mitigasi.

Validasi metodologi inventarisasi dan perhitungan penurunan emisi.

Penyediaan rekomendasi berbasis sains dan teknologi rendah karbon.

Section 38 of the Well-being of Future Generations Act requires Public Service Boards (PSBs) to take account of the latest UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (CCRA) when preparing their Well-being Assessments.

BBNPA is an invited member of Powys PSB, with 66% of the park area, and 70% of it population residing with the local authority of Powys.

Including in it's overlap with the National Park area - to inform a resilience/adaptation plan for the region. 

Alongside this, PSBs in the South of the Park area, including Cardiff Capital Region which overlap the Park in Rhondda Cynon Taf, Merthyr Tydfil, Torfaen, Caerphilly, Blaenau Gwent and Torfaen are also conducting a climate risk and vulnerability assessment. 

The long-term ambition for BBNPA is to combine this work to produce an overarching assessment which covers the whole of the National Park area.

Powys PSB has developed a framework for area based climate action. 

This framework provides a structure for evidence-based, coordinated area-based action planning and delivery towards net zero and climate resilience. It is a tool to support the public sector to lead, catalyse and support area-based climate action for a fairer, more sustainable and healthier future.


The framework is based on extensive research and analysis and peer review. It is still being nuanced with input from a wide range of stakeholders.


It creates the possibility for:

· Clarity about which public body needs to lead on which part of the climate solutions locally (WG, CJCs, PSBs, individual public bodies)

· Systematic collaboration and coordination between public bodies, and with other sectors.

· The application of all the WFGA ways of working in practice including supporting more systematic local stakeholder and local public involvement - which is crucial for a just transition.

Local involvement will be increasingly important to achieve future carbon budgets which are progressively more reliant on whole society behaviour change.

The Framework is particularly shaped by analysis that:


· Public bodies can multiply their impact by mobilising society-wide creativity, action and resources, rather than just focusing on their own direct operations and services. Local authorities have direct control over around 2-5% of local emissions but can have significant influence over around 30% of emissions locallyi.


· Coordinated public body action has the potential to be even more effective than local authorities alone in leading, catalysing and supporting this local society-wide climate action.


· Public bodies do not have all the funding or the local supply chains and skills needed to meet their net zero by 2030 decarbonisation goal (relating to their direct operations and procurement). County-wide climate action will make achieving the goal more possible.

Work to embed and socialise the use of the framework amongst neighbouring local authorities and public bodies is being developed in conjunction with the Welsh Centre for Public Policy, and the Future Generations Commissioners Office, who's role is to: <Promote the sustainable development principle, in particular to act as a guardian of the ability of future generations to meet their needs and encourage public bodies to take greater account of the long-term impact of the things they do. Monitor and assess the extent to which well-being objectives set by public bodies are being met.=

The National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) is Greece's strategic roadmap for the energy transition, aiming to achieve climate neutrality by 2050. It sets specific energy and climate targets till 2050 and describes the necessary policies, priorities and measures to achieve them. According to the revised NECP (2024), 75,7% of electric energy will be produced by renewables by 2030 and 96,2% by 2035. It also stipulates that carbon dioxide emissions will be reduced by 58% compared to 1990 by 2030 and by 69% by 2035. National targets are incorporated in municipal planning and by the elaboration of local energy action plans. 
At the same time, the recently adopted European Directive on the Energy Performance of Buildings sets ambitious targets for reducing overall energy use in buildings. For residential buildings, the target is to reduce average primary energy use by 16% by 2030 and by 20-22% by 2035. For non-residential buildings, each Member State is committed to ensure the renovation of 16% of the worst performing buildings by 2030 and of 26% of them by 2033.
As part of the “Covenant of Mayors” since 2010 and the new 'Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy' since 2017, Ilion Municipality has committed to reduce carbon dioxide emissions (and potentially other greenhouse gases) in its territory by at least 40% by 2030, through energy upgrade interventions and greater use of renewables.

Target 6:Reduce net greenhouse gas emissions in Protected Landscapes to net zero by 2050 relative to 1990 levels.

The National Park Management Plan is a statutory plan that involves a partnership between the National Park Authority and local partners, such as local government, and departments of central government (e.g. Historic England, Forestry Commission, Forestry England, Natural England). The Plan is renewed every 5 years with the current plan effective from 2025-2030 (note: the plan has been adopted by members but is currently awaiting publication). 

By 2040 the National Park will be resilient and responsive to the impacts of climate change, storing more carbon each year than it produces. 
The Plan contains Ambitions (with each Ambition having associated objectives to achieve that Ambition) that relate to Climate mitigation and adaption. Mitigation objectives are:

B1: Work with farmers and landowners to support food production through the use of regenerative farming practices, working with natural processes, across at least 100 farm holdings (c15,000 ha) by 2030.

B3: Work with farmers and landowners to encourage creation of 6,000 ha of native broadleaf and mixed woodland, including, scrub, wood pasture and natural regeneration by 2031, to create a network that increase resilience to climate change and reduce downstream flood peaks.

B5: Support more services along the Settle-Carlisle Railway and the reinstatement of other rail lines, increase bus and shared transport links to surrounding towns, and improve infrastructure for electric vehicles, so as to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from travel by 50% by 2030 (compared to 2019).

B6: Support initiatives to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and increase smallscale and community renewable energy schemes, so as to reduce energy costs and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from industrial, commercial and domestic properties by 50% by 2030 (compared to 2019).

D1: Support farmers and land managers to maintain and improve the outstanding landscape, geology, wildlife and heritage of the National Park, so that at least 80% of land managers have adopted nature-friendly farming or land management on at least 15% of their land by 2030.

D2: Maintain the National Park as a place where a true sense of tranquillity and remoteness can still be found, including taking action to retain international 'Dark Sky Reserve' status

D5: Support farmers and landowners to enhance the Dales' landscape, and support nature, climate and farming resilience, including planting field trees to mitigate the impact of ash dieback on tree cover outside woodlands, , and creating or restoring 60 km of hedgerows by 2030 (from 2022 baseline).

E1: Establish an integrated National Park farm advisory service to: support regenerative farming; increase take-up of national agri-environment schemes and green finance opportunities; and, so support the viability and retention of low input livestock farming across the National Park.

E2: Provide advice, training and support for rural and land-based businesses to help them to innovate, diversify, and secure investment in their natural assets and create 'green jobs', so as to retain at least the same number of jobs within the sector. 

E3: By 2030 provide at least 30 apprenticeships or traineeships, and wider programmes of training in land management, heritage and green skills, including the new skills needed by businesses to support more nature-friendly farming and tackle climate change.

F6: Produce local plans to improve connections for walking, cycling, wheeling and horse-riding, so it is easier for residents and visitors to travel for work, for school and to access key services and visitor destinations without needing a car, and create at least 2 new multi-use routes by 2030, including one linking Garsdale-Hawes.

A7: Support farmers and landowners to restore or create 5,000 hectares of new wildlife-rich habitats outside protected sites by 2030 (from a 2022 baseline). 

A8: Support farmers and landowners to bring 75% of woodland into sustainable management by 2030, including positive management of conifer plantations to increase habitat for red squirrels and black grouse 

B2: Work with farmers and landowners to bring all remaining degraded peatland (c28,000 ha) into initial restoration and management by 2035.

O município de Vitória de Santo Antão (PE) mantém engajamento contínuo com os níveis estadual e federal por meio de programas e instrumentos cooperativos voltados à ação climática, adaptação e resiliência urbana.

Atualmente, Vitória integra o Programa Adapta Cidades, iniciativa coordenada pelo Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima (MMA) em parceria com o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Meio Ambiente (PNUMA) e com apoio técnico do Instituto Alziras e da ICLEI América do Sul. O município foi selecionado entre as 10 cidades pernambucanas contempladas na etapa estadual do programa, o que representa o reconhecimento de seu potencial institucional e territorial para desenvolver uma agenda climática estruturante.

No âmbito do Adapta Cidades, Vitória de Santo Antão vem participando de capacitações, oficinas e diagnósticos integrados voltados à elaboração de seu Plano de Ação Climática Municipal, com ênfase na adaptação baseada em ecossistemas (AbE), no fortalecimento da governança local e na articulação intersetorial entre meio ambiente, planejamento urbano, recursos hídricos, defesa civil e educação ambiental.

Esse engajamento com o governo federal e o governo estadual (via SEMAS-PE, que atua como articuladora territorial) tem permitido alinhar o planejamento municipal aos instrumentos nacionais de política climática, como o Programa Cidades Verdes Resilientes (PCVR) e o Plano Nacional de Adaptação à Mudança do Clima (PNA), bem como acessar informações técnicas, metodologias e apoio para captação de recursos.

A AMASVISA (Agência Municipal do Meio Ambiente e Sustentabilidade de Vitória de Santo Antão), em conjunto com a Secretaria Municipal de Planejamento, é o ponto focal local para o Adapta Cidades e demais políticas climáticas, mantendo comunicação ativa com as equipes técnicas do MMA, do ICLEI e da Secretaria de Meio Ambiente e Sustentabilidade do Estado de Pernambuco.

Em síntese, o engajamento federativo de Vitória de Santo Antão é estruturado e permanente, fundamentando-se em cooperação técnica, integração de dados e fortalecimento institucional no contexto da transição climática brasileira.

Abington Township Pennsylvania was accepted into the PA Dept of Environmental Protection's (PA DEP) Local Climate Action Program (LCAP) (see https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/residents/climate-change/local-climate-action-program ). 
The PA LCAP provides free technical and personnel assistance to local governments that want to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and address climate change. Over the course of the 6 years it has been running, LCAP has trained 81 cities, townships, boroughs, counties, and regional organizations, representing over 450 municipalities across the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
Abington Township was one of the 21 cohort PA jurisdictions to be selected during the 2020-2021 cohort. Through PA LCAP, the Township was trained by ICLEI to conduct a climate risk and vulnerability assessment, a GHG community inventory and construct a Climate Action Plan.
In addition, the merit of the Township's proposed CAP garnered additional PA LCAP assistance by being selected for the Shared Energy Manager program (PA LCAP SEM - see https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/residents/climate-change/local-climate-action-program/shared-energy-manager ) to receive professional energy manager to conduct energy assessments, renewable energy studies, and other services to implement their climate action plans. The free provided state-contracted SEM provides reviews of existing plans and project proposals, make recommendations, and perform assessment services to reduce energy costs and greenhouse gas emissions.

These services are tailored to each municipality's needs and goals and are not a “one size fits all” approach to energy management. Examples of specific technical assistance tasks which have been performed for participating local governments include:

Energy Benchmarking
Energy Star Certification Facility Verification
Audits & Energy Conservation Measure (ECM) analysis and recommendation for:
Municipal Buildings
Streetlighting and Traffic Lighting
Wastewater Treatment Facilities
Renewable Energy Feasibility Evaluation, including Solar Photovoltaic (PV) and renewable thermal technologies
Fleet Electrification Analysis, including alternative fuel vehicles and Small Rolling Equipment
Energy Management Plan creation
ECM specification and implementation assistance

Abington Township received PA LCAP SEM assistance during 2022-2023 and 2023 and 2024 in order to develop an optimal plan to replace the HVAC system for its municipal and police administration building (2022-2023) as well as 1. create an engineering plan to install electric vehicle charging stations (EVCS) ; 2. obtain municipal, state, and private funding to install EVCS; and 3. create an electric vehicle transition plan to transition the Township's muncipal fleet to EVs.

La evaluación de vulnerabilidad en San Borja se realizó como parte del proceso de planificación para enfrentar el cambio climático, en coordinación con lineamientos del Ministerio del Ambiente (MINAM) y en el marco del programa EDUCCA. Este análisis tuvo como objetivo identificar los sectores, territorios y poblaciones más expuestas a los impactos climáticos, con el fin de diseñar medidas de adaptación eficaces.

Se aplicó una metodología basada en tres componentes clave: exposición, sensibilidad y capacidad adaptativa. Primero, se identificaron los factores de exposición, como olas de calor, lluvias intensas y baja cobertura vegetal. Luego, se evaluó la sensibilidad de la población ante estos eventos, considerando variables como densidad poblacional, grupos vulnerables (niños, adultos mayores), infraestructura crítica, y calidad del entorno urbano.

La información fue obtenida mediante estudios técnicos, datos censales, mapeo geoespacial y talleres participativos con actores locales. Asimismo, se evaluó la capacidad del distrito para adaptarse a los cambios climáticos, considerando su infraestructura, servicios ambientales, gestión institucional y participación ciudadana.

El resultado fue un diagnóstico integral que sirvió como base para priorizar acciones climáticas en el Plan Local de Cambio Climático, enfocado en reducir riesgos y aumentar la resiliencia de las zonas más vulnerables del distrito.

San Borja elaboró su Plan de Acción frente al Cambio Climático para responder de manera integral y estratégica a los desafíos ambientales que afectan al distrito, garantizando un desarrollo sostenible y resiliente frente a los impactos del cambio climático.

El distrito reconoce que fenómenos como el aumento de temperaturas, lluvias intensas, eventos climáticos extremos y la degradación ambiental tienen efectos directos sobre la calidad de vida de sus habitantes, la infraestructura urbana y los recursos naturales. Por ello, el plan busca mitigar las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI) y promover acciones de adaptación que reduzcan la vulnerabilidad de la población y los ecosistemas.

Además, San Borja se alinea con las políticas nacionales e internacionales de lucha contra el cambio climático, cumpliendo con compromisos establecidos en el Acuerdo de París y la Agenda 2030 para el Desarrollo Sostenible.

El Plan de Acción también es una herramienta para articular esfuerzos multisectoriales, involucrando a la comunidad, el sector privado y las instituciones públicas, permitiendo priorizar inversiones y gestionar recursos de manera eficiente.

En resumen, el Plan de Acción fue desarrollado para fortalecer la capacidad del distrito frente a los retos climáticos, proteger el bienestar de sus ciudadanos y fomentar un futuro más sostenible e inclusivo.

San Borja ha establecido metas claras para mitigar el cambio climático y avanzar hacia un desarrollo sostenible y resiliente. Una de las principales metas es reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI) en un 30% para el año 2030, tomando como base los niveles de emisión del año 2020. Para lograrlo, se promueve la implementación de energías renovables y la mejora de la eficiencia energética en edificaciones públicas y privadas.

Asimismo, se busca fomentar la movilidad sostenible aumentando el uso de transporte público limpio y modos no motorizados, como la bicicleta y la caminata, en un 40% para el 2030. Esto implica desarrollar infraestructura adecuada, como ciclovías y zonas peatonales seguras.

En gestión de residuos, la meta es alcanzar un 60% de reciclaje y compostaje, reduciendo la cantidad de desechos que terminan en rellenos sanitarios, minimizando así las emisiones derivadas.

Además, San Borja apunta a aumentar en un 25% las áreas verdes urbanas para mejorar la captura de carbono y la calidad del aire. Finalmente, se incentiva que al menos el 50% de las nuevas construcciones cumplan con estándares de eficiencia energética para el año 2027.

Estas metas son parte del compromiso del distrito para contribuir activamente a la lucha contra el cambio climático.

Una de las metas principales es mejorar la gestión de riesgos asociados a eventos climáticos extremos, como lluvias intensas e inundaciones, mediante la implementación de sistemas de drenaje pluvial sostenible y la rehabilitación de áreas verdes urbanas para absorber el agua de lluvia.

Otra meta clave es aumentar la capacidad de adaptación de la infraestructura pública, promoviendo construcciones resistentes y el mantenimiento adecuado de espacios públicos, garantizando que estén preparados para soportar fenómenos climáticos adversos.

San Borja también busca fortalecer la sensibilización y participación ciudadana, implementando programas educativos que fomenten prácticas responsables en el uso del agua, manejo de residuos y conservación ambiental, priorizando la inclusión de grupos vulnerables como niños, adultos mayores y personas con discapacidad.

Además, se promueve la protección y recuperación de áreas naturales y corredores ecológicos, esenciales para conservar la biodiversidad y mitigar los efectos del calentamiento local.

Estas metas son fundamentales para que San Borja avance hacia un desarrollo urbano sostenible y una comunidad más preparada y resiliente frente al cambio climático.

O município mantém diálogo contínuo com o Governo do Estado de Minas Gerais e com o Governo Federal em temas relacionados à agenda climática. Exemplos incluem:
Apoio técnico da Secretaria de Estado de Meio Ambiente e Desenvolvimento Sustentável (SEMAD) na atualização do Plano Municipal de Saneamento Básico e no acompanhamento do Plano de Gestão Integrada de Resíduos Sólidos.
Participação em capacitações e editais promovidos pelo BDMG e FEAM, voltados para eficiência energética, resíduos sólidos e adaptação às mudanças climáticas.
Interação com o Governo Federal por meio de programas do Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima e do Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária, especialmente em projetos de agricultura sustentável e bem-estar animal.
Esse engajamento fortalece a capacidade técnica e financeira do município para implementar ações de mitigação e adaptação, integrando políticas locais com estratégias estaduais e nacionais.
